ILLVSTRISSIMO PRINCIPI, ET DOMINO, D. FRIDERICHO, Palatino comiti ad Rhenum, Electoralis Palatinatus haeredi, Bavariae Duci, Rectori magnifico Heidelbergensis Acade- miae, Domino clementissimo, Gratiam, pacem, salutem a Deo Patre & Domino Iesu Christo.
units.tr: TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE AND LORD, LORD FREDERICK, Count Palatine of the Rhine, heir of the Electoral Palatinate, Duke of Bavaria, magnificent Rector of the Heidelberg Academy, my most gracious Lord: grace, peace and salvation from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: VAE fuerunt causae, Illustrissime Princeps, Rector magnifice, eaeque pergraves (nisi me animus fallit) quae me ad exarandum hoc breve σύνταγμα his paucis diebus adduxerunt: juventutis studiosae commodum, & hujus Academiae. Etenim quae res juventuti in studiorum suorum ratione sint commoda, utilia, atque salutaria, majores nostri providerunt sapientissime, legibusque optimis procuraverunt: quid Academiae huic nostrae sit necessarium, nos omnes docuit proximi superioris anni calamitas. Ac commune quidem bonum hujus Academiae nostrae existimationemque in eo maxime versari constat, ut doctissimus vir omnique doctrinarum genere instructa, sanctis legibus circummunita, potentissimorum Principum & patronorum (quorum in numero est C. T.) praesidio firmata perfler, omnique instrumento suo apte occupato & collocato sancte legitimeque gubernetur: hoc vidit antiquitas, hoc nostra tempora experta sunt, & boni sentiunt. Quae omnia si per Illustrissimum Principem, heroemque fortissimum, D. IOANNEM CASIMIRUM, patruum ac tutorem tuum, Dominum nostrum clementissimum, & per T. C. assequimur (assequimur autem, & in dies magis ac magis assequemur) optime cum hac celebri Academia actum iri per Dei gratiam & benedictionem confidimus. Studiosae vero juventutis commoda, quum certa via & ratio in-
units.tr: There were causes, most illustrious Prince and magnificent Rector, and very weighty ones (unless my mind deceives me), which led me to write this short treatise in these few days: the advantage of the studious youth and of this Academy. For our forefathers wisely foresaw what in the course of their studies is advantageous, useful and wholesome for young people, and provided for it by excellent laws. The disaster of last year taught us all what this Academy needs. It is certainly agreed that the common good of this Academy and its reputation depend chiefly on its being governed holily and lawfully: it should be staffed by a most learned man, equipped with every kind of learning, surrounded by sound laws, strengthened by the protection of most powerful princes and patrons (among whom is Your Highness), and every instrument of it should be fittingly employed and placed. Antiquity saw this, our own times have experienced it, and good men perceive it. If we obtain all these things through the most illustrious Prince and bravest hero, Lord John Casimir, your uncle and guardian, our most gracious Lord, and through you (and we do obtain them, and shall obtain them more and more each day), we trust, by the grace and blessing of God, that this famous Academy will fare very well. The advantages of the studious youth, when a certain path and plan of study is prescribed by law, when the stages are arranged, honours are bestowed, and their authority is honourably granted to those who have bravely climbed to some height of honour: that these advantages are very well secured by the ancient and praiseworthy institutions of the Academies, and are advanced with great praise and incredible profit, experience itself has long shown most clearly.

units.la: ij studiorum cursu legibus prescribitur, disponuntur gradus, honores tribuuntur, & facultas sua iis qui ad honoris fastigium aliquod fortiter conscenderunt, honeste decernitur, illius ergo commoda ex priscís illu & laudabilibus Academiarum institutis optime procurari, & summa cum laude atque incredibili fructu promoveri, jamdiu ipsa quoque experientia commonstravit luculentissime. Qua quidem via si juventus pietatis & eruditionis amans, fidem habens majorum institutis praeceptorum ā suorum hortationibus, ad metam aliquam legitime vellet contendere, speraremus omnino fore, ut plures solide docti & vere utiles Ecclesiis Rebuspub. exsisterent. Pauciores certe stulta scientiae & eruditionis persuasione proper e inflati, velut folles vento, sese turpiter daturi essent (ut αὐχάδες nomines sunt Δαναύρωτι) & per αὐωρίαν navigationis sua, naufragium facientes alios secum in periculum naufragii ejusdem abriperent. Nam quemadmodum olim dicebat Euagrius, τὸ στρεδαῖον ἐν νέῳ ἔναι ἐχέγυον & ἐνλιμον ἐν γήρᾳ ἐσεσθαι, sic εὑρὰ τὸ κενόσπυδον ἀλμίας ἐχέγυον. Hic vero plurimum judicia variant. Nam qui juvenes sunt, gravia esse in Academiis haec legum praescripta putant: viri graves inania ducunt atque levissima: sic ab omnibus fere negliguntur in hoc tempore, quae priscoillo saeculo studiosissime religiosissimeque colebatur. Quid est autem, objecro, in hac re tota, quod videri usque adeo grave juventuti possit? An quod studia quasi cancellis describuntur? at hoc imperitis & imprudentibus (peritiam vero prudentiamque juvenis quis sibi arroget?) utile est ac necessarium: si non credunt, falsem nauticam, vel tectonicam, vel Iuboriam consulant, & observent quid quis praestare possit commodè fine lege & modo tyrocinii. An quod gradus honorum ex studiorum modulo dispositi fuerunt legibus? at hoc juventutis optimum est (ut Ambrosii utamur voce) incentivum, praemium cursus praeteriti, futuri incitamentum, ne quis forte in specie potius aut praesumtione eruditionis quam in re & veritate conquiescat,
units.tr: If young people who love piety and learning, trusting in the teachings of their elders and in the exhortations of their teachers, were willing to strive lawfully toward some goal along this path, we would altogether hope that more men would arise who are soundly learned and truly useful to the Churches and the commonwealth. Certainly fewer would foolishly puff themselves up with the conviction of their knowledge and learning, like bellows with wind, and shamefully expose themselves (as boastful men are, like Danaus' ...), and, by the swaying of their voyage, wrecking themselves, would drag others with them into the danger of the same shipwreck. For as Evagrius once said, that to be moderate in youth is self-restraint [τὸ στρεδαῖον ἐν νέῳ ἔναι ἐχέγυον] and to be ... in old age [ἐνλιμον ἐν γήρᾳ ἐσεσθαι], so, in the same way, [εὑρὰ τὸ κενόσπυδον ἀλμίας ἐχέγυον]. Here, however, opinions vary greatly. For those who are young think these prescriptions of the laws in the Academies are burdensome; serious men regard them as empty and very trivial. Thus in this age almost everyone neglects what in that older age was cultivated most eagerly and most devoutly. But what, I ask, is there in this whole matter that could seem so burdensome to the young? Is it that studies are laid out as though within barriers? But this is useful and necessary for the inexperienced and the unwise (for who among the young would claim for himself experience and prudence?). If they do not believe it, let them consult a pilot, a builder or a physician, and observe how no one can profitably do anything without rule and the measure of an apprenticeship. Or is it that the grades of honour are arranged by law according to the measure of study? But this is the greatest incentive for the young (to use Ambrose's word), a reward for the course already run and a spur for the course to come, so that no one may rest in mere appearance or presumption of learning rather than in the substance and truth of it, and so that no one, through overconfidence in some knowledge, may offer his ignorance to everyone as a laughing-stock. Or finally, is it that certain ceremonies and symbols are employed in the Academies in accordance with the prescriptions of the laws? Yet these symbols are human, not arising from any damnable superstition, but from human institution and agreement, free from superstition, and observed by good men without superstition. They signify either the completion of the labours of study, or the present fruit of learning, or the ability and grace (as they call it) to undertake just duties with praise, and to receive their advantages. What of these can young people reasonably mock? I certainly would not think (to run briefly through these points one by one) that young men devoted to virtue, humanity and purer learning would shrink from this, so that their past labours in their studies might not become known through public attestation. For they studied in order to become known, and to devote their learning to the common good. If not, what is more wretched than a treasure buried in the ground, and a good lying idle? But if they refuse the attestation of others, and indeed of their teachers, of the Academies in which they lived, and of learned men, I should like them to consider two things with themselves. First, that the individual's own distinguished work (which we certainly praise and admire) may become known, so that, according to his ability and dignity, he may be advanced by public judgment to what he deserves. Second (granting that they may remain hidden, or may spend their work wherever they think fit, by their own judgment rather than another's), with what good faith the best Academies could bear this: that men found fit for weightier tasks should lose their standing in lesser ones and stand aloof from the common good, for the sole reason that those men were not commended by public attestation, and were thrust from the school into the arena of the army, or the civil or ecclesiastical service. If they refuse to take up the present fruit of virtue and learning, that is, the honour they have earned, I acknowledge their singular modesty, I praise it, cherish it and revere it. But how far this judgment of theirs is better than public judgment, I still cannot see. For by this very abstaining from such a kind of honour, they snatch from their teachers and the Academies through which they have made progress the honour they owe them. What more? They are ungrateful towards those who deserve well, while they pride themselves on the name of modesty, wherever this principle of gratitude is commanded by the laws. But if (as we said in the last place) they desire rather to show their ability by their own deeds, and to obtain their functions and advantages by their own labour rather than by another's recommendation, they err in two ways, and not slightly.

units.la: ʼ feat, fiduciaá alicujus scientiæ ridendam propinet omnibus inscientiam suam. An denique illud, quòd ceremonias quasdam & symbola ex præscripto legum in Academiis adhibentur? Atqui humana sunt symbola, non ex damnabili superstitione ulla, sed ex hominum instituto & conventione profecta, a superstitione aliena, & citra superstitionem à viris bonis observata: eáq; aut labores studiorum perfunctos, aut præsentem scientiæ fructum, aut facultatem & πίχαρὸν (quod vocant) in justis functionibus cum laude capessendis & percipienda earum commoda significât. Quid horum juventus cum ratione potest eludere? Equidem non putaverim (ut singula hæc percurram paucis) ïâvenes virtutis, humanitatis, & puriorus doctrinæ studiosos id subterfugere, ne anteactï labores sui in studiis testificatione publica innotescant. Studuerunt enim, ut innotescerent, & scientiam suam in bono communi occuparent. Si non, quid miserius thesauro in terra fosso, & otioso bono? Quòd si alienam, & quidem præceptorum suorum aut Academiarum in quibus vixerunt doctorumque hominum testificationem nolunt, duo velim reputet cum animis suis: unum quotusquisque suæ singulari operâ (quam laudamus certè & admiramur) commodè innotescat, ut pro facultate & dignitate ad ea quibus dignus est, judicio publico provehatur: alterum (ut demus ipsos latere posse, aut suam operam ubicunque visum fuerit, suo potius judicio quàm alieno consumere) qua fide optimæ Academiæ id perferre possint, ut qui rebus gravioribus apti comperti sunt, fordescant in tenuioribus, & a communi bono abstineant, hoc solum nomine quòd illi homines testificatione publica non fuerint commendati, & de ludo in arenam militiamq; detrusi aut fortensem, aut Ecclesiasticam. Si præsentem virtutisque & scientiæ fructum, id est, honorem meritum, detrectant carpere, agnosco modestiam singularem, laudo, & colo, & veneror: sed quanto hoc ipsorum judicium publicæ iudicio præstet, nondum videre possum. Nam hoc ipse quod ab isto honorum genere abstinent, honorem quam debent praeripiunt suis praeceptoribus & Academiis, per quas profecerunt. Quid plura? Iunt ingrati in benemerentes, dum sibi gratificantur bujus modestiae nomine, ubicunque haec ratio ευχαριστίας legibus est imperata. Si autem (quod postremo loco dicebamus) ipsi facultatem suam reipsa magis cupiunt ostendere, & functiones commodaque assequi per se & labore suo quam aliena commendatione, duobus modis errant non mediocriter.
units.tr: ...feat, and with confidence in some branch of learning, offers everyone a laughable display of its own ignorance. Or is it that the ceremonies and symbols prescribed by the laws are adopted in the universities? But these symbols are human. They did not arise from any damnable superstition but from human institution and agreement. They are free of superstition, and good men observe them without superstition. They signify either the completion of the labours of study, or the present fruit of learning, or the ability and favour (what they call charis [χάριν]) to take up just offices with credit and to enjoy their advantages. Can young people reasonably mock any of these? I do not think (to go through these points briefly, one by one) that young men devoted to virtue, humane learning and purer teaching would shun them, so that their earlier labours in study should not become known through public attestation. For they studied in order to become known, and to put their learning to the common good. If not, what is more wretched than treasure buried in the ground, or a good that lies idle? But if they refuse the attestation of others, and indeed of their teachers, the universities where they lived, and learned men, I would have them weigh two things in their own minds. First, how few will become known through their singular work (which we certainly praise and admire), so that they may be advanced by public judgment, according to their ability and standing, to the positions they deserve. Second (granting that they may remain unknown, or that they may spend their work wherever it seems fit, on their own judgment rather than another's), with what good faith the best universities could endure this: that men found fit for weightier matters should waste away in humbler ones, and be kept from the common good for the single reason that they were not commended by public attestation, and that they were thrust from the school into the arena of war, whether civil or ecclesiastical. If they refuse to seize the present fruit of virtue and learning, that is, the honour they have earned, I acknowledge their singular modesty, I praise it, cherish it and revere it. But I cannot yet see how their judgment in this matter is better than public judgment. For by abstaining from this kind of honour, they snatch from their teachers and the universities through which they advanced the honour they owe them. What more is there to say? They are ungrateful to those who deserved well of them, while they flatter themselves with the name of modesty, wherever the law has commanded this practice of gratitude [εὐχαριστίας]. But if (as we said last) they desire rather to show their ability in fact, and to obtain offices and advantages by themselves and by their own labour rather than by another's recommendation, they err in two ways, and not slightly.

units.la: Primum enim (quod vulgo dici solet) non est per plura faciendum, quod per pauciora potest: superfluo autem labore seipsos cumulat, qui suo Marte enituntur, ut in consilio, in foro, in plebe valeant omissa Academiarum testificatione: praesertim cum vix cosilium ullum sine fumo, forum sine invidia, plebs sine imperitia in judiciis constare possit. Deinde si re ipsa ostendere cupiunt qui viri sint, hic ubi ipsis gymnasium fuit facultatis, hic inquam palaestra facultatis est, hic moderatores certi ac periti studiorum, hic agonothetae, hic explorati facultatis και της οᾁσίας arbitri: hic licet ipsis decurrere, hic nervos animi contendere, hic omnibus modis qui erunt opus, induistria peritiamque sua apud peritos & incorruptos judices ac testes exponere. At abhorret fortasse juvenes isti, velut Catones, a nugis & caeremoniis. Atqui ne Catones quidem ipsi a functionibus in Republ. suscipiendis, & ab earum symbolis abhorrebant. Civile institutum est, civili honoris, dignitatis, praemiorum que civile documentum, lege & more receptum, superstitionis expers. Quae cum ita sint, quid est quod juventus pia, virtutis & politiorus doctrinae studiosa, ex animo horreat, reprehendat verbis, aut factis refugiat tantopere, firem ipsam introspexerit expenderitque diligentius?
units.tr: First, as is commonly said, what can be done by fewer means should not be done by more. Those who struggle by their own strength, so that they may be effective in council, in the law courts and among the common people, while setting aside the attestation of the universities, load themselves with needless labour. This is especially so since no council can stand without smoke, no court without envy, and no common people without ignorance in matters of judgment. Second, if those who want to show in fact what men they are, here, where the gymnasium of their ability was, here, I say, is the wrestling ground of ability: here are the certain and skilled overseers of studies, here the presidents of the games, here the proven judges of ability and of substance [καὶ τῆς οὐσίας]. Here they may run their course, here they may strain the sinews of their minds, and here, by every means that is needed, they may set forth their industry and skill before skilled and incorruptible judges and witnesses. But perhaps those young men, like Catos, shrink from trifles and ceremonies. Yet not even the Catos themselves shrank from taking up offices in the commonwealth, or from the symbols that go with them. This is a civil institution, a civil lesson of honour, dignity and rewards, received by law and custom, and free of superstition. Since this is so, why should a devout youth, devoted to virtue and to purer learning, shrink from it with all its heart, rebuke it in words, or flee from it in deeds so strongly, when it has not looked into the matter itself and weighed it more carefully?

units.la: Ad alios veniemus graves aetate, doctrina celebres, auctoritate praestantes viros, qui pietate, doctrina, judicio, perinde que sua perspecta apud omnes clari, judicant haec inania, levia, tricas apinas esse. Hi duobus telis plurimum videntur sibi iflas Academiarum nostrarum leges confodere: rationibus & exemplis. Rationibus, quia plurima sunt inquiunt, superflua & puerilia, abusus multi, omnia profecta a Pontificis. Exemplis, quia contemsit Basilius magnus, aliíq; magni & praestantes viri, prisca Patrum, majorumq; memoria & nostra. De his, quambrevissimè fieri a nobis poterit, videbimus. Primùm ergo objicitur multa inesse superflua & puerilia. Nego aut superflua esse, aut puerilia, quae legitimè & suo tempore observantur in Academiis, sine superstitione & injuria ulla. Nam superflua sunt ac puerilia, quae aut reipsa ita sunt, aut significatione. Haec autem proprie neque reipsa superflua aut puerilia, neque significatione dicenda sunt. Quis enim studiorum metas, gradus, honores, probationes, testimonia solennia in scholis & Academiis superflua & puerilia esse putaverit? quas res illi ipsi graves & praestantes viri, si liberos instituunt, in familia servant: si scholas servarint inter pueros & adolescentes jubent, in quas vocat promotionibus, & honorarijs studiorum inter promovendum praemijs honorificè liberaliterq; constituti. Quinetiam novi de illo ipso summorum doctissimorum q; hominum (quos colo) numero, qui non raro apud me & alios conquestì sunt, & cum animis suis sepe multumq; dolent, quòd iusto illo studiorum ordine quasi per gradus ad altiora non fuerunt ducti, sed confuse perturbateq; instituti olim, postea incredibili labore suo tandem eò pervenerunt, quò ludibundi fermè (prout ingenio valent) pervenissent, si tantum bonum, quod lege Academiarum caveretur, ipsis contigisset. Deinde verò (ut aliquid dem oppugnantibus legem & ceremoniam) fateor eamdem rem suo tempore neq; superfluam, neque puerilem esse, quae alieno tempore supervacanea & puerilis futura esset. Exempli causa, ridicula futura est promotio primanorum in Paedagogiis, si ultimis tribuatur, vel contrà: ita promotio Doctorum ineptè iis tribuatur qui Baccalaurei ad summum creandi & renunciandi sunt in Academia. Atque haec vera est ratio, qua homines sanè non indoctì fallutur, quum de summis gradibus & symbolis eorum judicant. Fallsum enim.
units.tr: Next we come to men who are advanced in years, famous for their learning, and outstanding in authority, whose piety, learning and judgment are known to all. They judge these practices to be empty, trivial and mere trifles. These men seem to assail the laws of our Academies chiefly with two weapons: arguments and examples. Their arguments are that there are many superfluous and childish things, many abuses, and that all of it has come from the Pope. Their examples are that Basil the Great and other great and distinguished men, both in ancient times and in our own memory, despised these things. We shall examine these points as briefly as we can. First, it is objected that many superfluous and childish things are present. I deny that those things are superfluous or childish which are lawfully and properly observed in the Academies, without superstition or any harm. Things are superfluous and childish either in reality or in their meaning. But these things are properly called neither superfluous nor childish, either in reality or in meaning. For who would think that the goals, grades, honours, examinations and solemn testimonials of studies in schools and Academies are superfluous and childish? Those same grave and distinguished men, if they educate their children, keep these things in their households; if they establish schools for boys and young men, they require them, and they honour and reward with prizes those who advance through the stages of study, and who are appointed with honour and generosity to these promotions. Indeed, I know of some of the most learned men (whom I cherish) who have often complained to me and to others, and who grieve often and deeply in their hearts, that they were not led through that proper order of studies, step by step, to higher things. Instead they were taught in a confused and disordered way, and at last, after incredible labour, they reached the point which they would have reached almost in play, as far as their talent allowed, had they enjoyed the great advantage that the Academies' laws provide. Then again (to grant something to those who oppose the law and its ceremony), I admit that the same thing is neither superfluous nor childish at its proper time, though at the wrong time it would be pointless and childish. For example, the promotion of freshmen in the colleges would be ridiculous if it were given to the final-year students, or the reverse. Likewise, the promotion of Doctors would be unfittingly given to those who are to be created and proclaimed Bachelors in the Academy. And this is the true reason why men who are by no means unlearned are deceived when they judge the highest degrees and their symbols. For the inference is false: if the highest things seem superfluous, and these things seem childish, it does not follow at once and simply that these things are purely and simply childish and superfluous. The examples just mentioned most clearly prove this. (The Greek phrase τὸ ἔθος is not needed here.)

units.la: axioma illud est, si summus viri superfluasunt hac videntur quæ puerilia, continuò purè simpliciterq́ puerilia & superflua dici oportere: quod proximè precedentia exempla evidentissimè arguunt. Sint sanè illus Coryphæis supervacanea in se, & puerilia videantur: attamen neque instituto legis puerilia aut superfluasunt, neque ex quibus lege decursa sludiorum suorum via ab Academiis reportant testimonium, neq; iis postremò qui ad eundem cursum hac testificatione solenni provocantur. Quorum causa æquius esse id semper duxi, ut doctissimi viri causa publici ordinis legibus publicis, ubi lata sunt atq; opus est, obsequantur, quàm ut propter se de jure publico & more non malo derogatum velint. Jam verò quòd abusus multi in hac re obiiciuntur nobis, non est de nihilo. Atque utinam omnes boni in Academiis εμοφυμαδὸν operam darent ut omnis abusus facesseret, atque id solum quod necessarium, quod ἀχαυον, quod legitimum est, obtineret. Sed ulsum rei legitimæ neilli quidem virtute & eruditione præstantes viri propter indignum abusum illius tollendum esse contenderint. Quidni autem? dixerit quispiam: ista enim sunt a Pontificiis ad nos derivata. Esto sanè: ut dem a Pontificiis manavi isse ista, an vero quicquid boni, quicquid honesti, quicquid ordinati a Pontificiis habemus acceptum, id propterea sumus rejecturi, quia fluxerit ex Pontificiis? Quin potius quicquid boni, honesti, & ordinati apud se habent Pontificii, id communes habeamus cum ipsis, si ferunt: si non ferunt, servemus saltem æque ac illi, & retineamus ad commune bonum. Verum non ita est ut opinio est illorum: nam hac a majoribus, a Carolo Magno & sapientissimis Principibus, alijs per Pontificios ad nos transfmearunt. Nos autem siquid bonum est in Pontificiis, siquid bonum & utile per Pontificios defluxit ad nos, absit ut idipsum in sano Pontificiorum odio abrepti depellamus. Siquid ἀνοιχείον Academia, siquid abusione, si superstitione contaminatum est, id per nos tollatur licet: nihil tergiversabimur. Sed rem sanê constituta utiliterq́ observatam iniquum est propter abusum damnari, ubi instituta est durum, propter opinionem quorundam neglegi. Iam vero quid ad exempla dicturi sumus? Publicas leges a Basilio magno contemtas aut omissas fuisse non memini. Id quidem meminii legere, & ita Nazianzenus refert, illum cum admiratione omnium legitimo examini satisfecisse Athenis pro eruditione sua: postea quam vero (ut idem refert) omnes viderunt τὸ ἔ ἠθος αὐτοῦ σώφρον, ἡ τὸ ἐν λόγοις καλόν, τί γὰρ; μόνος χρεῖον τῶν ἀπονυμένων τὴν κοινὴν διαφυγὴν νόμων, κρείττονος ἢ ἐχ' ἐνλὼ ἀξιωθῆναι ἡμῖν: ut inquam animadvertebant constantiam morum in eo, & sermonum commoditatem, quid tandem factum est? solus fere eorum qui Athenis agebant liber fuit a communi lege, & ampliore dignus honore habitus quam novi advenae haberi solent: quomodo autem? quia non fuit ut ceteri, cum pompa traductus per forum, clamoribus exceptus, deductus in balneum, &c. sed simpliciter ξ̓ τὸ δεῖγμα Φιλοσοφικὸν (ut illi vocabant) consalutatus Magister seu Doctor philosophiae. Superavit ergo Basilius non refugiet ista, quae legitima fuerunt, cum auctoritate praestans; quae ludicra, auctoritate & gratia diluens. Quid vetat, quominus idem a viris bonis aetate doctrinaque praeditis, in Academia quaque optima retineatur? De viris bonis atque literatis, siquando vocantur ad Academias, judicium idem. Sua causa ne faciant sane, neque facturi sint: at legum publicarum causa, exemplique publici tamen facturi sunt, ne dum ritus humanos gravitas sibi vindicent fugere, morosè (ut ita dicam) superstitiosi homines ducantur esse. Certè non in venustè illud de Academiis, earumque in fluidis humanioribus ordine praestituto a nobis praedicari apud juventutem poterit, quod ille olim de sua Ithaca, Τρηχεῖ, ἀλλ' ἀγαθὴ κυρτοειδὲς, ἐπ' ἐγαγε Ης γαίης δωάματ' γλυκερώτερον ἄλλο ἰδεῖν.
units.tr: Granted, those highest things may in themselves be superfluous and may seem childish. Yet they are neither childish nor superfluous in the design of the law, nor for those by whose completion of the course of study they receive testimony from the Academies, nor finally for those who are called to the same course by this solemn testimony. In their cause, I have always thought it fairer that learned men should obey public laws, where they have been enacted and are needed, than that, for their own sake, they should wish to detract from public right and from a good custom. As for the many abuses that are charged against us in this matter, the charge is not without ground. Would that all good men in the Academies would work together so that every abuse might disappear, and that only what is necessary, honourable and lawful might remain. But men outstanding in virtue and learning have never contended that the lawful thing itself should be abolished because of its unworthy abuse. Why not? someone may say, for these things have been handed down to us by the Papists. Granted, let us suppose these things did flow from the Papists. Are we therefore to reject whatever good, honourable and orderly things we have received from the Papists, simply because they came from the Papists? Rather, whatever good, honourable and orderly things the Papists hold, let us hold in common with them, if they allow it; if they do not allow it, let us keep them just as they do, and retain them for the common good. But the matter is not as their opinion has it, for these things were handed down to us from our ancestors, from Charlemagne and the wisest princes, and reached us through the Papists. But if anything good is in the Papists, if anything good and useful has flowed down to us through them, far be it from us, carried away by a sick hatred of the Papists, to cast that out. If anything in the Academy is unseemly, or is contaminated by abuse or superstition, let it be removed by us; we shall not hesitate. But it is unjust that a thing rightly established and usefully observed should be condemned on account of abuse, or neglected because of the opinion of some. Now what shall we say about the examples? I do not recall that Basil the Great despised or omitted the public laws. I do recall reading this, and Nazianzen reports it: that he satisfied the lawful examination at Athens, to the admiration of all, for his learning. Afterwards, however (as the same author reports), when everyone saw the modesty of his character and the charm of his speech, what happened? He alone, almost, of those who were then at Athens, was free from the common law, and was regarded as worthy of a greater honour than newcomers usually receive. And how? Because he was not, like the others, led through the forum in procession, greeted with shouts, and taken to the bath, and so on, but was simply greeted as Master or Doctor of Philosophy, by the so-called philosophical proof, as they called it. Basil therefore surpassed them, not by refusing those lawful things, but by excelling in authority, and by dissolving frivolous things through his authority and grace. What prevents the same thing from being retained in the best Academy by good men, who are endowed with age and learning? The same judgment holds for good and learned men, if at any time they are invited to the Academies. They may not do so for their own sake, nor will they wish to, but for the sake of public laws and public example, lest, while they claim to avoid human customs out of gravity, they be thought to be morose and, as I may say, superstitious. Certainly, what that poet once said of his Ithaca cannot be preached to youth with any elegance about the Academies and the order of the humanities laid down by us: "Rugged, but a good nurse of youth; nor do I know anything sweeter to see than one's own land" [Τρηχεῖ', ἀλλ' ἀγαθὴ κουροτρόφος· οὐδέ τι γαίης τῆς ἄλλης γλυκερώτερον ἄλλο ἰδέσθαι].

units.la: quam rembus licentiosissimus temporibus nostris juventus studiosu vix vnquam creditura est. Cum ita que animadverterem non mediocriter hac in re utrobique peccari; tum quòd juventus nostra &c. ἐπιπος παρακινδυνεύειν ἀλόγιστος, ἢ ἀχαλίνωτος feratur, in studia sine lege, sine ordine, arbitratu suo, id unum sibi in primis gratulans si vivere potest ἀνυπέυθυνος; tum quòd Academiarum sanctarum, legum indignè concidit autoritas in hac studiorum confusione & temporum, nisi Deus de cælo prospexerit, & omnes boni se ad laudatum hoc ædificium opera sua, labore, industriâ, statuminandum & surrigendum contulerint: non alienum ab officio meo putavi fore. Si ea quæ de Academiarum ortu, legibus, effectus, causis ψυχικῶς simpliciter, dicenda videbantur, in σωματικόν aliquod unum compingerem, & a prepositeris adeo quini quis multorum judiciis. pro eo ac possum, opella mea vindicarem.
units.tr: In these most licentious times of ours, the studious youth will scarcely ever believe it. Since I noticed that errors are made to a considerable degree on both sides in this matter, and since our youth is carried headlong into studies, without law, without order, at its own pleasure, rejoicing above all that it can live unaccountable, and since the authority of the holy Academies has been shamefully broken down by this confusion of studies and of the times, unless God looks down from heaven and all good men contribute their work, labour and diligence to shore up and raise this praised edifice, I thought it would not be foreign to my duty. If I were to compile into one body what seemed to be worth saying about the origin, laws, effects and causes of the Academies, speaking in a general way, and were to defend it, as far as I can, with my little work against the judgments of many, I would be doing what I can.

units.la: Hanc verò, cui cuimodi est, Illustrissime Princeps, visum est T. C. & M. θεός Φωνῆν multis nominibus. Nam primum eadem studia pro tua ætate colis studiosè quæ colunt Academiæ: præterea honorem summum hoc anno (qui quartus ipsi Iubilæus est) huic Academiæ habuisti, quum fasces ipsius submisse tibi oblatos non es dedignatus et clementer suscipere: postremò autem hoc ipsum qualecunque officium quodam jure suo flagitare a me visa est Academia, ut palàm testatum fieret, illud ipsum vulnus quod incredibili dolore nostro & adversariorum lætitia sibi fuerat impositum superiore anno, jam te Rectore hoc anno depositum & curatum esse, tuámque C. & M. (quod sanctè pronunciabas nuper) omnibus & votis & officiis hunc nostrum ordinem & Academiam ornare velle. Hæc vota, sponsiones, officiáque gratiosissima T. C. & M. recordatus, cum animo meo lætor, nobis gratulor, agnosco palàm, & apud omnes prædico, tuaque C. & M. gratias immortales habeo, cum meo ipsius nomine, tum ordinis totius nostri & Academiæ: Deumque oro æternum Patrem æterni & ὁμοούσιον filij Iesu Christi Domini & Seruatoris nostri, a quo omnis bona donatio proficiscitur, cælesti benedictione sua velit efficere, ut T. C. & M. firmissimo sit præsidio huic Academiæ, & hæc vicissim tibi ornamento quàm diutissimè ad gloriam suam & commune bonum patriæ, Ecclesiæ Christianæ, & Reipublicæ. Amen.
units.tr: It seemed right to me, most illustrious Prince, to offer this little work, such as it is, to Your C. & M. for many reasons. First, you cultivate the same studies, suited to your age, that the university cultivates. Moreover, this year you held the highest honour this university could give (it is its fiftieth year, its jubilee), when you did not disdain to accept graciously the staff of office that was humbly offered to you. Finally, the university itself thought it had a right to demand from me this small duty, so that it might be openly attested that the wound inflicted on us last year, to our great grief and the delight of our opponents, has now, under your rectorship this year, been dressed and healed. Your C. & M., as you solemnly promised recently, wishes with all its prayers and services to adorn this order of ours and this university. I gladly remember these wishes, promises and most gracious services of Your C. & M. I rejoice in them with all my heart, I openly acknowledge them, and I proclaim them to everyone. In my own name and in the name of our whole order and university, I give Your C. & M. undying thanks. I pray to God the eternal Father, and to his consubstantial [ὁμοούσιον] Son Jesus Christ, our Lord and Saviour, from whom every good gift comes, that by his heavenly blessing he may make Your C. & M. a most firm protection to this university, and that in turn this university may be an ornament to you for as long as possible, to his glory and to the common good of the fatherland, the Christian Church and the commonwealth. Amen.
