units.tr: FRANCIS JUNIUS: THE ACADEMY.

units.la: CAPUT PRIMUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER 1.

units.la: De origine vocis Academia.
units.tr: On the origin of the word Academia.

units.la: CADEMIAE nomen Athenis primùm inclaruisse apud omnes ferme autores convenit: sed dubia controversaque origine, & significatu vario. Etenim Graecorum alii civitatem, alii lavacrum, gymnasium alii interpretati sunt, prout ex diversis fontibus putant ductum. Qui civitatem, hi Academiam vocant ἀγλω̃ ἡ δὲ ἀγωγλὼ τῶν δήμων, id est, honoratam aliquam tribuum & familiarum collectionem atque conventum compositam voce dixerunt: quèadmodum ἀσὶ, ἀσὶ Terentius, pro systemate vel congregatione, ex ἀ, quod est ὁμοῦ, simul, & verbo ἱσταμαι, stare. Qui lavacrum (ut Hesychius autor est) appellauerunt nomine Academiae, ii ex Hebraeo fonte παρὰ τὸ κάζειν, τὸ κοσμεῖν, id est, ab ornando Academia dici voluerunt, eo quod lotionis usu corpora colerentur fierentq; elegantiora. Atq; hanc lavacri significationem duobus argumentis sibi visi sunt Attici confirmare, situ loci, & ritu illius Academiae. Situ, quia lavacrum fuit prope urbem cum nemore junctum Academiae: Ritu, quia studiosos juvenes solebant ex eo abluere, quum ad certos quosdam & legitimos studiorum gradus conscendisset: ut suo loco postea ex Nazianzeno dicturi sumus. Qui autè pro gymnasio acceperunt, pleriq; omnes statuunt fuisse nomen impositum ex Academo sive Hecademo, laudato viro. Hunc enim autorem fuisse tradunt Academiae, eiq; de suo nomine, quum ex privata possessione publicum faceret studiorum causâ, indidisse nomen.
units.tr: THE name Academia is almost universally agreed by authors to have first become famous at Athens, but its origin is disputed and its meaning varies. The Greeks did not agree: some explained it as a city, others as a bath, and others as a gymnasium, according to the different sources from which they thought it derived. Those who took it to mean a city say that Academia was called by a word meaning an honoured assembly of tribes and families, a gathered body of the demes [ἀγλω̃ ἡ δὲ ἀγωγλὼ τῶν δήμων], just as Terence says asi, asi [ἀσὶ, ἀσὶ] for a system or gathering, from a [ἀ], which means together [ὁμοῦ], and the verb histēmi [ἱσταμαι], to stand. Those who called it a bath (as Hesychius reports) derived the name Academia from the Hebrew source, from adorning [παρὰ τὸ κάζειν, τὸ κοσμεῖν], that is, they wished it to be named from ornamenting, because bodies were beautified and made more elegant by the use of washing. The Athenians thought they could confirm this meaning of bath by two arguments, the situation of the place and the custom of that Academy. The situation: the bath was near the city, joined to the grove of the Academy. The custom: young students used to be washed there when they had climbed to certain fixed and lawful stages of study, as we shall say in its place later from Gregory Nazianzen. Those who took it to mean a gymnasium mostly hold that the name was given after Academus, or Hecademus, a famous man. They report that he was the founder of the Academy, and that when he turned a private estate into a public place for study, he gave it his own name.

units.la: Paufanias Atticis, Extra urbem proxime heroum virorum, fortium sepulcra est Academia, privati olim hominis agar, nunc gymnasium. Laërtius Platone, Reversus Athenas Plato commorabatur in Academia. Est autem hoc gymnasium suburbanum, nemorosum, a quodam heroe, cui nomen fuit Academus dictum: quæ admodum & Eupolis in Æstateutis dicit, ἐν Ἀκαδημίας ἡρώεσιν Ἀκαδήμου Ἥρου, In ambulacris Academi umbrosis dei:
units.tr: Pausanias, writing about the Athenians: Outside the city, near the tombs of heroic men and brave warriors, is the Academy, once the estate of a private man, now a gymnasium. Laertius, writing about Plato: On returning to Athens, Plato stayed in the Academy. This gymnasium lies in the suburbs, among trees, and is named after a hero called Academus. Just as Eupolis says in his Summer: In the shady walks of Academus, the hero [ἐν Ἀκαδημίας ἡρώεσιν Ἀκαδήμου Ἥρου].

units.la: & Timon quoque de Platone sermonem habens, inquit; Τῶν ἀπάντων δ' ἡγέτο πλατύσαρ@, ἀλλ' ἀγορητής Ηδυεπής, τέτλιξιν ἰσόγραφος ἰδ' Ἀκαδήμου Ἀινδρεῖ ἰφεξόμενοι ὕστα λεπίστωσαν ἰέσι. id est, His Plato dux cunctis humeros latissimus ibat, Oremelos perfuave sonans, & quale HecademiArboribus grata modulantur voce cicadæ.
units.tr: Timon too, speaking of Plato, says: Plato, broad of shoulder, led them all, a speaker of sweet speech, who with his voice sounded like the cicadas that sing sweetly in the trees of Hecademus [Τῶν ἀπάντων δ' ἡγέτο πλατύσαρ@, ἀλλ' ἀγορητής Ηδυεπής, τέτλιξιν ἰσόγραφος ἰδ' Ἀκαδήμου Ἀινδρεῖ ἰφεξόμενοι ὕστα λεπίστωσαν ἰέσι].

units.la: Quam in sententiam item dicebat Horatius libro 2. Epistolarum,
units.tr: Horace also said the same thing in the second book of his Epistles:

units.la: Atque inter sylvas Academi quærere verum.
units.tr: And to seek the truth among the groves of Academus.

units.la: Hactenus de recepta apud autores illos etymologia: Hoc autem etymologiarum genere antiquitas plurimum abundavit, ut aliqua religionis specie cum auctoritatem locis, tum suis narrationibus fidem compararet. Etsi plerumque; perfugio isto fuisse videtur usa, ut in tabulis pictores & Geographi solent: nempe quum aut vetustas historiam, aut vocum peregrinitas rem ipsam significationem que obscuravit. Quæ res quia in hoc quoque exemplo accidit, videndum nobis est, ut ex ruderibus priscæ historiæ & linguarum exterarum comparatione id quod verum est eruamus.
units.tr: So much for the etymology accepted by those authors. Antiquity especially abounded in this kind of etymology, so that by a certain show of religion it could win authority for its places and credibility for its stories. Yet it seems to have often used this refuge, as painters and geographers do on their maps, namely when either age has obscured the history or the foreignness of the words has obscured the meaning itself. Since this has happened in this example too, we must see to it that, by means of the ruins of early history and the comparison of foreign languages, we dig out what is true.

units.la: Cadmus vel potius Kadmus, Phœnicium nomen est ex Hebrea matre lingua ductum: & significat antiquum vel anticum, ut promiscue scribebant veteres. Quemadmodum autem vocem antiquum, Latini olim, & Latinorum progenitores Tyrrheni, id est, Osci & Ethrusci a Phoenicibus orti usurpabant; sic Phoenices suam appellationem Kadmi. Nam ab his Tyrrheni & per hos Latini, ut filij nepotesque ab avis & maioribus suis, voces quàm plurimas, usum verò universum linguarum suarum acceperunt. Illis igitur Kadmus, his anticus vel antiquus dictus est, quisquis tempore, situ, loco, ordine, dignitate, officio, vel actione & procuratione ante stabat ceteris. Tempore, ut quum Maro diceret,
units.tr: Cadmus, or rather Kadmus, is a Phoenician name derived from the Hebrew mother tongue, and it means ancient or former, as the ancients wrote indiscriminately. Just as the Latins long used the word antiquum, and the Latins' forebears, the Tyrrhenians, that is the Oscans and Etruscans, descended from the Phoenicians, did the same, so the Phoenicians took their own name, Kadmi. For from these people the Tyrrhenians, and through them the Latins, received very many words, and indeed the whole use of their languages, as sons and grandsons receive from grandfathers and forefathers. So Kadmus was the name for them, and anticus or antiquus for the Latins, for whoever stood before others in time, position, place, order, rank, duty, action or management. In time, as when Virgil says:

units.la: Vrbs antiqua fuit, Tyrii tenuere coloni,
units.tr: There was an ancient city, which Tyrian colonists held,

units.la: Karthago Italiam contra, &c.
units.tr: Carthage, facing Italy, etc.

units.la: atque hoc sensu Tullius eleganter Attico, Tres, inquit, epistolas tuas accepi postridie Idus: erant autem III. I. III. pridie Id. datae: igitur antiquissima cuique primum respondebo. Situ aut Sɨc, ut quû antica aut postica pars tepli ex auguraculo designabatur, qua ratione veteres antica, ait Verrius, pro janua posuere. Atq; hoc per literà c scribi Alexandrinus jam usus obtinet. Loco, ut quû ea quę ante nos sunt in cospectu nostro volumus intelligi, & ortû Solis anticam caeli partê nominamus, quemadmodû Hebrei & Syri Kedem. Ordine, ut quum principes in Senatu Rom. sententiam rogabantur, quem vocat Tullius antiquiorem in Senatu sententia dicendae locum, & victores in ludis antegerionem (sic enim habetur in Glossario vetere) obtinere. Dignitate & pretio, ut est apud Virgilium,
units.tr: And in this sense Cicero elegantly writes to Atticus: I received your three letters on the day after the Ides; they were dated the third, the first, and the third before the Ides; so I shall answer the oldest first. In position, or Sic, as the front or back part of a temple was marked out from the augural place; by this reasoning, Verrius says, the ancients used antica for the door. And the Alexandrians now commonly write this with the letter c. In place, as when we want things that are before us to be understood as in our sight, and we call the eastern part of the sky the front, as the Hebrews and Syrians do with Kedem. In order, as when the leaders were asked their opinion in the Roman Senate, which Cicero calls the more ancient place for giving an opinion in the Senate, and when winners in the games obtained the first place (for so it is found in an old glossary). In rank and value, as in Virgil:

units.la: Nec mihi jam patriam antiquam spes ulla videndi:
units.tr: Nor is there any hope for me of seeing my ancient homeland again.

units.la: & narrat Cicero antiquiorem Regi Deiotaro fuisse laudem & gloriam, quàm regnû & possessiones suas. Officio dignitate coniuncto, ut quum in templis & sacris Antistites, in Academiis Antecessores dicerentur, nimirum quia officio placuit dignitatem & locum respondere.
units.tr: And Cicero reports that glory and fame were more ancient to King Deiotarus than his kingdom and possessions. Where office is joined with rank, as when in temples and sacred matters they were called Antistites and in academies Antecessores, obviously because rank and place correspond to office.

units.la: Actione denique & procuratione, vt quum homines aut etiā ordines alii aliis occurrunt, & fiunt quolibet cōgressu inter se obviam: quomodo anteveniendi verbum prisci Latini vsurparūt: & Κάδμον hominem cæcum, qui in omnia incurrit & impingit obvia, dixerunt Salaminii.
units.tr: Finally, in action and management, as when men or even orders encounter one another and meet face to face in any encounter; this is how the early Latins used the verb anteveniendi, and the Salaminians called a blind man who runs into and strikes everything in his path Kadmos [Κάδμον].

units.la: Ac Kadmum quidem illum, cuius historiæ frequenter meminerunt, nec a tempore antiquum dici constat, nam fuerunt longe antiquiores alii: nec a situ aut loco, nam magis Orientales alii, quàm hic fuit, pariter in Græciam migraverunt: ordine multo minus, nam αὐτόχθονες Græci homini extero primas nunquam fuisse concessuri, & in Illyricum deinde pulsus est Græcorum invidia, vt narrat historici. Restat igitur, ut aut a dignitate officioque (ut credibile est) aut ab actionibus suis habuerit appellationem Kadmi. A dignitate ergo officioq; cum dignitate iuncto, velut πρωτεῖα, fuisse apud suos dictum res ipsa loquitur, & præclaras actiones ejus ex officio consequutas. Kadmi enim hæc fuit dignitas, quòd filius fuerit Agenoris Tyriōrū regis in Phœnice agro: officiū quòd dux fuerit migrantibus copiis a patre: actio, quòd & opere & sermone omnibus præiverit. Hunc vero autores alii Ægyptium, alii Phœnicem, alii Milesiū fuisse putāt: alii diversos fabulantur exstitisse: sic innumeræ fabulæ ex hoc, ut equo Trojano & progenie Cadmea, prodiverunt. Etenim Ægyptii hunc hominem vindicare sibi cupientes, a fe prædicabant ortum. Ἀγρὸ Μισῶρ (inquit Philo apud Eusebium ex Samconiathone) Τάαυτ(Θ)· ὃς ἐξ ἀρετῶν τῶν πρώτων τοῖς χαίρων χεαφλᾶν Αἰγύπτιοι μὲν Θωθ (legε Θωθ) Αλέξανδρος δὲ Θωθ, Ἑλλῆνες δὲ Ἑρμῆς ἐκάλεσαν. id est, Ex Mifor (hic autem est Ægyptius) genitus ejus Taautus, qui primorum elementorum scripturam invenit: hunc Ægyptii Thooth, Alexandrei Thouth, Graeci vero Mercurium Ἑρμῆν.
units.tr: Now it is agreed that the Kadmus whose history they often mention was not called ancient in time, for others were far more ancient; nor by position or place, for other Orientals, more so than he, migrated to Greece equally; and much less by order, for the native Greeks would never have granted first place to a foreigner, and he was then driven out to Illyricum by Greek envy, as the historians relate. It remains, then, that he had the name Kadmus either from his rank and office (as is credible) or from his actions. That he was called by his people first, from rank joined with office, as it were, the thing itself declares, and his famous actions followed from his office. For Kadmus's rank was that he was the son of Agenor, king of the Tyrians in the land of Phoenicia; his office was that he was the leader of the troops that migrated under his father; his action was that he went before everyone both in deed and in speech. Some authors think he was an Egyptian, others a Phoenician, others a Milesian; others invent that there were several. So countless stories arose from him, such as the Trojan horse and the Cadmean race. For the Egyptians, wanting to claim this man for themselves, proclaimed that he was born among them. Philo, quoted by Eusebius from Sanchuniathon, says: From Misor (and he was an Egyptian) was born Taautus, who invented the writing of the first letters; the Egyptians called him Thooth (read Thoth), the Alexandrians Thouth, but the Greeks called him Hermes Mercurius [Ἑρμῆν].

units.la: Lib.1.præf. Eusebius Chron. parat.Euseb. §el.ca.vlt. [?] appellaverunt. Eumdem sibi Libyes arrogant, Herculem appellantes. Fuisse Tyrium Phoenices gloriantur, & fatentur Graeci. Verumtamen hi, ut aliquid deripiant de Phoenicum laude & vertant in rem suam, Cadmum alterum fuisse narrant genere Milesium, qui primus oratione prosa condere instituit historiam. Omnes autem unum & eundem fuisse fatentur Mercurium, qui literas Aegyptios & Graecos docuerit, quamvis diversis appellationibus, & in Africam praeterea detulerit. Hic ergo Hermes Graecorum sive Mercurius propterea Kadmus fuit nominatus, quod quum literarum ornamento instructus esset, ab omnibus est princeps habitus dignitate officioque, & hominum congressus expolivit humaniorum literarum & studiorum adjumento. Atque hoc iam olim fuit Mercurii in Graecia epitheton, Varino teste: ex quo Baeoti illum [?] dixerunt Καδμίλον, ut est apud Lycophronem.
units.tr: Book 1, preface; Eusebius, Chronicle, preparation; Eusebius, last chapter. [?] called him. The Libyans claim him for themselves too, calling him Hercules. The Phoenicians boast that he was from Tyre, and the Greeks admit it. Yet the Greeks, so as to snatch something from the glory of the Phoenicians and turn it to their own advantage, say that there was another Cadmus, of Milesian birth, who first began to write history in prose. But all admit that he was one and the same Mercury, who taught the Egyptians and Greeks letters, though under different names, and who also carried them into Africa. So this Hermes or Mercury of the Greeks was called Kadmus for this reason: since he was furnished with the ornament of letters, he was regarded by all as chief in rank and office, and by the assistance of humane letters and studies he refined the company of men. This was already long ago an epithet of Mercury in Greece, according to Varro; hence the Boeotians called him [?] Kadmilos [Καδμίλον], as in Lycophron.

units.la: Hic autem ipse, sive Kadmus sermone Phoenicio, sive Taautes vel Taautus Aegyptio, sive Libyco Hercules, sive Hermes & Cadmilus Graeco, pro sua sapientia, ubicunque locorum fuit, instituit literarum ludos, & homines ad vitam humaniorem & liberalia studia revocavit, fodinas lapidum metalloruḿ, & conflaturam, (ut ajunt) invenit; ut ego sentio, demonstravit multis: exposuit denique congressuum, commerciorum, & negotiationum commoda navigationibus. Quapropter etiam navigium, comparatum ad navigationes instrumentum, Hebraeis & Syrisappellatur Thebba, quam Graeci appellant [?]: ex quo urbes Thebae apud Aegyptios & Graecos dictae, regio Thebam, & conjugata omnia.
units.tr: This same man, whether he is called Kadmus in the Phoenician tongue, Taautes or Taautus in Egyptian, Hercules in Libyan, or Hermes and Cadmilus in Greek, wherever he was in the world, by his wisdom established the games of letters. He called men back to a more civilised life and to the liberal studies. He discovered (as they say) the quarries of stones and metals and the smelting of ore. As I think, he showed many people how to do these things. Finally, he set out the advantages that voyages bring to meetings, trade and business. For this reason the ship, the vessel made for voyaging, is called Thebba by the Hebrews and Syrians, and the Greeks call it [?]. From this word the cities Thebes among the Egyptians and Greeks were named, and the region Thebam, and all the words related to them.

units.la: Horum vero beneficiorum omnium vestigia passim remanserunt. Hinc enim Cadmea sive Cadmia in re metallica, & Cadmitis dicta in gemmario genere. In primis autem nobilia & illustria rei literariæ documenta comparent in locorum appellationibus. Nam in Ægypto, Heptanomorum regio atq; Thebaica nomos Chinnuc-politen (quem corruptè Cynopolitè dixerūt) Hermopoliten, Hera- cleopolitén, Athenopolitēn, Lycopolitēn vel Lyceopolitēn, Hermonthitēn habuit: opida Chinnuc polin vulgo Cynópolin dictam, Hermópolin, Antæos, Lyceópolin sive Lycópolin, Hera- cleópolin, Hermium, Hermónthida, & innumera idgenus alia ex adventu & institutione Kadmi. Vt verò in Ionia commigravit, eam cōplevit iisdem fermè nominibus. Mons Cadmus habitationi fuit, regio Lyconia, gymnasia secundūm flumen Lycum, Heraclea duplex, &ex Kadmilo per aphærefin Miletus dicta (unde literæ Milesiæ pro magicis, & vicus eodē nomine quondam) Bargilia, Milassa quam Mylassam scribunt, mons Phœnix, & vicus eodem nomine, &c. ut in Africa Libyphœnices sub Karthagoniis, & opidum Hermæa dictum. Ex Ionia verò in Bæotiam processit Kadmus, ubi Cadmēam sive Cadmiam arcem Thebarum gymnasiúmque statuit, Thebas, Tánagram, Gĕphyram, pro eo quod est Cephyram vel Cephuram, id est πλέξης, initiationis & purgationis locum; & montem Helycónem effecit celebrem, qui vulgo non sine vitio scribitur Helicon. Postea Argivi Cadméos, Bæóti Gephyræos Tanãgrica sede ejecerunt. Itaque hi Athenas diverterunt, id est, in Athenarum δήμως sive pagos: a quibus in civitatem recepti, doctrinisquàm plurimis, præsertim literarum studiis humanioribus coluerunt illam, ut Herodotus in Terpsichore narrat & confirmat luculentissimé. Qua autem ratione Thebis in Bæotia gymnasium Kadmēa siue Cadmia fuit appellatum eadem quoque Athenis fastum. Etenima Tanagræ, id est (sictymon spectes) ame- exἐχάδωνς studiorum exponentibus in medium hospitibus Athena dictæ sunt, vt sedes τ πεςεχάδωνς doctrinarum q; omnium, & Αθῆνα dea studiorum ficta, Minerva seu Pallas: a Cadméis verò Kadméa sive Kadmia appellata, locus studiorum a Gephyræis advenis institutus. Est enim hæc prosthesis, a vel e, Cadmeo generi cùm in Libya, tum in Atthide usitata. Libyes & Afri φαὶ Ἐστοαm dicunt, Stephanum Ἐστεφάνωμ, Cholam Acholam, Tzephin, Aspin opidum, & similia multa. Attici verò in eumdem modum ςεχωὶ ἀσεχωὶ, ςεφίδα ἀσεφίδα, Θλὼαν Αθλώαν, Θλώας Αθλώας, Αυχῶνα ἐλυχῶνα (male ἐλιχῶνα) Kadμείαν sive Kadμίαν quoque Ἀκαδημίαν vel Ἐκαδημίαν pronunciant. Atque hæc quidem satis de vocis origine.
units.tr: The traces of all these benefits remain everywhere. From him comes Cadmea or Cadmia in metallurgy, and Cadmitis in the class of gemstones. The most noble and famous proofs of his literary work appear in the names of places. In Egypt, the district of the Heptanomis and the Theban nome had Chinnuc-politen (which they wrongly called Cynopolites), Hermopoliten, Heracleopoliten, Athenopoliten, Lycopoliten or Lyceopoliten, Hermonthiten. The towns were Chinnuc polin, commonly called Cynopolis, Hermopolis, Antaeos, Lyceopolis or Lycopolis, Heracleopolis, Hermium, Hermonthis, and countless other names of the same kind, from the arrival and teaching of Kadmus. When he moved into Ionia, he filled it with almost the same names. Mount Cadmus was his dwelling place, the region was Lyconia, there were gymnasia along the river Lycus, there were two Heracleas, and Miletus, named from Kadmilus by aphaeresis (whence the Milesian letters, meaning magical writings, and a village of the same name once existed), Bargilia, Milassa, which some write as Mylassa, Mount Phoenix with a village of the same name, and so on. In Africa there were the Libyphoenices under the Carthaginians, and a town called Hermaea. From Ionia Kadmus went on into Boeotia, where he set up the Cadmea or Cadmia, the citadel and gymnasium of Thebes. Around it were Thebes, Tanagra, Gephyra, named for what is really Cephyra or Cephura, that is [πλέξης], a place of initiation and purification. He also made famous the mountain Helicon, which is commonly and wrongly written Helicon. Later the Argives drove the Cadmeans out, and the Boeotians drove the Gephyraeans out of the seat of Tanagra. These men went to Athens and settled in the demes or villages of Attica. Once they were received into the city by its citizens, they cultivated it with many learned arts, especially the humane studies of literature, as Herodotus relates and confirms most clearly in his Terpsichore. By the same reasoning, the gymnasium at Thebes in Boeotia that was called Cadmea or Cadmia was also named in Athens. For the place where the guests gathered to set out their studies was called Athens, as the seat of all learning, and the goddess of studies was feigned under the name Athena, that is Minerva or Pallas. It was called Cadmea or Cadmia by the Cadmeans, a place of study set up by the newcomers from Gephyra. This prefixing of a or e is common in the Cadmean dialect both in Libya and in Attica. The Libyans and Africans say [φαὶ Ἐστοαm] for ..., they say Stephanus [Ἐστεφάνωμ], Chola [Acholam], Tzephis, Aspis (a town), and many similar words. The Attic speakers in the same way say [ςεχωὶ] for [ἀσεχωὶ], [ςεφίδα] for [ἀσεφίδα], [Θλὼαν] for [Αθλώαν], [Θλώας] for [Αθλώας], [Αυχῶνα] for [ἐλυχῶνα] (wrongly [ἐλιχῶνα]), and they also pronounce Kadmeia or Kadmia as [Ἀκαδημίαν] or [Ἐκαδημίαν]. So much for the origin of the word.

units.la: CAPUT SECUNDUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER TWO.

units.la: Quid sit Academia, & quæ sint ejus appellationes.
units.tr: What an Academy is, and what its names are.

units.la: Est igitur proprie quidem Academia, συνημα vel coetus hominum exercentium studia literarum, & in iis sese occupantium: metonymicè verò locus ubi exercentur studia docendo discendóque. Nam quòd Athenienses olim suæ illi Academiæ speciatim hoc nomen arrogaverunt, & alij κατ' ἐξοχὴν ei tribuerunt; id ambitione illorum factum est, & horum ignoratione. Ambitio fuit Atheniensium, quòd qui αὐτόχθονες vel Aborigines semper in Græcia haberi voluerunt, ii gloriosa isthæc studiorum nomina suæ ipsorum genti ac soli vindicaverunt; & certas eorum origines plerumque de industria corruperunt, ut omnem scientiæ doctrinarúmque laudem aliis præriperent. Nam etiam (quod longè fuit gravius, & factu indignissimum) eos turpiter oppresserunt per quos profecerant. Gephyræos enim vel Cephuræos advenas,
units.tr: Properly speaking, then, an Academy is a collective [συνημα] or gathering of men who pursue the study of letters and occupy themselves with it. By metonymy, it is the place where the study of letters is carried on through teaching and learning. The Athenians long ago claimed this name for their own academy in particular, and others attributed it to them as the academy par excellence [κατ' ἐξοχὴν]. This came about through the Athenians' ambition and the ignorance of others. The ambition was the Athenians': since they always wished to be regarded as autochthonous or Aborigines [αὐτόχθονες], they claimed these glorious names of learning for their own nation and soil, and often deliberately corrupted their true origins, so as to snatch from others all the praise of knowledge and learning. Indeed, and what was far graver and most unworthy to do, they shamefully oppressed those through whom they had made progress. The Gephyraeans or Cephurae, immigrants who had adorned Attica itself with letters, they received on the harshest and most bitter terms, as Herodotus attests. They never rested until that people's name was nearly wiped out, so that their goddess Pallas was regarded as the parent of learning and culture, while the Athenians themselves were held to be the true nurslings and servants of learning.

units.la: • qui ipsam Atthida literis exornaverant, exceperūt durissimis & acerbissimis conditionibus, teste Herodoto: nec unquam, nisi deleto fermè illorum nomine, potuerunt conquiescere; vt dea ipsorum Pallas pro studiorum & humanitatis parente, ipsi vero pro germanis studiorum alumnis & administris soli haberentur. Sed illa insignis fuit in aliis gentibus ignoratio, quòd ex inscientia historiæ veteris exterarúmque linguarum imperitia laborantes, id quodam modo cesserunt Atheniensibus, quod priùs ad ipsos quàm ad Athenienseis pervenerat. Cur enim Iones? cur Bæoti parem laudem non fuissent assumturi sibi? Nempe maluerant ipsti Kadmeos & Academias ejicere ex suis finibus, quàm exterorum ferre diu consuetudinem: illi vero τυεχνικώτερον Kadmeis a Gephyra pro mancipiis abusi sunt, dignitatē vero scientiæ & gloriam Academiarum sibi refervarunt. Sic injuriam fecerunt Iones & Bæoti Cadméis semel; Athenienses eisdem semper, dum stetit ipsorum Respub. Anhoc fortasse nomine Athenienses ingeniis Bæotis illuserint, & aures Bæoticãs proverbio salso vellicaverint? Qua proter Romani jure optimo (quorum majores a Phœnicibus humana studia & politiores literas acceperant) Phœnicas suos ϖεφόνες quodammodo vindicaverunt, & celebre illud nomen Academiæ, opus, & gloriam ad posteros Phœnicum ab hostibus, id est, a Græcis ad gentem suam transtulerunt. Atq; hoc pacto id confequuṫū est, quod poëta Claudianus scribit in Panegyrico de Manlii Theodori consulatu,
units.tr: Other nations showed a notable ignorance. Lacking knowledge of ancient history and unskilled in foreign languages, they in a sense yielded to the Athenians what had come to the Athenians before it came to them. For why would the Ionians or Boeotians not have claimed an equal praise for themselves? They preferred to expel the Cadmeans and the Academies from their territories rather than long endure foreigners among them. More cleverly, they treated the Cadmeans as slaves from Gephyra, but kept the dignity of learning and the glory of the Academies for themselves. Thus the Ionians and Boeotians did injury to the Cadmeans once; the Athenians did it always, as long as their commonwealth stood. Perhaps it was on this account that the Athenians mocked the Boeotian talents and plucked at Boeotian ears with a salty proverb? Therefore the Romans, with the best right (their forefathers had received human learning and more refined letters from the Phoenicians), in a sense claimed their Phoenicians for themselves. They transferred the famous name of the Academy, with its work and glory, from the Phoenicians' enemies, that is the Greeks, to their own nation for posterity. In this way there was achieved what the poet Claudian writes in his Panegyric on the consulship of Manlius Theodorus:

units.la: In Latium spretis Academia migrat Athenis.
units.tr: "Athens being despised, the Academy migrates into Latium."

units.la: Cùm igitur Academia commune fit omnium conventuum vel collegiorum nomen, quæ institui ad rem literariam & haberi solent: ad ejusmodi autem aliquod συνμα omni tempore certa loca fuerint disposita apud omneis omnes gentes: age, expediamus paucis quæ de locorum illorum appellationibus dicia a nobis videntur oportere. Quamquam non est consilii nostri, ut omnes in hunc locum omniúmve gentium appellationes accumulemus pariter; quod nemo homo præstare posset pro linguarum & gentium varietate ac multitudine: sed eas tantummodò quæ ab Hebræis ad Phœnicas & Ægyptios, ab iis ad Græcos, hinc ad Romanos & nostros homines transfiverunt.
units.tr: Since "academy" has become the common name of all the assemblies or colleges that are set up and usually kept for literary purposes, and since for such a society certain places have at all times been set apart among all peoples, let us now briefly set out what seems to me must be said about the names of those places. Yet it is not my purpose to gather together all the names of that kind of place from every people, which no one could do given the variety and number of languages and nations. I will deal only with those names that passed from the Hebrews to the Phoenicians and Egyptians, from them to the Greeks, and from there to the Romans and to our own people.

units.la: Animadverti quatuor esse capita, ex quibus nomina Academiarum fermè deducta sunt: personas, officia, loca, & adjuncta. Ac mihi quidem videntur autores Græci cùm exterarum linguarum & priscæ historiæ ignoratione, tum religionis injiciendæ & conciliandæ authoritatis studio, nomina quàm plurima ad fictos illos antiquitatis Deos retulisse, & collegiis quasi singulis singulos præfecisse. Nam Athenienses & Bœoti summis collegiis suis, puta Academiæ Minervam, Lycéo Apollinem, Cynosargei Herculem Tutanum sive Tutelinum præsidémque assignabant. Sed quia hoc loco potiùs historiæ veritatem quàm mendaciorum infinitatem (quibus abundauerunt Græci) cupimus expositam; dabimus operam, ut de vero & genuino appellationum ortu dicamus solùm: illorum verò mendacia, si forte, cursim uno aut altero verbo, data occasione, perstringemus.
units.tr: I have noticed that the names of academies are derived mainly from four heads: persons, offices, places, and attributes. It seems to me that the Greek authors, partly through ignorance of foreign languages and ancient history, and partly from a desire to impose religion and win authority, referred very many names to those fictitious gods of antiquity and set a god over each college as if over each one separately. For the Athenians and Boeotians assigned Minerva as the patron and guardian of the Academy, Apollo to the Lyceum, and Hercules Tutanus, or Tutelinus, to the Cynosarges. But since in this place we want to set out the truth of history rather than the endless mass of lies with which the Greeks abounded, we will take care to tell only of the true and genuine origin of the names; their falsehoods we will touch on briefly, with a word or two, if the occasion arises.

units.la: A personis ergo nomina bifariam deducuntur: alia enim sunt ab autoribus, alia ab affectis ibi agentibus. Ab autoribus (quorum plerosque fecerunt Deos antiqui propter egregia ipsorum merita, ut ait Tullius) dicuntur Academia, Cadmea Thebis, gymnasium Ptolemæi ad forum, gymnasium Adriani Cæsaris Athenis, ut refert Pausanias: itemque (ut gětibus olim visum est) Athenæum,
units.tr: So names are derived from persons in two ways: some come from founders, others from those who work there. From founders (many of whom the ancients made gods because of their outstanding merits, as Tully says) come the names Academy, Cadmea at Thebes, the gymnasium of Ptolemy at the forum, and the gymnasium of the Emperor Hadrian at Athens, as Pausanias reports; likewise the Athenaeum, as the peoples once thought fit,

units.la: B
units.tr: B

units.la: Apollónium, Heracleum, Hermeum sive Hermium, Museum, quod inepte Musæum pleriq; scribunt, & quæcunque a singulari suo autore ἀληθῶς ἢ δοξαστικῶς obtinuerunt nomen, prout ubique ferè memoria nostra observatur. Sed hæc infinita sunt, neque a nobis opus est percenseri. A personis verò ibi agentibus denominata sunt Cœnobium, Collegium, domus Prophetarum, Lyceum, Mandra, Synagoga, & siqua sunt huiusmodi: quorum alia in rebus sacris tantum modo & Ecclesiastica historia, alia in omnibus promiscuè vsurpantur. Ab officiis & functionibus orta sunt hæc nomina, Ascetérium, Athenæum, Apollónium, Cynosarges, Diátriba, Didascalium, Domus vel locus doctrinæ, Heracleum, Hermeum vel Hermium, Ludus, Μελετητήριον, Museum, phrontistérium, Schola, studium, & cætera id genus.
units.tr: Apollonium, Heracleum, Hermeum or Hermium, Museum, which many write wrongly as Musaeum, and whatever names have been obtained from a single founder, either truly or by supposition, as is almost everywhere observed in our own memory. But these are endless and there is no need for us to list them. From the persons who work there are named the cenobium, collegium, house of the prophets, lyceum, mandra, synagogue, and any others of this sort. Some of these are used only in sacred matters and in ecclesiastical history, while others are used promiscuously in every context. From offices and functions come these names: asceterium, athenaeum, apollonium, cynosarges, diatriba, didascalium, house or place of teaching, heracleum, hermeum or hermium, ludus, meletēterion, museum, phrontisterium, school, study, and others of that kind.

units.la: A loco item, Gibhá sive Gabaá, id est, collis, Labrathá sive Lebrathán, Monastérium, Peripatos, Stoa, & siqua sunt præterea ad genus istud pertinentia.
units.tr: Likewise from place come gibha, or gabaa, that is hill; labratha or lebrathan; monasterium; peripatos; stoa; and whatever else belongs to that class.

units.la: Ab adjunctis denique dicta fuerunt olim Amalthea sive Amaltheum, Gymnasium, Xystus, & quæcunq; forte de signis idolorum suorum denominationem apud cæcos idololatras habuerūt olim. Hæc autem singula, quia non omnia omnibus satis perspecta sunt, ordine eodem ac modo adducta sunt, deinceps explicabimus.
units.tr: Finally, from attributes were formerly named the Amalthea, or Amaltheum, the gymnasium, the xystus, and whatever names the blind idolaters once gave them from the images of their idols. These individual items, since not all are sufficiently well known to everyone, have been brought forward in this order and manner, and we will explain them in turn.

units.la: Ἀκαδημία, sive (ut olim) Ἀκαδήμεια Græcis, Latinis Academia vel Academia, aut etiam tenuiore sono Ἀκαδημία, antiquissima Atheniensium schola, a Kadmo Agenoris filio, vel potiùs Kadméis autoribus fuit appellata, qui a Bæotis Tanagra, Gephyra, Thebis, Helycone expulsi, aliisque sedibus, Athenas commigraverant: ut antè ex Herodoto confirmavimus. Nam veterum sententiam, quòd ab Academo vel Hecademo fuerit constituta, superiore capite explosimus. Attica autem hæc appellatio Academiæ rectè ad alia quævis gymnasia commeavit, quæ literarum & studiorum causa publicè aut privatim fuerunt comparata. Hujusmodi fuit Arpinas illa, & Tusculana, & tertia illa Ciceronis inter Avernum lacum Puteolosque sita, olim percelebris: ut refert Plinius libro 31. naturalis historiæ, capite 2. etsi Tusculanam plurimùm donavit Lycei nomine Ἀλσκεφῖλ. Athenæû, Apollónium, Heracleum, Hermeum, Museum, & siqua sunt ejusmodi omnia hæc vetustas impia & insscia veri adscripsit Deorum suorum nominibus, ut quæ veritatem religiosæ fidei & historiæ gestæ pariter ignoraret. Sed hæc omnia sequentibus locis commodiùs exponentur. De singularibus autem gymnasiis (ut antè diximus) hoc loco tacebimus, quia nec prodest, nec potest fieri ut pervestigentur & conscribantur singula.
units.tr: Akadēmia [Ἀκαδημία], or formerly Akadēmeia [Ἀκαδήμεια], is what the Greeks call it; the Latins call it Academia or Academia, or even with a thinner sound Akademia. It was the most ancient school of the Athenians, named after Cadmus, son of Agenor, or rather after the Cadmean authors, who had been driven out by the Boeotians from Tanagra, Gephyra, Thebes, and Helicon, and from other seats, and had migrated to Athens, as we confirmed earlier from Herodotus. For we have already refuted the opinion of the ancients that it was founded by Academus or Hecademus in the preceding chapter. This Attic name of Academy has rightly passed to any other gymnasium that was set up at public or private expense for the sake of letters and studies. Of this kind was that Arpinate one, and the Tusculan, and that third one of Cicero's, placed between Lake Avernus and Puteoli, once very famous, as Pliny reports in book 31 of his Natural History, chapter 2, although he gave the Tusculan one largely the name of Lyceum. All of these, the Athenaeum, Apollonium, Heracleum, Hermeum, Museum, and any others of this kind, ancient impiety, ignorant of the truth, ascribed to the names of its gods, as it was ignorant alike of the truth of the religious faith and of recorded history. But all of these will be set out more conveniently in the following places. Concerning the individual gymnasia, as we said before, we will remain silent here, because it is neither useful nor possible to investigate and describe each one.

units.la: Cadmëa sive Cadmía, Καδμεία, olim urbs Thebarum dicta, Strabone teste, & arx quoq; Thebarum fuit appellata, ut autor est Plutarchus in Pelopida. Gymnasiũ verò cùm apud Thebanos, tum apud Bœotos reliquos Καδμεία, Cadméa, fuit appellatũ a Cadmo, sive Cadméis autorib.
units.tr: Kadmea or Kadmia [Καδμεία], formerly called the city of Thebes, according to Strabo, and also called the citadel of Thebes, as Plutarch states in his Life of Pelopidas. But the gymnasium, both among the Thebans and among the other Boeotians, was called Kadmeia, Cadmea, from Cadmus, or from the Cadmean authors.

units.la: Quæ autem nomina a personis in literarum studia incubentibus fuerūt imposita, ea se habent in hūc modum.
units.tr: The names that were imposed from the persons who devoted themselves to the study of letters are as follows.

units.la: Cœnobium κοινόβιον, locum, vbi communis quædam vita agitur ad sacrationem studiorum commoditatem & ad bonos mores, pia vetustas appellavit, ex quo in prisca Ecclesia licuit ascetéria pietatis colere, & juventutem in rebus sacris informare. Hinc Cœnobiarchæ. Hodie servatur nomen.
units.tr: Coenobium [κοινόβιον]: the pious antiquity called a place where a common life is led, for the sake of consecrating studies, for convenience, and for good morals, a coenobium. From this it was permitted in the early Church to cultivate asceteria of piety and to form young people in sacred matters. Hence the coenobiarchs. The name is still kept today.

units.la: Collegium proprie quidem societas vel cœtus eorum est qui ad rem, functionem, militiámve aliquam (ut lurecos.vocant) simul allegantur: non enim a legendo, sed a legando,id est, allegando dictum. Metonymice vero locus appellatur, idque κατ' ἐξοχὴν, ubi corpus & societas eorum est qui literarum studiis operam daturi sunt. Hic quoque in prisca Ecclesia Christi fuit usus olim: cujus rei vestigium non sane obscurum est in vulgo, quòd hac etiam memoria nostra quædam in Pontificiis Ecclesiæ collegiatæ nominantur.
units.tr: A collegium, properly speaking, is a society or body of those who are summoned together for some business, office or military service (as the jurists say). It is not named from legere (to read) but from legare, that is, from allegare (to send for). By metonymy, however, the word is also used of a place, and in its chief sense it denotes the body and fellowship of those who are going to devote themselves to literary study. This usage also existed in the early Church of Christ. Some trace of it is clearly still visible in the common speech, since in our own time some institutions among the Papists are called collegiate churches.

units.la: Domus vel locus Prophetarum σπηνέων, ἀγγελ​ε​ί​ο​ν, in prisca Iudæorū Ecclesia dicebatur locus ubi divini illi & sancti Prophetæ discipulos, ut patres filios, docebant instituebántque in vera pietate, doctrina fidei, morúmque probitate,& consulentibus respondebant. Nam utrique, Doctores inquam & discipuli ipsorum, Prophetæ dicebantur communi voce: Ἀλλαxε​ί​π​ν​ω​ς vero hi filii Prophetarum,& illi patres,ut Scriptura passim testis est.
units.tr: The house or place of the Prophets was called among the early Jews σπηνέων, ἀγγελεῖον [σπηνέων, ἀγγελεῖον]: the place where those holy and divine prophets taught their disciples, as fathers teach their sons, in true piety, the doctrine of faith and integrity of life, and gave answers to those who consulted them. For both the teachers and their pupils were commonly called prophets, and the pupils were called sons of the prophets [ἀλλαχῶς], and the teachers fathers, as Scripture bears witness in many places.

units.la: Lycéum,sive Lycium (ut Spartianus vocat in Adriano Cæsare) Λύκειον, Græci vindicant sibi fabulosissimè. Hoc enim deducunt alii a Lycio Pandionis filio, ut Pausanias:alii ab Apolline Lycéi præsidé (ut ante oftedimus) qui dictus est a Græcis Lycius: alii a lupo sacro Apollini, cujus signum in Lycéo fuit:alii ἀπὸ τῆς Λύκης, a luce, sive propter doctrinæ lucem quam inde percipiebat studiosi, sive quòd clarior esset locus,& plus haberet lucis umbræque minus quàm Academia, cujus ambulationes umbrosas Eupolis appellauit. Fabulæ. Hebræum nomen est lahakà 1.Sam.19.20. coetum atque conventu significans: & per syncopen Hebraeis frequentatam laka, ut sunt Babat, bat, laat, vel labat, lat, similiáque multa. Hinc ergo Phœnices duxerunt scholasticorum conventuum suorum appellationem: a quibus regiones illas Ioniæ quas incoluerunt primùm, Lyciam & Lycaoniam, gymnasiis ipsorum exornatas, fluuiúmque Lycum dixerunt. rúnt, quòd fecundùm eum gymnasia operâ ipsorum fuerint instituta in minore Asia : itémque in Ægypto Lycaópolin fiue Lycópolin:Nomónq, Lycopolitén,&c.deinde verò in Boeotia Helyconem motem Mufarũ, quivulgo Helicon (vt capite 1.docuimus) & fexcenta alia. Exhoc autem fonte manavit Graecorum Latinorumq;, λέγω, πl συλλέγω, & nomen λόγ, συλλογὴ, qua homines λογάδλω, id est,turmatim vel manipulatim congregantur, & λογέιον, ὁ πσὰρ συλλογὴς, &c. forteetiam Latinorum lucus: quod ego quidem putauerim. Atque ex hac significatione Αυκείου vel λογείου, aut etiam(fi ita placet)συλλογὴς, hæc opidorum nomina profecta sunt : Lucotecia Parifiorum, quæ per syncopen Lutecia póstdiéta:& Lucodunum, in priscis lapidibus Lugodunum vel Lugudunum,vulgo Lucdunum fiue Lugdunum, olim etiam Lugodinium corrupta voce (nam dunum apud veteres significabat molem,vt doctissimus Turnebus doctè mernet in Adversariis)quasi dicas molem conventui hominum recipiendo & continendo accomodam. Hoc autem nomine appellantur, primùm quidem emporium illud celebre quòd nomen dedit Lugdunensi Gallic,tum alterum Germaniæ magnæ non procul a fluuio qui Albis dicitur, itemque nobile illud hoc tempore Batavorum Lyceum quod Leydam vocant,praeterea quæ illud Aquitanicum ad Pyrenæos saltus,cujus in conventu fuerunt populi Convenæ ex causa illa quam modò diximus appellati, & in opidum contributi, vt Plinius autor est libro 4. natur. hiftor. cap.19. quo ex loco (vt in transcursu moneam)Ptolemæũ libro 2..Geographicῶν, cap.7.opus est emendari. Nam quod de Lygdo vel Lugdo autore prædicant quidam , id per me fabulis deputetur licet. Quod vero a L.Munatio Plaço alii princeps illud GalliæLugdunensis opidum dictum volunt, Strabonis auctoritate & narratione ita convellitur, vt qui hoc sentiùt autorem illum gravem non legisse, aut certe parum meminisse videantur. Fuit autem Lyceum vel Lycium Athenis quidem gymnasium Aristotelis & Peripateticorum, ex quo discesserunt ab Academia. Sed proprie tamen atque universè (ut justa vocis notatio postulat) gymnasium significat habendo coetui & colendis studiis accommodum. Ac propterea non inepte Tullius gymnasium a se in Tusculano suo constitutum donavit Lycei nomine, libro 1. de divinatione: & constitutæ ad hanc rem scholæ eleganter eodem nomine ornari possunt. Mandra μανδρα, ex Hebraeo ductum nomen apud Phoenicas Ægyptiosq; habet epenthesin literæ n. Temporariam quamvis habitationem significat, vel commorationis locum. Qui autem ex Græco ducunt, spelunçam aut spæcum interpretantur, quo se ab imbre & procellis pecudes solent recipere: & in Ecclesia illa vetere sic dictam fuisse putant eorum habitationem, qui & contemplationis studio & mundi istius tædio religiosam vitam vivebant solitariè. Omnino mandra propria notatione sua est communis habitatio quædam, id est (quod ante diximus) coenobium. Quod autem Græci de pecore dixerunt, id quoque Phoenicibus & Cadmeis debent. Atque hinc passim Αρχιμανδρίτης, Archimandrita, in historia Ecclesiastica nominantur οἱ τῶν μοναςηρίων καὶ μανδρῶν πρωτοςῶτες: quorum Iustinianus Imperator meminit 1.7.C. de summa Trinitate & fide catholica.
units.tr: The Lyceum, or Lycium (as Spartianus calls it in his life of Hadrian), the Greeks claim for themselves [Λύκειον] in a very fabulous way. Some derive the name from Lycus, son of Pandion, as Pausanias does; others from Apollo, the patron of the Lyceum (as I showed earlier), who was called Lycius by the Greeks; others from the wolf sacred to Apollo, whose image stood in the Lyceum; others from light [ἀπὸ τῆς Λύκης], either because of the light of learning that students received there, or because the place was brighter and had less shade than the Academy, whose shady walks Eupolis called… Fables. The Hebrew word is lahaka [לַהֲקָה] (1 Sam. 19:20), meaning a company or assembly; and by the contraction common among the Hebrews it becomes laka, as in Babat, bat, laat or labat, lat, and many similar forms. From this the Phoenicians took the name for their scholarly assemblies; and from these the regions of Ionia which they first inhabited, Lycia and Lycaonia, adorned with their gymnasia, and the river Lycus, received their names. For according to this view the gymnasia were founded by their labour in Asia Minor; and likewise in Egypt Lycaopolis or Lycopolis, and the Lycopolite nome, and so on; then in Boeotia Helicon, the mountain of the Muses, which is commonly called Helicon (as we showed in chapter 1), and countless other names. From this same source flowed the Greek and Latin λέγω, συλλέγω [to gather], and the noun λόγος, συλλογή [collection], by which men are gathered in troops or bands, and λογεῖον, the place for gathering, and so on; and perhaps also the Latin lucus, which I for my part would think likely. From this meaning of Αὐκεῖον or λογεῖον, or even (if you like) συλλογή, the names of these towns derive: Lucotecia of the Parisii, later shortened by contraction to Lutecia; and Lucodunum, in old inscriptions Lugodunum or Lugudunum, commonly Lucdunum or Lugdunum, and once, by a corrupted form, Lugodinium (for dunum among the ancients signified a mass or heap, as the very learned Turnebus rightly observes in his Adversaria), as if you were to say a mass fit for receiving and holding a gathering of people. This name is given first to that famous trading town which gave its name to Gallia Lugdunensis; then to another in Great Germany, not far from the river called the Elbe; likewise to that noble Lyceum of the Batavians, now called Leiden; and besides these, to the town in Aquitaine at the passes of the Pyrenees, whose inhabitants, the Convenae, were so called for the reason just given and were gathered into one town, as Pliny attests in book 4 of his Natural History, chapter 19. In passing I would note that Ptolemy, Geography book 2, chapter 7, needs correction on this point. As for the claim of some that the name comes from an author called Lygdus or Lugdus, let it be counted as a fable so far as I am concerned. But the view of others that the town of Gallia Lugdunensis was named after L. Munatius Plancus, the first ruler, is refuted by the authority and account of Strabo, so that those who hold it seem either not to have read that grave author or certainly to have remembered him poorly. The Lyceum or Lycium at Athens was the gymnasium of Aristotle and the Peripatetics, from which they separated from the Academy. Yet properly and generally (as the strict meaning of the word requires) it signifies a gymnasium suited for holding an assembly and for cultivating studies. Accordingly Tully did not inappropriately name the gymnasium he founded at his Tusculan villa with the name of Lyceum (book 1, On Divination), and schools established for this purpose may elegantly be adorned with the same name.

units.la: Synagogam, συναγωγὴ, quam Hebraei (Cenesith) vocant, significare locum non solum coetibus Ecclesiasticis, verumetiam scholasticis habedis apud Iudaeos olim destinatum, magis notum est quàm ut resegeat explicatione: & ita non obscurè accepit Lucas Act.6.9. Templis enim concionalibus, id est, σχολαστηρίοις scholæ plurimùm erant iunctæ: ut post in vocem Gabaa dicturi sumus.
units.tr: The word mandra [μάνδρα], derived from the Hebrew and used among the Phoenicians and Egyptians, has an epenthetic n. Although it signifies a temporary dwelling, or a place of sojourn, those who derive it from Greek explain it as a cave or den, to which flocks are accustomed to retreat from rain and storms; and they think that in that ancient Church the dwellings of those were so called who lived a religious life in solitude, devoted to contemplation and weary of this world. In its proper sense, however, mandra is simply a common dwelling, that is (as we said before) a coenobium. What the Greeks said of a flock they owe also to the Phoenicians and Cadmeans. Hence the Archimandrite [Ἀρχιμανδρίτης] is often named in ecclesiastical history as those who are first among the monasteries and folds [οἱ τῶν μοναστηρίων καὶ μανδρῶν πρωτεύοντες]; the Emperor Justinian mentions them in 1.7 C., On the Most Holy Trinity and the Catholic Faith.

units.la: Atque hæc de nominibus quæ a personis instituentibus ducta sunt, aut de causa eorum qui ad literarum studia eódem conveniunt, fuerunt imposita. Sequuntur quæ ab officiis.
units.tr: These are the names given to places from the persons who founded them or from the purpose of those who gather there for the study of letters. Next come those named from their duties.

units.la: Ascetérium, ἀσκητήριον, Græca origine in prisca Ecclefia gymnasium sacrum vocabatur, in quo ascéte aut ascétriæ, id est, viri aut fœminæ se in meditatione rerum sacrarum & officiorum exercitatione occupabant, ut postea aliquo habitu ad eam rem comparato, quum probati essent & idonei judicati, functionem justam susciperent in Ecclesiis, scholis, aut dochiis Christi. Sic appellant Leo & Anthemius Cæsares in l. omnia 35. C. de episcopis & clericis.
units.tr: Asketerium [ἀσκητήριον], a word of Greek origin, was in the ancient Church called a sacred gymnasium. There men and women, called ascetics, occupied themselves with meditation on sacred things and the practice of their duties. Later, once they had been equipped for the task with a certain dress, and had been tested and judged fit, they undertook proper office in the churches, schools, or teaching places of Christ. Leo and Anthemius, the emperors, so call them in law 35, C. de episcopis et clericis.

units.la: Athenæum, ἀθήναιον, olim dicebatur locus gymnasiumque publicum, ubi rhetores & poetæ exercebantur palám. Sic Lampridius in Alexandro Severo, Ad Athenæum, inquit, audiendorum & Græcorum & Latinorum Rhetorum vel Poetarum causa frequenter processit. Hoc autem abrara Αθήναις, id est, Palladis plerique omnes putant appellatum: qualis fuit Lugduni olim ad Rhodanum, ut Iuvenalis Satyra 1. testis est his versibus: Palleat, ut nudá pressit qui calcibus anguem, Aut Lugdunensem Rhetor dicturus ad aram.
units.tr: Athenaeum [ἀθήναιον] was formerly the name of a public place and gymnasium where rhetoricians and poets practised openly. Lampridius, in his life of Alexander Severus, says: He often went to the Athenaeum to hear both Greek and Latin rhetoricians or poets. Most people think it was so named from Athens [Αθήναις], that is, from Pallas. There was such a place at Lyons on the Rhône of old, as Juvenal attests in Satire 1 in these verses: "Let him turn pale who, barefoot, trod on a naked snake, or the rhetorician who is about to speak at the altar of Lyons."

units.la: Erat enim gymnasium eo in loco celebre, ut innuit Strabo, ad confluentem Rhodani & Araris: cuius rei hodie documentum superest, puta cœnobii quod in eo tractu situm est vernacula appellatio. Verum (quod bona veterum pace dictum velim, qui exoticas literas nesciverunt) neque Athenarum, neque Aθηνᾶς, id est, decus ipsius Palladis partus est Athenæum, fiad summum & verum illius ortum respexeris: sed Phœnicia est appellatio, perinde significans ac si doctorum vel doctrinæ locum, doctrinæve celebrem appellaveris. Phœnices enim & Syri doctrinam a tradendo nominant quasi παράδοσιν, disciplinam vero a percipiendo quasi παραλημμένην, quia doctrina a magistris & præceptoribus traditur, & disciplina ab audientibus percipitur: doctum vero hominem appellant Thanai vel Thani. Atque ex eo Aθηνᾶ docta Minerva & doctrinæ dea; Aθηνᾶ, vrbs Athena quas doctas Ovidius vocat, unde humanitas, doctrina, religio, fruges, jura, leges orta, atque in omnes terras distributa putantur, ut ait Tullius: Athenæum doctrinæ, doctorumque hominum doctrinam suam fideliter tradentium locus, & literarum sedes: Ἀνταῖοι deniq; κατὰ μετάδοσιν & Athenopolites Ægypti nomos, & compositum Tanagra, quod capite 1. expositum. Apollonii, ἀπολλώνιον dixerunt alii quod Athenienses Lyceum: id quidem ab Apolline (ut Græcorum vanitas argutabatur olim) sed longe alio respectu quam putabant illi. Nam ut Græci Λοξίαν, ita Phœnices Apollinem a caligine & obscuritate dixerunt respondentium ejus: quæ adeo flexiloqua erant & obscura, inquit Tullius, ut interpres egeat interprete. Apollonium vero gymnasium non tam ab Apolline (ut putatur) dictum est, quam a rerum obscurarum & quæ in vulgo nesciuntur declaratione. Id enim proprium virorum est literatorum munus, & gymnasiorum ornamentum: ex quo opida quam plurima variis in regionibus confequuta sunt Apolloniæ nomen, & in Thebaide Ægypti fuit Apollopolis vel Apollinis civitas, & abea Nomos Apollopolites apud Plinium lib. 5. natur. hist. cap. 9.
units.tr: The athenaeum [ἀθήναιον] was once the name for a public place and gymnasium where rhetoricians and poets practised openly. So Lampridius, in his life of Alexander Severus: He often went forth to the Athenaeum, he says, for the purpose of hearing both Greek and Latin rhetoricians or poets. Most people think this word was named from Athens, that is, from Pallas; such a place was once at Lugdunum on the Rhone, as Juvenal's first satire attests in these lines: Let him turn pale who pressed a naked snake with his heels, or the rhetorician who is about to speak at the altar of Lugdunum. For there was a famous gymnasium at that spot, at the meeting of the Rhone and the Arar, as Strabo indicates; and today the vernacular name of a monastery situated in that district still bears witness to it. But (and I would say this with due respect to the ancients, who did not know foreign letters) the Athenaeum is not named from Athens or from Athena, that is, from the glory of Pallas herself, if you look to its highest and true origin. It is a Phoenician name, meaning just as much as if you had called it the place of learned men or of celebrated learning. For the Phoenicians and Syrians name teaching from handing down, as if paradosis, and discipline from receiving, as if paralēmmenē, because teaching is handed down by masters and teachers, and discipline is received by hearers; and they call a learned man Thanai or Thani. From this comes Athēnā, learned Minerva and the goddess of learning; Athēna, the city of Athens, which Ovid calls learned; whence, as Tully says, humanity, learning, religion, crops, rights and laws are thought to have arisen and to have been spread into all lands. The Athenaeum is the place of learning, of learned men faithfully handing down their learning, and the seat of letters. Finally, the Antaioi through exchange [κατὰ μετάδοσιν], the Athenopolite nome of Egypt, and the compound Tanagra, which was explained in chapter 1. Others have called it the Apollonium [ἀπολλώνιον], because the Athenians had a Lyceum; and this is named from Apollo (as the vanity of the Greeks used once to argue), but with a much different reference from what they supposed. For just as the Greeks called him Loxias, so the Phoenicians called Apollo by a name meaning the one who answers from darkness and obscurity; and his responses were so ambiguous and obscure, says Tully, that the interpreter himself needed an interpreter. The gymnasium of Apollo is named not so much from Apollo (as is supposed) as from the explanation of obscure things and of things unknown to the common people. For this is the proper duty of learned men and the ornament of gymnasia; and from it very many towns in various regions have taken the name Apollonia; and in the Thebaid of Egypt there was Apollopolis, or the city of Apollo, and from it the Apollopolite nome, according to Pliny, Natural History book 5, chapter 9.

units.la: Cynosarges,κυνόσαργες, gymnasium olim Atheniensium fuit proxime urbē, ubi maximè docuit Cynicorum natio, Herculi sacrum (vt μυθολόγοις placet) dictum à cane albo, qui sacrificium quoddam Herculi oblatum eripuerat. Scilicet ante illud tempus locus sacer fuit, sed carebat nomine. Germanæ gerræ. Imò vero Cynosarges Phœnicium nomen est à Kadmeis (ut alia) inditū, quod in eo loco iuventus eruditione & institutione augeretur, quasi prælucente face. Nam Chinnúk farég apud Syros nihil sibi vult aliud quàm ordinare institutionem, & doctrinam ordine certo tradere: quod nomen cui loco melius, obsecro, quàm gymnasiis literariis aptari potest? Atque hinc illa quoque gymnasiorum & civitatum nomina de quibus capite primo, Cynon, Cynospolis vel Cynopolis, & siqua sunt eiusmodi: quorum ortum ignorantes Græci & alii sequuti Græcos Circæo poculo suo ex eruditis hominibus fecerunt canes: & eruditionis locum (indignum facto) in maledictionis formulam transmutarunt vulgato proverbio, ἐς κυνός Capyrς.
units.tr: Cynosarges [κυνόσαργες], once a gymnasium of the Athenians close to the city, where the Cynic school mostly taught, was sacred to Hercules (as the mythologists like to say) and named after a white dog which had snatched away a sacrifice offered to Hercules. Clearly the place was sacred before that time but had no name. German nonsense! Rather, Cynosarges is a Phoenician name, given by the Cadmeans as were other names, because in that place young people were improved by learning and instruction, as if guided by a leading torch. For Chinnúk farég among the Syrians means nothing other than to set out instruction and to teach doctrine in a fixed order. What name, I ask you, could suit a literary school better? Hence also the names of gymnasia and cities discussed in the first chapter, Cynon, Cynospolis or Cynopolis, and any others of that kind. The Greeks, and others who followed the Greeks, ignorant of their origin, used their Circean cup to turn learned men into dogs, and turned a place of learning (an insult to its purpose) into a formula of abuse by the common proverb [ἐς κυνός], "to the dogs."

units.la: Diátriba, διατριβή, locus exercitationum disputationumque dicitur, ex sermone Græco.
units.tr: Diatriba [διατριβή] is the term, from the Greek language, for a place of exercises and disputations.

units.la: Didascalium item, διδασκαλεῖον, doctrinæ exponendæ & tradendæ locus.
units.tr: Likewise didascalium [διδασκαλεῖον], a place for expounding and imparting teaching.

units.la: Domus explicationis & declarationis, Beth-gelja: domus doctrinæ vel eruditionis, Beth-ulphana: domus perquisitionis seu pervestigationis, Beth-midras seu medrás apud Syros dicitur, à justo scholarum vel gymnasiorum usu. Hinc Bargilia locus Ioniæ Syræ appellatus, quasi agrū vel campum declarationis dicas in Caria non procul Iaffo, quam Bargylam Plinius, Mela Bargylon scribit, Ptolemæus Bargylliam: item ἀλφάσις apud Græcos disciplina morum dicta, & conjugata quàm plurima. Heraclêum, ἡρακλεῖον, ab Hercule Libyco dictum volunt, de quo ante capite 1. pauca. Nos verò fontem huius appellationis paulo post dicturi sumus.
units.tr: The house of explanation and declaration is Beth-gelja; the house of teaching or learning is Beth-ulphana; the house of inquiry or investigation is Beth-midras, or among the Syrians medrás, from the proper use of schools or gymnasia. Hence Bargilia, a place in Syrian Ionia, as if you were to call it a field or plain of declaration, in Caria not far from Iasos; Pliny calls it Bargyla, Mela Bargylon, and Ptolemy Bargyllia. Likewise ἀλφάσις [alphasis], called among the Greeks the discipline of morals, and very many related words. They say Heracleum [ἡρακλεῖον] is named after the Libyan Hercules, about whom we said a little in chapter 1. But we shall speak of the source of this name a little later.

units.la: Hermæü, ἑρμαῖον, eruditionis locus Mercurio (vt Graeci putaverunt) sacer, dicebatur illis tam privatus quàm publicus: nam hoc quoque nomine in Augustali sive praetorio Cæsaris dictam fuisse legimus apud Tranquillûin Claudio Cæsare. Est autem Hermes Phœnicia origine proprie ἀνὴρ πολυταλαγχθεὶς (ut Homeri utamur voce) varia & multa peregrinatione excultus, peritus, versutus, doctus: attributum Kadmi illius Tyrii, vt ante ostendimus. Ex eo igitur fonte derivatû est Hermaeum, doctorû virorum peritorumq; locus, gymnasium literatorum hominum, ubi res abditæ pervestigâtur, ignotæ docêtur, obscurae declarantur, iterdeniq;, instrumenta, artes, scientiæ, omnia ad sapientiam veram pertinentia proponûtur. Quapropter etiam Hermes sive Mercurius cômune fuit omniû Academiarum & gymnasiorû signum: vnde proverbium, κοινὸς Ἑρμῆς. Cicero Attico, Quod ad me de Hermathena scribis, per mihi gratum. est ornamentū Academia proprium meæ: quòd & Hermes cômune omniû, & Minerva singulare est infigne ejus gymnasii. Hinc autem profectæ sunt plurimæ locorum appellationes simplices & compositæ in Asia minore, Ægypto, Libya, Græciaq;: vt Hermæa, Hermaum, Hermopolis, Hermopolites Nomos, & compositum Hermonthis, indeq; Hermonthites Nomos forma Ægyptia, pro eo quod variores Graeci fuissent dicturi Hermathenaida, & Hernathenaiten Nomon, ex patria sua ἑρμαθηναῖος appellatione.
units.tr: Hermaeum [ἑρμαῖον], a place of learning sacred to Mercury (as the Greeks thought), was called by them both private and public. We also read this name applied to the Augustal or praetorium of Caesar, in Suetonius' Claudius Caesar. Hermes, of Phoenician origin, is properly "a man much tossed about" (to use Homer's word), experienced, crafty, learned, refined by varied and long wandering. He is an attribute of that Tyrian Cadmus, as we showed before. From that source, then, is derived the Hermaeum, a place of learned and skilled men, a gymnasium of literary people, where hidden things are investigated, unknown things taught, obscure things explained, and finally instruments, arts, sciences, and everything pertaining to true wisdom are set forth. Therefore Hermes or Mercury was also the common sign of all academies and gymnasia, whence the proverb "Hermes for all." Cicero writes to Atticus: "As to what you write to me about Hermathena, it pleases me greatly; it is an ornament proper to my Academy, since Hermes is common to all, and Minerva is the special emblem of that gymnasium." From this came very many place names, simple and compound, in Asia Minor, Egypt, Libya and Greece: Hermaea, Hermaum, Hermopolis, the Hermopolite nome, and the compound Hermonthis, and from it the Hermonthite nome in an Egyptian form, where the Greeks would more correctly have said Hermathenaida and the Hermathenaite nome, from their own designation ἑρμαθηναῖος.

units.la: Ludus metonymicè Latinis dicitur pro loco ludi literarii: nâ omnem scholam, inquit Asconius, ludum dixere Romani, quia liberali ingenio ludus est, quû literas, artes, historias, scientiasque discit. Quamobrem eleganter ludum discendi
units.tr: Ludus is used by the Latins, metonymically, for the place of a literary school. For Asconius says that the Romans called every school ludus, because it is a liberal pursuit, since one learns letters, arts, histories and sciences there. Wherefore, elegantly, ludum discendi

units.la: Lib.1.epist. 4.ad Attic. discendi non lusionis Tullius ad Q. Fratrem appellavit.
units.tr: (book 1, letter 4 to Atticus) Tully called it "the sport of learning, not of play," in writing to his brother Quintus.

units.la: Μελετητήριον, Græcum est nota origine, meditationis & exercitationis locus, q. d. meditatorium; ut ascetērium, phrontisterium, & similia.
units.tr: Meletētērion [μελετητήριον] is a Greek word of known origin, meaning a place of meditation and exercise, as if to say "meditatorium," like ascetērium, phrontisterium, and similar words.

units.la: Museūm vel Musiū (ut Spartianus vocat) gymnasiū est, Musarum locus privatus, publicusve, à Musis dictus, ut vana Græcia credidit. At Musæ ipsæ, o Græculi, unde hîc aqua hæret: μωσαι, μυωσαι, μελωδεσαι, ὁμὲσεσαι, inquiunt illi: & quid nō? ager medacii feracissimus omnia affert, præterquā veritatē unam. Hebræū est, Phœniciū est verbum Mus in perscrutandi & pervestigandi significatione. Hæc igitur studia, atq; hi studiorū duces fuerunt olim appellatione hac apud veteres figurati: hæc appellatio prædicat autores suos, quam tamen eo quòd ignota esset, simplex vetustas in deas ignotas stollidè transformavit. Sic Dei nomine luditur, quod alicujus viri nomine facere vix quisquam impunè audeat.
units.tr: Museum, or Musiu (as Spartianus calls it), is a gymnasium, a private or public place of the Muses, named after the Muses, as vain Greece believed. But the Muses themselves, you little Greeks, where does the water stick here? They say mōsai, muōsai, melōdesai, homesesai [μωσαι, μυωσαι, μελωδεσαι, ὁμὲσεσαι], and what not? The field of falsehood yields everything in abundance, except for one truth. It is a Hebrew word, a Phoenician word: Mus, in the sense of searching out and investigating. These studies, and the leaders of these studies, were therefore figuratively designated among the ancients by this name. The name proclaims its authors. But because the name was unknown, simple antiquity foolishly turned it into unknown goddesses. Thus the name of God is mocked, which hardly anyone would dare to mock with the name of a man and go unpunished.

units.la: Phrontistērium, φροντιστήριον, nota satis origine vel notatione vocis, à Socrate primùm nomē habuisse dicitur: cujus discipuli appellabantur φροντισταί, quòd alii officiosè curarēt alios ex humano Socratis instituto. Aptissima sanè gymnasiorū, vt vocant, collegiatorū denominatio.
units.tr: Phrontistērium [φροντιστήριον], whose origin and etymology are well enough known, is said to have first received its name from Socrates. His disciples were called phrontistai [φροντισταί], because they dutifully cared for one another, following Socrates' human method. It is a most apt name for what are called collegiate gymnasia.

units.la: Schola, σχολὴ ἢ σχολεῖον, diatriba, gymnasium, ludus ubi studiorum causa juvenes ab occupationibus cæteris otiantur, nomen est translatitium. Ausonius, --- Grajo schola nomine dicta est, Iussa laborifera tribuantur ut otia Musis.
units.tr: Schola [σχολὴ ἢ σχολεῖον], a place of discussion, a gymnasium, a school where young people are freed from their other occupations for the sake of study, is a transferred name. Ausonius: "It was named schola from the Greek; let the leisure that bears toil be given to the Muses."

units.la: Studium recentiores & homines nostri per insolētem quamidam abusionem dixerunt scholam. Sed ἀλλ᾽ ὅμως.
units.tr: Recent writers and our own people, by a certain unusual abuse of the word, have called a school a studium. But ἀλλ᾽ ὅμως [all' homōs], nevertheless.

units.la: Deinceps consequuntur ea quæ a loco aut situ dicta.
units.tr: Next come those names derived from place or situation.

units.la: Gibhá, sive Gabaá, ut vulgo legitur, item q; Gᴄbah & Gᴀbc Geographis dicta, apud Hebræos & Syros collem significat vel locum editū. Hoc nomine locus olim donabatur in populo Dei qui habendis conuentibus Ecclesiasticis vel scholasticis destinatus esset. In causa fuit hujus appellationis mos ille antiquissimus, quòd plurimùm ad hos conventus eminens sedes in editioribus quibusq; locis eligeretur. Hic autem summum locum templa sive E'xxλnσιασηρια proximū scholæ obtinebāt. Atq; hæc non raro fuit Prophetarū docentium sedes, vt ex Saulis historia 1. Sam. 10. colligitur: ideoq; domus vel locus Prophetarum dicebatur vulgo, quemadmodū suprà ostendimus. Atq; hinc profecta est vetus (vt in transcursu moneamus) illa Gabiorum apud Volscos in finibus Latii appellatio, quos alii dura cōpositione a Galaćto & Bio Siculis fratribus duxerunt nuncupatos. Dionysius Halicarnassæus lib. antiquitat. Rom. 1 de Romulo & Remo loquens ita scri- bit, ἠνίκα ἡ πηςὸν τῷ γάλακτι τροφῆς ἀπηλάγη τὰ παιδία, δοθῆναι πρὸς τῶν τρεφόντων εἰς Γαβίας, πόλιν ἡ μακραὶ ἀπὸ τῆς Παλαιστίνης κατὰ ἐν Ὀλυμπίᾳ, ὡς ἐλλάδα παιδείαν ἐκπαιδευθῆναι, &c. id est, postquā verò infantes a lacte depulsi sunt & cibo lacteo, ab altoribus fuisse traditos ut deducerentur Gabios, civitatem non procul a Palantio sitam, in qua disciplinam Græcam edidicerent. Fuit enim Gabiis Latinorū schola Volscorumq; quam Phœnices Cadmei, & prognati eorum Tyrrheni, Osci, sive Ethrusci statuerūt, nomine imposito de sermone suo.
units.tr: Gibhá, or Gabaá as it is commonly read, also called Gibeah, Gibah or Gabah by the geographers, means in Hebrew and Syriac a hill or raised place. By this name a place in God's people was once designated, set aside for holding ecclesiastical or scholastic assemblies. The cause of this name was that most ancient custom, that a prominent seat was chosen on higher ground for these gatherings. Here the highest place was held by the temples or ekklēsiastēria, next to the school. This was often the seat of the teaching prophets, as is gathered from the history of Saul, 1 Sam. 10. Therefore it was commonly called domus vel locus Prophetarum, "the house or place of the prophets," as we showed above. From this also came the old name (let us note it in passing) of the Gabiorum among the Volsci, on the borders of Latium, whom others, by a harsh compounding, have derived from the Sicilian brothers Galatus and Bius. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in book 1 of the Roman Antiquities, speaking of Romulus and Remus, writes thus: [ἡνίκα δὲ πρὸς τῷ γάλακτι τροφῆς ἀπηλλάγη τὰ παιδία, δοθῆναι πρὸς τῶν τρεφόντων εἰς Γαβίους, πόλιν οὐ πολλὰ ἀπὸ Παλλαντίου κειμένην, ἵνα ἑλληνικὴν παιδείαν ἐκπαιδευθῆναι]: "When the children were weaned from milk and milk food, they were handed over by their foster-parents to be taken to Gabii, a city not far from Palatium, to be educated in Greek learning." For Gabii had a school of the Latins and Volsci, which the Phoenician Cadmeans, and their descendants the Tyrrhenians, Oscans or Etruscans, had founded, giving it a name taken from their own speech.

units.la: Labratha vel Lebrathan, Ægyptiis, Afris, & Armenis (quos Hebræi & vicini Hebræorum Phœnices literas suas docuerunt) est declivis vel acclivis locus, abeo quòd descenditur in profundum dictus. Nam illis verbum Labarà est descendere. Et inde Lubár, Labrà, tota παροικία in declivitate posita & subiecta synagogæ suæ: Labratha, synagoga: Lebrathenum, οἱ ... ως. εἰς μίαν συναγωγὴν παροικοῦντες : Labarum siue Labo- rum vexillum sacrum sive principale: λάβηρ[?], fossa, profunditas: & conjugata pleraque alia, quæ omnia κατὰ [?] literæ l, ex Hebræo derivata sunt. Hic vero opus est, vt obscuram istam atque inauditam hominibus nostris exterarum vocum συζυγίαν exponamus latiùs. A verbo igitur Labara, quod est descendere, dicitur mons Armeniæ Λαβάρ, Lubar. Epiphanius in Scythismo, sub principium sui Panarii, Μετὰ δὲ τὴν καταικλυσμὸν ἀπηρίσεως τῆς Λάρναχος ἡ Νῶε ἐν τῇς ὄρεσι τῆς Ἀρμενίας ἀνὰ μίαν Ἀρμενίαν [?] Καρδυαῖων, ἐν τῷ Λαβὰρ ὄρει καλεμένῳ, σκέσε πρῶτον κατοίκησις γίνεται τῶν ἀνθρώπων, &c. Nicolaus vero Damascenus apud Flavium Iosephum libro i. antiquit. Iudaic. cap.4.ait, ἐν ὑπὲρ τῶν Μιννάδα μέγα ὄρος κατὰ τὴν Ἀρμενίαν Βάρις λεγόμενον, εἰς ὃ πολλὰς συμφυγόντας ἐπὶ ἡ καταικλυσμῷ λόγον ἔχει περίσωσιν. Post diluvium autem, inquit Epiphanius, quum arca Noë consistisset in montibus Ararat, inter Armenios & Cardyeos, monte cui nomen est Lubar: inde primum habitationes hominum fuerunt constitutæ. Nicolaus vero, est supra Minyada, inquit, mons magnus secundùm Armeniam, qui vocatur Barù, in quem fama est confugisse multos tempore diluvii, & servatos esse. Id autem observandum est, illius Lubar, & huius Barin idem esse, si hoc exceperis, quòd prius in principio syllabam habet ψιλόν ex Orientalium & Afrorum usu, posterius purum est & accessione carens. Ex hoc nomine formatum est alterum illud Λαβρά, labrá, id est, tota parœcia atque vicinitas, quæ uno quasi colle aut clivo disterminata est, & ad conventum Ecclesiæ unius pertinet. Idem Epiphanius ἐξ τῶν Ἀρεομαγιτῶν his verbis rem totam explicat: ὅσῳ γὰρ ἐκκλησίαι τῆς καθολικῆς Ἐκκλησίας ἐν Ἀλεξανδρεία, ἵνα ἕνα Ἀρ- χιεπίσκοπον ἐπ' ἐμὲ ἀπὸ ἱδίων ζώντων. Ἀπολαμβάνει εἰς πρὸς-
units.tr: Labratha or Lebrathan, among the Egyptians, Africans and Armenians (whom the Hebrews and their Phoenician neighbours taught their letters), is a sloping or rising place, so called from the descent into a depth. For in their language Labarà means to descend. Hence Lubar, Labrà: the whole parish, set on a slope and below its synagogue. Labratha: a synagogue. Lebrathenum: those [οἱ ... ως] dwelling in one synagogue [εἰς μίαν συναγωγὴν παροικοῦντες]. Labarum or Laborum: the sacred or principal standard. λάβηρ [labēr]: a ditch, a depth. And most of the other related words, all of which are derived from the Hebrew, in the letter l. Here it is necessary to explain more fully this obscure and unheard-of combination of foreign words for our people. From the verb Labara, which means to descend, the mountain of Armenia is called Λαβάρ, Lubar. Epiphanius, in the Scythismus at the beginning of his Panarion: [Μετὰ δὲ τὴν καταικλυσμὸν ... ἐν τῷ Λαβὰρ ὄρει καλουμένῳ, σκηνὴ πρῶτον κατοίκησις γίνεται τῶν ἀνθρώπων], and so on: after the flood, when the ark of Noah had come to rest in the mountains of Armenia, between the Armenians and the Cardyaeans, on the mountain called Lubar, the first habitation of men was established there. Nicolaus of Damascus, in Flavius Josephus, Antiquities book 1, chapter 4, says: [ἐν ὑπὲρ τῶν Μιννάδα μέγα ὄρος κατὰ τὴν Ἀρμενίαν Βάρις λεγόμενον, εἰς ὃ πολλοὺς συμφυγόντας ἐπὶ τοῦ καταικλυσμοῦ λόγος ἔχει περισωθῆναι]: "Above Minyas there is a great mountain in Armenia called Baris, into which, as the story goes, many took refuge at the time of the flood and were saved." Epiphanius says: "After the flood, when the ark of Noah rested in the mountains of Ararat, between the Armenians and the Cardyaeans, on the mountain called Lubar, the first habitation of men was established." Nicolaus says: "Above Minyas is a great mountain in Armenia called Barù, into which, it is said, many fled in the time of the flood and were saved." It must be noted that the Lubar of the former and the Barin of the latter are the same, except that the former has a psilon at the beginning, according to the usage of Orientals and Africans, while the latter is pure and lacks the addition. From this name was formed the other word Λαβρά, labrá, that is, the whole parish and neighbourhood, which is marked off by one hill or slope, as it were, and belongs to the assembly of a single church. Epiphanius himself explains the whole matter in these words, from the Areiomagitae: [ὅσῳ γὰρ ἐκκλησίαι τῆς καθολικῆς Ἐκκλησίας ἐν Ἀλεξανδρείᾳ ... ἕνα Ἀρχιεπίσκοπον ... ἀπὸ ἰδίων ζώντων ... ἀπολαμβάνει εἰς πρὸς-]: "For as many churches of the catholic Church as there are in Alexandria ... one archbishop ... living from their own ... he takes ... to"

units.la: quaecunque Ecclesia, inquit Epiphanius, Alexandriae adcatholicam Ecclesiam pertinent, unifubfunt Archiepiscopo: speciatim vero Presbyteri sive Seniores illis praefecti sunt, propter necessitates Ecclesiasticas habitatorum suam Ecclesiam accolentium, regionumque circumstantium vel paroeciarum, quae voce patria dicuntur Labrae ab iis qui urbem Alexandriam colunt. Ex his autem verbis facile intelligitur, qui fuerit olim Ecclesiarum ordoin amplioribus opidis: nā opida in labras (parochias hodie vocāt) fuisse distributa, singulis labrīs suum Presbyterium, omnibus autem simul Archiepiscopum & Antistitem praefuisse. Tum plerumque in summo labrae istius editissimoque loco fuit labratha, sive Lebrathan de qua hic agitur, id est, synagoga, Ecclesia, locus conventui Ecclesiastico & scholastico dictus: atque hunc in locum familiae contributae (παροικοι, parochi vulgo) appellabantur Lebrathenin, id est, Lebrathēni, qui corrupte (ut fit in migratione exterarum vocum & transplantationibus plurimum) a Graecis dicti sunt Libertini.
units.tr: Whatever churches, says Epiphanius, in Alexandria belong to the catholic Church are subject to one Archbishop; and in particular the presbyters or elders are set over them, on account of the ecclesiastical needs of the inhabitants who dwell around their church and of the surrounding regions or parishes, which in the native tongue are called labrae by those who live in the city of Alexandria. From these words it is easily understood what the order of the churches was formerly in the larger towns. For the towns were divided into labrae (which today they call parishes), each labra having its own presbytery, and over them all together an archbishop and bishop presided. Then, generally, in the highest and most elevated spot of that labra there was the labratha, or Lebrathan, which is the subject here, that is, a synagogue, a church, a place called for ecclesiastical and scholastic assembly. The households gathered into this place (paroeci, commonly parishioners) were called Lebrathenin, that is, Lebrathēni, who, corrupted (as happens much in the migration and transplanting of foreign words), were called Libertini by the Greeks.

units.la: Sic enim illa Lucae verba accipimus, Exorti sunt autem quidam e synagoga quae dicitur Libertinorum tum Cyrenaeorum tum Alexandrinorum, & eorum qui sunt ex Cilicia & Asia, disputantes cum Stephano, &c. Ab eadem origine sunt (ut cursim ea perstringamus quae ad eruditae antiquitatis intelligentiam faciunt) alia σύζυγα vel conjugata praefixum l habentia, aliáque carentia. Habent enim lhaec nomina, Λάζαρος, fossa profunda, & Labarum sive Λάβαρον Sozomeno, vexillum praetorium, principale, sive Augustale, ut antè diximus. Sine l vero ex eodem fonte manantia leguntur ista: βῆρυτος, Beryt sive Berytus, urbs Phoeniciae clarissima, ubi juridicam Academiam instituit Iustinianus Cæsar: Thabor mons Iudææ: Thabrus, qui vulgo Taurus mons, Ciliciam Armeniámque disterminans: & Atabyria, Plinio teste, olim Rhodus dicta. His adde coronidis loco cántabrum, vocem compositam, apud Tertullianum, Minutium, & alios autores classicos: quo nomine significatur stylus, scapus, vel hastile labarorum, id est, signorum pensilium quæ Imperatoribus olim præferebantur, ritu ab Armeniis regibus translato. Hæc enim vexilla ea a cæteris commodè distinguebantur, quòd labara de suo kané, id est, scapo vel hastili deponi poterant ut exemtilia, reliqua autem omnia erant operis continentis: ac propterea ubique vexillis cantabra opponuntur. Tertullianus Apologetico, Suppara illa vexillorum, & cantabrorum flola, crucium sunt. Minutius, Nam & signa ipsa, & cántabra, & vexilla castrorum, quid aliud quàm inaurata crucesfunt & ornata? Sed ad rem.
