units.tr: For so we understand those words of Luke: Certain of the synagogue which is called the synagogue of the Libertines, both of the Cyrenians and the Alexandrians, and of those who are from Cilicia and Asia, disputed with Stephen, etc. From the same origin come (to touch briefly on those things which help the understanding of learned antiquity) other words, syzygies or conjugates, some with a prefixed l and some without. Those with the l are these: Lazarus, a deep ditch; and labarum or Λάβαρον in Sozomen, the principal or imperial praetorian standard, as we said above. Without the l, however, these words flow from the same source: Berytus, Beryt, a most famous city of Phoenicia, where the Emperor Justinian established a school of law; Thabor, a mountain of Judaea; Thabrus, commonly called Mount Taurus, which separates Cilicia from Armenia; and Atabyria, which, according to Pliny, was formerly called Rhodes. To these add, as a crown, cantabrum, a compound word found in Tertullian, Minucius and other classical authors, by which is signified the stem, staff or shaft of the labara, that is, of the hanging standards which were formerly carried before the emperors, a custom transferred from the Armenian kings. For these standards were distinguished well from the others in this way: the labara could be taken down from their kané, that is, their staff or shaft, as detachable parts, whereas all the rest were of one continuous piece of work. Therefore everywhere cantabra are set against vexilla. Tertullian in the Apologeticus: Those trappings of the banners and the fringes of the cantabra are crosses. Minucius: For the very standards, and the cantabra, and the banners of the camp, what else are they than gilded and adorned crosses? But to the matter.

units.la: Monastérium μοναστήριον, Græca appellatione afceterium est vel phrontistérium monachorum, quos μοναχὸς, μοναχὸς, vel μονάζοντας antiquitas nuncupavit, id est, eorum qui solitariam vitam colebant in Ecclesia vetere, ut pietatem semoti a reliquo mundo commodius exercerent, fèque in contemplatione rerum sacrarum occuparent, donec legitimè ad sacras functiones & ministeria apta vocarentur.
units.tr: Monastery, monasterium, from the Greek μοναστήριον, is the name for the dwelling or school of monks, whom antiquity called monachi, μοναχοί, or μονάζοντες, that is, those who lived a solitary life in the ancient Church, so that they might more conveniently exercise piety, withdrawn from the rest of the world, and occupy themselves in the contemplation of sacred things, until they were lawfully called to sacred functions and ministries suited to them.

units.la: Peripatos, περίπατος, Lycei locus ἐγκύκλιος, ut ab Aristotele sæpenumero appellatur, in quo ambulantes solebant agere de rebus philosophicis Peripatetici. Hæc enim ambulatio a rotunda ipsius forma dicta est illis περιπατητικός, aut etiam κύκλος, & ἐγκύκλιοι nimirum πάντα: Latini circum, vel circulum dicunt.
units.tr: Peripatos, περίπατος, was the circular place of the Lyceum, ἐγκύκλιος, as Aristotle often calls it, in which the Peripatetics used to walk and discuss philosophical matters. For that walking was called peripatetic by them from the round shape itself, and also kyklos, and enkyklioi, that is, all-round studies. Latin writers say circum or circulus.

units.la: Stoa, στοά, cognomento ποικίλη dicta, poecile Spartiano, id est, varia, ubi depicti erant fortes illi & præstantes viri qui in pugna Marathonia pro patria occubuerant, gymnasium fuit Zenonis Stoicorúmque, situm ex adverso fermè ipsius Academiæ ad urbem Athenarum. Generatim vero porticum structuramque oblongam significat, qualia plerumque sunt basilicarum & magnificorum operum vestibula, a Stoa illius Atticæ similitudine: ut Ioan.5.2.&10.23.
units.tr: Stoa, στοά, also called by the cognomen poikile, Poecile in Spartianus, that is, varied, where were painted those brave and excellent men who had died for their country in the battle of Marathon, was the gymnasium of Zeno and the Stoics, situated almost opposite the Academy itself, near the city of Athens. In general, however, it signifies a portico and an oblong structure, such as are commonly the vestibules of basilicas and magnificent buildings, named from the resemblance to that Attic stoa, as in John 5.2 and 10.23.

units.la: Restant pauca nomina ex adjunctis attributa.
units.tr: A few names remain, which are given from attached features.

units.la: Amalthea sive Amalthæum ἀμαλθεια, ἀμαλθεῖον, gymnasium Bibliotheca instructissimum & confertissimum, ex origine Hebræa dicitur. Nam vox Almah Hebræis, & Syris significat plenum. Sic vocat Tullius in epistolis ad Atticum.
units.tr: Amalthea or Amalthaeum, ἀμαλθεια, ἀμαλθεῖον, a gymnasium most richly and densely stocked with books, is named from a Hebrew origin. For the Hebrew and Syriac word almah means full. So Tully calls it in his letters to Atticus.

units.la: Gymnásium, γυμνάσιον, proprie nominatur locus in quo nudi athletæ exercebantur, ut vocis notatio indicat: dicitur vero κατ' συνηθεσιν de quolibet exercitationis loco, & και ἐσχολῆ de ludo literario & Academia. Nam huius in accessu erat gymnasium exercendis juvenum corporibus institutum, ne obtorpesceret assidua studiorum μελέτη. Pausanias in Atticis.
units.tr: Gymnasium, γυμνάσιον, properly denotes the place where naked athletes trained, as the etymology of the word shows; but by common usage it is applied to any place of exercise, and by extension to a school of letters and an academy. For at its entrance there was a gymnasium established for exercising the young, lest they grow numb from the constant practice (μελέτη) of studies. Pausanias in the Attica.

units.la: Heraclèum, ἡρακλεῖον, alii ab Hercule Lybico dictum volunt, alii a statua Herculis quæ ante gymnasia solebat poni, ut fortes esse docerentur quicunque ad literarum studia accedebant: nam Hercules apud veteres dictus est μυσταγωγὸς. Sed Hercules unde? Phœnicia est & Punica appellatio, virum peregrinationibus variis cultum significans & versatum, qui orbem terrarum pedibus obierit, multiplicémque sibi peritiam rerum & doctrinam διὰ σοφίας comparaverit, ut de nomine Ἡρα ante dicebamus. Nam ex eo quòd Hebræi virum peditem & vias tentantem explorantémque pedibus appellant Ragli, Phœnices & Pœni duxerunt nomen commune virorum omnium nium Regal vel Regla, quia solus ἀπὸς ἐμπειρίας aptus est, & τὸν ἐμπειρον nuncupauerunt Elragli: & inde ἡεχκλῆς. Atque hinc multæ Heraclea, & Heracleopoles in Asia tota, Ægyto, Græcia, & regionibus aliis, &c. ubi schola ad literarum studia floruerunt. Sed quia omnes putauerunt Herculem ante gymnasia in stadiis asceticisque locis propter robur statui oportere, dedimus illud opinioni vulgi, ut hoc nomen gymnasiorum in numerum eorum conferremus quæ exadjunctis ducta sunt.
units.tr: Heraclaeum, ἡρακλεῖον: some want it named after the Libyan Hercules, others from a statue of Hercules which was customarily placed before the gymnasia, so that whoever came to the study of letters might be taught to be brave; for among the ancients Hercules was called μυσταγωγός. But whence Hercules? Phoenicia and the Punic name denote a man versed and trained through varied travels, who has gone over the globe on foot and acquired manifold skill and learning through wisdom (διὰ σοφίας), as we said before about the name Hera. For from the fact that the Hebrews call a man on foot, who tries and explores the ways on foot, Ragli, the Phoenicians and Carthaginians drew a common name for all such men, Regal or Regla, because he alone is fit from experience (ἀπὸ ἐμπειρίας), and they called the experienced man Elragli; and thence Heracles. And hence many Heraclea and Heracleopolis across all of Asia, Egypt, Greece and other regions, where schools for the study of letters flourished. But since everyone thought Hercules ought to stand before the gymnasia in the stadia and exercise grounds for the sake of strength, we have yielded to the popular opinion, so as to count this name of gymnasia among those derived from accessories.

units.la: Xystus, ξυστὸς, lata porticus & ampla dicebatur, ubi exercebantur athletæ hiberno tempore, gymnasium tectum & quasi παράδοσις vestibulumque Academiæ. Hinc ἀλφὶ συνεκδοχῆς ipsam quoque Academiam nonnulli dixerunt Xystum. Sed hæc de nominibus plus satis.
units.tr: Xystus, ξυστὸς, was called a wide and spacious portico where athletes exercised in winter, a covered gymnasium and, as it were, a kind of vestibule and entrance hall of the Academy. Hence by synecdoche some have called the Academy itself the Xystus. But enough about these names.

units.la: CAPUT TERTIUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER THREE.

units.la: Quæ species Academiarum.
units.tr: What kinds of Academies there are.

units.la: EX tam multis σχολέων gymnasiorumque appellationibus una hoc tempore cæteris anteponitur: & vnum eorum genus est, quod ex communi usu jam sibi vindicat nomen Academiæ, proprio quodam & singulari jure, ut post dicturi sumus. Cum igitur illud ipsum genus quod καθ' ἰδίαν vocatur Academia, justa legitimaque ratione postulet, ut inter se distinguantur gymnasiorum formæ: nunc videndum nobis est, quid sit id in quo Academia aliis antecellit, & quamobrem sibi hoc nomen arroget.
units.tr: Of the many names given to schools and gymnasia, one is now preferred above all the rest, and it belongs to a kind of school that by common usage already claims the name Academy, by a proper and singular right, as we shall say later. Since that very kind, which is called Academy in its own right, requires that the forms of gymnasia be distinguished from one another on a just and lawful basis, we must now consider what it is in which the Academy surpasses the others, and why it claims this name for itself.

units.la: Ac primum quidem ponendum illud est, neque mechanica, neque palæstrica, neque παγγυπῶδη, neque σωματικῆς ἀσκήσεως ullius gymnasia hic a nobis agi: sed ea spectari solum in quibus animus humanus cognitione liberalium disciplinarum informatur, & ad veram pietatis formam,scientiæ,virtutisque ducitur.
units.tr: First of all we must lay down that by gymnasia we here mean neither those of the mechanical arts, nor the palaestra, nor the pancratic or any other gymnasia of bodily training. We are concerned only with those in which the human mind is formed by the study of the liberal disciplines and led to the true form of piety, knowledge and virtue.

units.la: Prima igitur gymnasiorum distinctio a materia ducitur in hunc modum. Gymnasiorum alia sunt quæ dicuntur παϊδαγωγὰ, alia quæ ἐνδεγτηρία: illa minoribus erudiendis instituta, hæc grandioribus & provectioribusætate studióque informandis plenius, ex quo principia in pædagogiis tradita bellè assequuti sunt. In pædagogiis autem duo traduntur potissimum: instrumenta doctrinarum, & principia sive rudimenta. Instrumenta appellamus linguas, artes instrumentales, & ornamenta earum historias. Linguas, Latinam & Græcam, omnis justa instituendi ratio pueris accuratè tradi postulat, & flagitat hæc memoria nostra: Hebræa non perinde ab omnibus desideratur. Desideratur tamen, eáque opus est plurimùm : quod bonum antecedentium seculorum barbaries diu ignoravit, & impendens bellorum clades porrò impeditura ç. , nisi Deus Christianum orbem respexerit misericorditer, & fortia juventutis piæ studia ad hoc officium accenderit, ut rumpatur Satan. Hic enim adversarius salutis nostræ jam fermè nihil tanu molitur, quàm ut in sermone illo suo non audiatur Deus, quo sermone suavissima illa mysteria exoptatissimæ salutis nostræ olim tradita atque perscripta sunt. Artes instrumentales, nimirum Grammaticam verborum ex usu, Logicam veritatis ex ratione, & Rhetoricam communis cultus ad eosdem res ex commoditate adhibendi artifices, necessarias esse qui ignorat, brutus est: suriosus, qui negat. Historias fiqui his cum iudicio & ratione adjungunt, non mediocre juventuti allectamentum ad amorem literarum humaniorum præbent, & sermoni, rationi, cultui denique in pueris confirmando.
units.tr: The first division of gymnasia, taken from their subject matter, runs as follows. Some gymnasia are called elementary schools [παϊδαγωγὰ], others are called higher schools [ἐνδεγτηρία]: the former are established for teaching younger pupils, the latter for forming those who are older and more advanced in age and in study, more fully, so that they may thoroughly master the principles handed down in the elementary schools. In the elementary schools, two things are chiefly taught: the instruments of learning, and the first principles or rudiments. By instruments we mean languages, the instrumental arts, and the histories that serve as their ornaments. Latin and Greek, every sound method of instruction demands that boys be taught thoroughly, and our own age insists on it. Hebrew is not demanded in the same way by everyone, yet it is still demanded, and it is very much needed. The barbarism of earlier centuries long ignored this good thing, and the threatening disasters of war will hinder it further, unless God looks upon the Christian world with mercy and kindles the strong zeal of devout young people for this duty, so that Satan may be broken. For this adversary of our salvation now attempts almost nothing so much as to stop God from being heard in that language in which the most sweet mysteries of our most desired salvation were once handed down and written. That the grammar of words, as practised in usage, logic of truth, as grounded in reason, and rhetoric, as the art of using the same things with fitting ornament, are necessary, only a brute would not know, and only a madman would deny. Those who add histories to these with judgment and reason provide no small inducement for young people to love the humane letters, and they bring great help in strengthening in boys speech, reason, and finally refinement of character.

units.la: {*} Mark on the text is printed; no further notes. mando magnum adferunt adjumentum. Principia five rudimenta duûm sunt generum, quæ in scholis pædagogicis si traduntur, bene est: si non traduntur, omnino tamen vnum eorum adhibeatur necesse est. Prius genus est pietatis, posterius philosophiæ. Pietatis rudimenta fermè cum latè ipso fugi atque imbibi oportere, quisquis pius est fatebitur: & qua fronte, obsecro, ossicium illud in pædagogica institutione omittatur? qua negligatur fide? Philosophiæ non peregrinalia exponi, sed aditus pueris reserari cupio: non omnes, sed eos saltem qui sunt de moribus: quam ad rem Tullius libris illis suis quos scripsit de officiis juventuti maximè commodavit. Hoc ergo pædagogiorum opus: cui si accesserit conveniens aliqua ad res Mathematicas (ut vocant) introductio, equidem juste pædagogium illud constitutum senserò, & quasi perfectum in suo genere. Quamquam non omnia pædagogia universo hoc instrumento sunt adornata, aut vero esse possunt: sed alia pro commoditate locorum, præceptorumque docentium, alia pro judicio variisque studiis hominum hanc aut illam partem depoposcerunt sibi, reliquas vero intactas sinunt. Exempli causa: literas quidem scire, id est, literaturam omnes fere cupiunt: sed linguam Latinam plerique, Græcam multi discunt, Hebræam paucissimi. Idem quoque eusvenit in tradendis artibus: passim Grammatica, multis in locis Logica & Rhetorica, sed quasi deartuata (ut ita dicam) exponitur, historia paucissimis. Sic gymnasia hæc pædagogica longè sunt alia præstantiora aliis: nempe quo melius feliciusque instrumenta ac principia rerum & quædam velut semina doctrinæ teneris puerorum mentibus ingeniisque subactis & cultis inseruntur.
units.tr: {*} Mark on the text is printed; no further notes. ...they bring great help. The first principles or rudiments are of two kinds. If these are taught in the elementary schools, well and good; if they are not taught, at least one of the two must necessarily be used. The first kind is piety, the second philosophy. Whoever is pious will admit that the rudiments of piety ought to be almost wholly poured into and absorbed by the pupil. And with what face, I ask, is that duty left out of elementary instruction? By what faith is it neglected? I wish that the elements of philosophy be not set out as something foreign, but that access to it be opened to boys: not all of it, but at least that part which concerns morals. For this purpose Tully, in those books of his which he wrote on duties, has been especially useful to young people. This, then, is the task of the elementary schools. If some suitable introduction to the so-called mathematical subjects is added to it, I would judge that elementary school to be rightly established and, in its own kind, nearly complete. Yet not all elementary schools are, or can be, furnished with this whole equipment: some, according to the convenience of places and of teachers, others according to the judgment and varied pursuits of men, have claimed for themselves this or that part and leave the rest untouched. For example, nearly everyone wishes to know letters, that is, to acquire literacy, but most learn Latin, many learn Greek, and very few learn Hebrew. The same happens in the teaching of the arts: grammar is taught almost everywhere, logic and rhetoric in many places, but they are set out, so to speak, in a lopped-off way, and history in very few. Thus some of these elementary schools are far superior to others, namely, to the extent that the instruments and first principles of learning, and certain seeds of doctrine, are better and more happily planted in the tender minds and trained natures of the boys.

units.la: Alterum autem illud gymnasicrum genus, quod ex grandiorum institutione Græcis ἐγκύκλιον diximus appellari, id ergo genus illud est quod initiatos literis & imbutos juvenes pleniore disciplinarum modo colit & perficit. Nam sive instrumenta in pædagogiis tributa respexeris, ea occupantur amplius atque excoluntur in hoc gymnasiorum genere: sive præcipuas quasque partes philosophiæ, quarum principia ex pædagogiis fuerunt hausta, ea demum hic perficiuntur atque absolvuntur: sive facultates illas summas, quæ primas in disciplinis humanis obtinent jure meritissimo, & ad communem Reipub. usum accedunt proximè, eæ in hoc ludo exponuntur commodè ad Reipub. & Ecclesiæ Christi utilitatem maximam. Ac primùm quidem linguarum uberior hic doctrina traditur; non autem peræquè ut in pædagogiis exilis ratio & σμικρόλογος adhibetur, ut oratores, poëtæ, atque historici Græci & Latini cum fructu percurrantur. Deinde verò facultatis philosophicæ, omnium remque artium & scientiarum instrumenta gravius, solidiùs, pressiùs ex classicis quibusque autoribus depromta, non ex rivulis aridioribus ducta aut in tenues alveos corrivata in medium afferuntur: quemadmodum tyronibus succrescentibus non solùm rerum nomina ad officinam suam pertinentium, sed usus etiam demonstrari solet suis gradibus certóque ordine. Præsertim autem id facto opus est, quum jam propè adest tempus quo incumbant illi in ampliora studia, alecámque judiciorum in palæstra hac literaria publicè nonnunquam subeant. Tum corpus totius philosophiæ quasi per anatomen confirmatis ipsorum mentibus, ut oculis, cernendū proponitur. Hic πρὸς ἀφαιρέσεως ὄντα, id est, Mathematicas disciplinas certo ordine juventuti percipiendas & tenendas tradit: illa τὰ ἐκ προσθέσεως ὄντα, quàm quam secundam philosophiam vocant ad res physicas pertinentem, eodemque fere contextu τὰ ἀσώλως ὑπὰ, id est, materiam primæ, vt loquuntur, & reconditioris philosophiæ enucleat argutè, doctè, breviter, familiariter: iste vero τὰ ἢ θικὰ, quibus circumscribuntur boni mores, sanctéque feruntur justi & injusti leges, ad singularem cujusque hominis institutionem, ad rem domesticam gubernandam, atque publicam necessarias. Succedunt tandem his facultates (ut appellantur) summæ, hominemque bene informatum & instructum in suo genere ad πραξλικὸν velut ducentes manu, θεολογικὴ, ῥομικὴ, ἰατρική. Quarum illa quæ Theologia appellatur fontes suos non alibi quàm in cœlo habet, rivi in homines verbo & Scriptura sacra ex mera Dei gratia defluxerunt: Hæ vero fontes suos ab orbis conditu in philosophiæ penetralibus, natura ipsa duce & teste habuerunt. Ethicam enim Iurisprudentia, Physicam Medicina quàm latissimè ad commoditatem generis humani privatim & publicè diduxerunt. Gymnasiorum igitur species fere quatuor ex hoc ordine (nam totidem fuerunt olim) constituti possunt: prima, eorum in quibus linguarum doctrina fuit expositá: secunda, in quibus instrumenta subministrantur & artes ad philosophiam præviæ: tertia, in quibus aperiuntur studiosis & patescunt recessus philosophiæ: quarta denique eorum, in quibus summæ illæ facultates, quas postremo loco diximus, juventuti explanantur ex usu Reipub. Omnia autem inde a principio studiorum, ex quo Cadmus literas intulit, apud Græcos Cadmiæ sive Academiæ nomine donata sunt.
units.tr: The other kind of gymnasium, which from the instruction of older pupils we have called by the Greeks encyclopaedic [ἐγκύκλιον], is the kind that cultivates and perfects, in a fuller course of the disciplines, young people already initiated in letters and steeped in them. For if you look at the instruments handed down in the elementary schools, these are taken up more widely and developed more fully in this kind of gymnasium. If you look at the chief parts of philosophy, whose first principles were drawn from the elementary schools, these are finally completed and brought to perfection here. If you look at those highest faculties, which rightly hold first place among human studies and come closest to the common use of the commonwealth, these are set out in this school, suitably and for the very great benefit of the commonwealth and of the Church of Christ. First, the languages are taught here more richly; not, however, with the same thin and niggling method as in the elementary schools, but so that Greek and Latin orators, poets and historians may be read through profitably. Then, the instruments of the philosophical faculty, of all the arts and sciences, are brought forward more weightily, more solidly and more closely, drawn from the classical authors, not from dry trickles or poured into thin channels: just as, when beginners grow, not only the names of the things belonging to their workshop are shown, but also their use, in due steps and in a fixed order. This is especially necessary when the time is near at hand for them to apply themselves to wider studies, and sometimes publicly to undergo the trial of judgment in this literary arena. Then the body of the whole of philosophy is set before the minds of the students, now made firm, as if to be seen with the eyes, as though laid open by anatomy. Here the subjects that are "by abstraction" [πρὸς ἀφαιρέσεως], that is, the mathematical disciplines, are handed down to be learned and retained by the young in a fixed order. Next, those that are "by addition" [τὰ ἐκ προσθέσεως], which they call the second philosophy and which pertain to natural things, and in nearly the same course the "unformed matter" [τὰ ἀσώλως ὑπὰ], that is, the matter of the so-called first and more hidden philosophy, are unfolded keenly, learnedly, briefly and familiarly. Then the ethical subjects [τὰ ἠθικά], by which good morals are circumscribed and the laws of just and unjust are rightly laid down, are needed for the training of each individual man and for the governing of household and public affairs. Finally, there follow the so-called highest faculties, which lead the man, well informed and equipped in his own kind, by the hand, as it were, toward the practical life: theology, law, and medicine. Of these, theology, the faculty so called, has its springs nowhere but in heaven, and its streams have flowed down to men from the sheer grace of God through the Word and Holy Scripture. The others, however, have had their springs from the creation of the world in the inner sanctuaries of philosophy, with nature itself as guide and witness. For jurisprudence has spread ethics, and medicine physics, as widely as possible for the advantage of the human race, both privately and publicly. Therefore, four kinds of gymnasia (for there were as many of old) can be established from this order: the first, those in which instruction in languages was set out; the second, those in which instruments and arts preparatory to philosophy are supplied; the third, those in which the recesses of philosophy are opened and laid bare to students; and the fourth, finally, those in which those highest faculties, which we mentioned last, are explained to young people for the use of the commonwealth. All these, from the beginning of study, from the time when Cadmus introduced letters, were among the Greeks given the name Cadmia or Academy.

units.la: Quamquam, si litcraturam exceperis, gymnasia olim perpauca, ac pene nulla in Græcia tota exstiterunt, ubi traditus fuerit linguarum usus. Singuli enim philosophi
units.tr: Although, if you except literature, there were once very few schools, and almost none in all of Greece, where the use of languages was taught. Each philosopher, and the leaders of the philosophers, travelled very diligently to foreign regions to bring back knowledge of things, but they strenuously concealed their knowledge of the languages they had learned along the way, for many reasons.

units.la: & philosophorum principes in regiones quidem exteras commigrabant diligentissime, unde rerum scientiam apportarent: sed linguarum, quas unà didicerant, notitiam dissimulabant strenuè multis nominibus. Primum illud est, quòd usque adeò sibi sapere videbantur ut res potius quàm linguas sua occupatione dignas judicarent. Secundum, quòd istud doctrinae genus magnis illis viris emporeticum magis esse quàm philosophicum videretur. Tertium, idque (ut mihi quidem videtur) maximè omnium verisimile, quòd mallent ipsi autores & inventores earum rerum quas docebant haberi apud suos, quàm aliis hominibus & linguis exteris laudem quam decerpebant tribuere: licet doctrinam suam, verissimam sementem laudum suarum, ab illis exteris accepissent. Itaque nec tum apud Graecos aliósve, nec diu post doctrina linguarum floruit, donec Romani scientiam exteram hausturi aliunde praeceptores & interpretes linguarum habere in Repub. sua curaverunt. Primùm enim religionum suarum causa Oscam sive Ethruscam linguam a Phoenicibus ortam, quâ in Sibyllinis, Pompilianis, Saliaribus, & Auguralibus libris utebantur, deinde verò longo post intervallo Graecam visum est edisserere. Quapropter Catonem illum senem pro miraculo habebat poëta Ennius, quòd trilinguis homo, id est, linguarum trium cognitionem adeptus esset, Latinae puta, id est, vernaculae, Oscaeque & Graecae. Adeo fera fuit linguarum disciplina.
units.tr: The first was that they thought themselves so wise that they judged things, rather than languages, to be worthy of their attention. The second was that this kind of learning seemed to those great men more mercantile than philosophical. The third, and to me the most probable of all, was that they preferred to be regarded as the authors and inventors of the things they taught, rather than to give credit to other men and foreign tongues for the praise they were gathering, even though they had received their doctrine, the very seed of their own renown, from those foreigners. So the study of languages did not flourish among the Greeks or others then, nor for a long time afterwards, until the Romans, who were going to draw foreign learning from elsewhere, took care to have teachers and interpreters of languages in their commonwealth. For first, for the sake of their religious rites, they judged it worthwhile to explain the Oscan or Etruscan language, which came from the Phoenicians and which they used in the Sibylline, Pompilian, Salian and Augural books; and then, after a long interval, the Greek language. For this reason the poet Ennius used to regard that old man Cato as a marvel, because he was a trilingual man, that is, had acquired knowledge of three languages: Latin, that is, his mother tongue, and Oscan and Greek. So wild was the discipline of languages.

units.la: Secundum genus, τὸ λογικὸν, floruit Athenis fuitque celebre, primùm quidem in Academia illa proprie apud Athenienses dicta, deinde verò in Lyceum & Stoam fuit derivatum. Etenim Lyceum, gymnasium alterum, omni instrumentorum & artium genere Aristoteles relicta Academia exornavit. Stoa verò Zenones duo, Cittieus & & Eleatæs auditor Parmenidis, & quicunque hos sequuntur, meliores argutiorésque omnes illi τῆς λογικῆς καὶ σοφιστικῆς artifices: quos optimè Ariston quondam similes prædicabat esse edentibus cancros & aštacos, qui propter exiguum alimentum pertenui cum fructu in ossibus & testis plurimis occupantur. Atque hoc sèrò quoque inurbem Romam ingressum est: & ubi ingressum est, perdiu jacuit, nec ita magno in pretio fuit. Nam rhetorum turba reiecta fuerunt omnia, inquit Tullius in primo de officiis: merces vero dialecticorum mina fuit habita, donec succedente Grammaticorum grege aucta est dialecticorum autoritas. Idem enim Romanis olim primò videbatur, ac cuidam apud Athenæum, qui medicos omnium futuros fuisse miserrimos affirmabat, nisi manipuli Grammaticorum exstitissent. Tandem verò istud doctrinarum genus in pretio & honore fuit, si Suetonio credimus: etiamnunc quidem ea autoritate est, ut nomen obtineat Academiæ.
units.tr: The second kind, the logical (τὸ λογικὸν), flourished at Athens and was famous, first indeed in that Academy properly so called at Athens, and then it was transferred to the Lyceum and the Stoa. For Aristotle, having left the Academy, adorned the Lyceum, the second gymnasium, with every kind of instrument and art. The Stoa was adorned by the two Zenos, the Citian and the Eleatic, a hearer of Parmenides, and by all who followed them, the cleverest and most subtle artisans of logic and sophistry. Ariston used to say that they were very like crabs and lobsters, which, feeding on little, are kept busy with meagre profit among many bones and shells. This too came late to the city of Rome, and when it came, it lay neglected for a long time and was not held in high esteem. For, as Tully says in the first book of On Duties, "the crowd of rhetoricians was rejected altogether"; the wares of the dialecticians were thought to be worth only a mina, until, with the grammarians' flock following, the authority of the dialecticians was increased. For the Romans at first seemed to think the same as a certain man at Athens, who used to maintain that all doctors would have been most wretched, unless bands of grammarians had come into existence. At last this kind of learning was held in esteem and honour, if we may believe Suetonius; even now it has such authority that it keeps the name of Academy.

units.la: Tertia gymnasiorum species φιλοσοφικὴ, vetissimè ex Athenensi illa & laudata Academia processit, quamvis ab exteris hausta & percepta primùm, & in ea culta & conservata sit quam diutissimè: posteà verò a Lyceo, Stoa, Cynosarge, aliisque; fœtibus (ut de Cadmea progenie poëtæ fabulati sunt) oppugnata est Academia, scilicet, & direxata maximè, ambitiosis multorum contentionibus. Tantus enim philosophorum estus τῆς καινῆς λογικῆς καὶ μαθηματικῆς fuit in suis dogmatis profundendis & pervicaciter afferendis, ut nationum fermè trecentarum examen in isto genere ad memoriam usque suam Themistius scripserit exstitisse. De hoc autem genere sic ait Tullius, Philosophia jacuit usque ad banc ætatem, nec ullum habuit lumen literarum Latinarum: quæ
units.tr: The third kind of gymnasium, the philosophical (φιλοσοφικὴ), came very early out of that famous Athenian Academy, although it was first acquired and taken up from foreigners, and was cultivated and preserved in it for as long as possible. Later, however, the Academy was attacked, and certainly broken up, by the Lyceum, the Stoa, the Cynosarges and others, offspring (as the poets fabled of the Cadmean progeny) springing from it, through the ambitious contentions of many. For there was such a fervour of the philosophers (τῆς καινῆς λογικῆς καὶ μαθηματικῆς) in propounding and persistently asserting their own opinions, that Themistius wrote that, down to his own memory, a trial of nearly three hundred nations had taken place in this field. Of this kind of learning Tully speaks thus: "Philosophy lay neglected down to this age, and it had no light of Latin letters; which..."

units.la: Lib. I. Tu. Scul. quæst.
units.tr: Book 1, Tusculan Disputations.

units.la: ·Heraclćum, ἡρακλεῶν, ab Hercule Libyco diũum volunt, de quo ante capite 1. pauca. Nos vero fontem huius appellationis paulo post dicturi sumus.
units.tr: Heraclaeum (Ἡρακλεῶν): they want it derived from Hercules of Libya, about whom a few things were said earlier in chapter 1. But we shall speak of the source of this name a little later.

units.la: Hermæū, ἑρμαῖον, eruditionis locus Mercurio (vt Græci putaverunt) sacer, dicebaturillis tam privatus quàm publicus: nam hoc quoq; nomine in Augustali sive prætorio Cæsaris dictam fuisse legimus apud Tranquillũ in Claudio Cæsare. Est autem Hermes Phœnicia origine proprie αὐτὴρ πολυτλαγχθὲς (ut Homeri utamur voce) varia & multa peregrinatione excultus, peritus, versutus, doctus: attributum Kadmi illius Tyrii, vt ante ostendimus. Ex eo igitur fonte derivatū est Hermæum, doctorū virorum peritorumq; locus, gymnasium literatorum hominum, ubi res abditæ pervestigātur, ignotæ docētur, obscuræ declarantur, iterdeniq; instrumenta, artes, scientiæ, omnia ad sapientiam veram pertinentia proponūtur. Quapropter etiam Hermes sive Mercurius cōmune fuit omniū Academiarum & gymnasiorū signum: vnde proverbium, κοινὸς Ἑρμῆς. Cicero Attico, Quod ad me de Hermathena scribis, per mihi gratum, est ornamentū Academiæ proprium meæ: quod & Hermes cōmune omniū, & Minerva singulare est infigne ejus gymnasii. Hinc autem profectæ sunt plurimæ locorum appellationes simplices & compositæ in Asia minore, Ægypto, Libya, Græciaq; : vt Hermæa, Hermæum, Hermopolis, Hermopolites Nomos, & compositum Hermonthis, indeq; Hermonthites Nomos forma Ægyptia, pro eo quod vaniores Græci fuissent dicturi Hermathenaida, & Hernathenaiten Nomon, ex patria sua ἑρμαθωνίας appellatione.
units.tr: Hermaeum (ἑρμαῖον), a place of learning sacred to Mercury (as the Greeks thought), was so called both privately and publicly; for we read that this name was also applied in the Augustal or praetorium of Caesar, in Tranquillus's Life of the Emperor Claudius. Now Hermes, of Phoenician origin, is properly "a man much tossed about" (αὐτὴρ πολυτλαγχθὲς, to use Homer's word), a man refined by varied and manifold wandering, skilled, shrewd, learned; an epithet of that Tyrian Cadmus, as we showed before. Therefore the Hermaeum, the place of learned and expert men, the gymnasium of men of letters, where hidden things are investigated, unknown things taught, obscure things made clear, and finally instruments, arts, sciences, and all things pertaining to true wisdom are set forth, is derived from that source. For this reason Hermes or Mercury was also the common sign of all academies and gymnasia; whence the proverb "Hermes is common" (κοινὸς Ἑρμῆς). Cicero to Atticus: "As to what you write to me about the Hermathena, it is as pleasing to me as an ornament peculiar to my Academy; for Hermes is the common emblem of all, and Minerva the singular badge of that gymnasium." From this origin there have come very many names of places, simple and compound, in Asia Minor, Egypt, Libya and Greece: Hermaea, Hermaeum, Hermopolis, the Hermopolite nome, and the compound Hermonthis, and from it the Hermonthite nome, in an Egyptian form, instead of what the more foolish Greeks would have called Hermathenais and the Hermathenaite nome, from their native name Hermathonias.

units.la: Ludus metonymicè Latinis dicitur pro loco ludi literarii: nā omnem schola, inquit Asconius, ludum dixere Romani, quia liberali ingenio ludus est, quū literas, artes, historias, scientiasque discit. Quamobrem eleganter ludum discendi non lusionis Tullius ad Q. Fratrem appellavit. Μελετητήριον, Graecum est nota originis, meditationis & exercitationis locus, q. d. meditatorium; ut ascetérium, phrontisterium, & similia.
units.tr: Ludus is used by the Latins metonymically for the place of a school of letters; for, as Asconius says, the Romans called every school a ludus, because it is a liberal occupation (ingenio ludus est) when one learns letters, arts, histories and sciences. Accordingly Tully, writing to his brother Quintus, elegantly called it "a ludus of learning, not of play." Μελετητήριον is Greek, of clear origin, a place of meditation and exercise, as it were a "meditatorium"; so too asceterion, phrontisterion, and similar words.

units.la: Musēūvel Musīū (ut Spartianus vocat) gymnasiū est, Musarum locus privatus, publicusve, à Musis dictus, ut vana Graecia credidit. At Musae ipsae, o Graeculi, unde?hinc aqua hæret: μαῶ(αι, μυᾶ(αι, μελωδὲ(αι, ὁμῶ ἔ(αι, inquiunt illi: & quid nō? ager medacii feracissimus omnia affert, praeterquā veritate unam. Hebraeū est, Phoeniciū est verbum Mus in perscrutandi & pervestigandi significatione. Haec igitur studia, atq; hi studiorū ducesfuerunt olim appellatione hac apud veteres figurati: haec appellatio praedicat autores suos, quam tamen eo quòd ignota esset, simplex vetustas in deas ignotas stollidè transformavit. Sic Dei nomine luditur, quod alicujus viri nomine facere vix quisquam impunè audeat.
units.tr: Museum or Musium (as Spartianus calls it) is a gymnasium, a place of the Muses, private or public, named after the Muses, as foolish Greece believed. But the Muses themselves, you little Greeks, where do they come from? Here the water sticks fast; these people say "μαῶσθαι, μυᾶσθαι, μελωδεῖσθαι, ὁμάεσθαι" and what not? The field of falsehood bears the richest crop of everything, except truth alone. The word Mus is Hebrew and Phoenician, with the meaning of searching out and investigating. These studies, then, and these leaders of studies, were of old figuratively designated by this name; this name proclaims its own authors, but because it was unknown, simple antiquity foolishly changed it into unknown goddesses. So the name of God is mocked, which hardly anyone would dare to do with the name of any man with impunity.

units.la: Phrontisterium, φροντιστήριον, nota satis origine vel notatione vocis, a Socrate primùm nomē habuisse dicitur: cujus discipuli appellabantur φροντισταί, quòd alii officiosè curarēt alios ex humano Socratis instituto. Aptissima sanè gymnasiorū, ut vocant, collegiatorū denominatio.
units.tr: Phrontisterium (φροντιστήριον), of a sufficiently well-known origin or derivation, is said first to have had its name from Socrates; his disciples were called phrontistai, because they carefully looked after one another in accordance with Socrates' human teaching. Certainly a most fitting name for what are called collegiate gymnasia.

units.la: Schola, σχολὴ ἡ σχολεῖον, diatriba, gymnasium, ludus ubi studiorum causa juvenes ab occupationibus caeteris otiantur, nomen est translatitium. Ausonius, --- Grajo schola nomine dicta est, Insta laboriferis tribuantur ut otia Musis.
units.tr: School (σχολὴ or σχολεῖον): a place of discussion, a gymnasium, a ludus where young men, for the sake of their studies, are released from their other occupations, is a borrowed name. Ausonius: "It was called schola by the Greeks; in it, let leisure be granted to the labour-bearing Muses."

units.la: Studium recentiores & homines nostri per infolestem quamdam abusionem dixerunt scholam. Sed ἀλς ἡρυεσ.
units.tr: Recent writers and our own people have, by a certain unusual misuse, called it studium, a school. But ... (the rest is corrupt).

units.la: Deinceps consequuntur ea quae a loco aut situ dicta.
units.tr: Next follow those names that are derived from place or situation.

units.la: Gibhá, sive Gabaá, ut vulgo legitur, item q; Gébah & Gabe Geographis dicta, apud Hebraeos & Syros collem significat vel locum editū. Hoc nomine locus olim donabatur in populo Dei qui habendis conuentibus Ecclesiasticis vel scholasticis destinatus esset. In causa fuit hujus appellationis mos ille antiquissimus, quòd plurimum ad hos conventus eminens sedes in editioribus quibusq; locis eligeretur. Hic autem summum locum templa siue ἐκκλησιαστήρια, proximū scholæ obtinebat. Atq; hæc non raro fuit Prophetarū docentium sedes, vt ex Saulis historia 1. Sam. 10. colligitur: ideoq; domus vel locus Prophetarum dicebatur vulgo, quemadmodū suprà ostendimus. Atq; hinc profecta est vetus (vt in transcursu moneamus) illa Gabiorum apud Volscos in finibus Latii appellatio, quos alii dura cōpositione a Galaćto & Bio Siculis fratribus duxerunt nuncupatos. Dionysius Halicarnassæus lib. antiquitat. Rom. 1 de Romulo & Remo loquens ita scri-bit, ἡνίκα ἡ τῆς ἐν τῷ γάλακτι τροφῆς ἀπηλλάγη τὰ παιδία, δοῦλον ... ποιήσας, ὡς ἐπὶ ἀγρὸν ... ; id est, postquam vero infantes a lacte depulsi sunt & cibo lacteo, ab altoribus fuisse traditos ut deducerentur Gabios, civitatem non procul a Palantio sitam, in qua disciplinam Græcam ediscerent. Fuit enim Gabiis Latinorū schola. Volscorumq; quam Phœnices Cadmei, & prognati eorum Tyrrheni, Osci, sive Ethrusci statuerunt, nomine imposito de sermone suo.
units.tr: Gibhá, or Gabaá, as it is commonly read, and also called Gébah and Gabe by the geographers, means in Hebrew and Syriac a hill or raised place. By this name a place was once given among the people of God that had been set apart for holding ecclesiastical or scholastic assemblies. The cause of this name was that most ancient custom, that a lofty seat was chosen in higher places for these gatherings. Here the highest place was held by the temples, or ekklesiasteria, and next to them the school. And this was often the seat of the prophets who taught, as is gathered from the history of Saul, 1 Sam. 10; and therefore the house or place of the prophets was commonly called so, as we have shown above. And from this comes the old name (to note it in passing) of the Gabii among the Volsci, on the borders of Latium, whom others, by a harsh compound, have derived as named after Galaktos and Bios, Sicilian brothers. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in the first book of his Roman Antiquities, speaking of Romulus and Remus, writes thus: when the children were weaned from the milk and milk food, they were handed over by their foster-parents to be taken to Gabii, a city not far from Palatium, in which they were to learn Greek learning. For Gabii was a school of the Latins, and of the Volsci, which the Cadmean Phoenicians, and their descendants the Tyrrhenians, Oscans or Etruscans, established, giving it a name from their own speech.

units.la: Labrathá vel Lebrathan, Ægyptiis, Afris, & Armenis (quos Hebræi & vicini Hebræorum Phœnices literas suas docuerunt) est declivis vel acclivis locus, ab eo quòd descenditur in profundum dictus. Nam illis verbum Labará est descendere. Et inde Lubár, ναρ ... ; Labrá, tota παροικία in declivitate posita & subiecta synagogæ suæ: Labrathá, synagoga: Lebrathenum, ὁ ... εἰς μίαν συναγωγὴν ἀθροισθέντες: Labarum siue Labo-rum vexillum sacrum sive principale: Λάβαρ, fossa, profunditas: & conjugata pleraque alia, quæ omnia κατὰ πεῖσιν literæ, ex Hebræo derivata sunt. Hic vero opus est, vt obscuram istam atque inauditam hominibus nostris exterarum vocum ἀνζυγίαν exponamus latius.
units.tr: Labrathá or Lebrathan, among the Egyptians, Africans and Armenians (whom the Hebrews and their neighbours the Phoenicians taught their letters), is a sloping or rising place, so called because one goes down into a depth. For in their language labará means to descend. From this come Lubar, [ναρ ...]; Labrá, the whole parish lying on a slope and subject to its synagogue; Labrathá, synagogue; Lebrathenum, those gathered into one synagogue [ὁ ... εἰς μίαν συναγωγὴν ἀθροισθέντες]; labarum or laborum, the sacred or principal standard; Λάβαρ, a ditch, a depth; and many other cognate words, all derived from Hebrew by a change of letters. Here it is necessary to explain more fully this obscure and unheard-of kinship of foreign words, which our people do not know.

units.la: A verbo igitur Labara, quod est descendere, dicitur mons Armeniæ Λυβὰρ, Lubar. Epiphanius in Scythismo, sub principium sui Panarii, Μετὰ δὲ τὴν καταικλυσμὸν σπείραν τῆς λάρναχος ἐν Νῶε ἐν τῇ ὄρει τῆς Ἀγχεῖαν ἀνὰ μέσον Ἀρμενίων καὶ Καρδυέων, ἐν τῷ Λυβὰρ ὄρει καλουμένῳ, ἐκεῖσε πρῶτον κατοικήσης γένετο τῶν ἀνθρώπων, &c. Nicolaus vero Damascenus apud Flavium Iosephum libro 1. antiquit. Iudaic. cap.4. ait, ἐν τῷ ὑπὲρ τῆς Μυυάδα μέχρι ὄρος κῶ τῆς Ἀρμενίας Βάρις λεγόμενον, εἰς ὃ πολλῆς συμφυγίζας δὴ ἓ καταικλυσμῷ λόγῳ ἔχει πεφασμένων. Post diluvium autem, inquit Epiphanius, quum arca Noë constitisset in montibus Ararat, inter Armenios & Cardyeos, monte cui nomen est Lubar: inde primum habitationes hominum fuerunt constitutæ. Nicolaus vero, est supra Minyada, inquit, mons magnus secundum Armeniam, qui vocatur Barii, in quem fama est confugisse multos tempore diluvii, & servatos esse. Id autem observandum est, illius Lubar, & huius Barin idem esse, si hoc exceperis, quod prius in principio syllabam habet ἀναρτήσεων ex Orientalium & Afrorum usu, posterius purum est & acceptione carens. Ex hoc nomine formatum est alterum illud Λαβρα, labra, id est, tota parœcia atque vicinitas, quæ uno quasi colle aut clivo disterminata est, & ad conventum Ecclesiæ unius pertinet. Idem Epiphanius ἡ τῶν Ἀπεροματιτῶν his verbis rem totam explicat: ὅσῳ γὰρ ἐκκλησίᾳ τῆς καθολικῆς Ἐκκλησίας ἐν Ἀλεξανδρείᾳ, ὑπὸ ἕνα Ἀρχιεπίσκοπον ἔστιν κατ' ἰδίαν ζώνως, ὁπηνίκα γυμνοῦσι εἰσὶ πρὸς-
units.tr: So from the verb labara, to descend, a mountain of Armenia is called Lubar (Λυβάρ). Epiphanius, in his Scythismus at the beginning of the Panarion, writes: "After the flood, when a fragment of Noah's ark came to rest on the mountain of Ararat, between the Armenians and the Cardyaeans, on the mountain called Lubar, there first men settled..." [Μετὰ δὲ τὸν κατακλυσμὸν ... ἐκεῖσε πρῶτον κατοικήσεως γένετο τῶν ἀνθρώπων]. Nicolaus of Damascus, however, in Flavius Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, book 1, chapter 4, says that beyond Minyas, as far as a great mountain of Armenia called Baris, to which many fled at the time of the flood and were saved, as is reported. Epiphanius: "After the flood, when the ark of Noah had rested on the mountains of Ararat, between the Armenians and the Cardyaeans, on the mountain called Lubar, from there the first dwellings of men were established." Nicolaus: "Above Minyas," he says, "there is a great mountain in Armenia called Barii, to which, it is said, many fled in the time of the flood and were preserved." It should be noted that Epiphanius's Lubar and Nicolaus's Barin are the same, except that the former, following the usage of the Orientals and Africans, has a prefixed syllable at the beginning, while the latter is pure and without it. From this name was formed the other word Λαβρα, labra, that is, the whole parish and neighbourhood, marked off as by a single hill or slope, and belonging to the assembly of one church. Epiphanius explains the whole matter in these words about the Aperomatites: "For whatever church of the catholic Church is in Alexandria, under one archbishop, in its own district, ..."

units.la: Συνήροι δὲ ὡς ἐκκλησιαστικὰς χρείας τῶν οἰκητόρων πλήσιον τῆς Ἐκκλησίας ὄντων, ᾧ ἀμφοδῶν ἦτι λαβρῶν ἀπηχωρέως καλυμένων ὑπὸ τῶν τῶ Αλεξανδρέων καταγωγῶν πλήν. Nam quacunque Ecclesia, inquit Epiphanius, Alexandriæ adiacet catholicam Ecclesiam pertinent, uniuersi sunt Archiepiscopo: speciatim vero Presbyteri sive Seniores illis præfecti sunt, propter necessitates Ecclesiasticas habitatorum suam Ecclesiam accolentium, regionumque circumstantium vel paræciarum, quæ voce patria dicuntur Labræ ab iis qui urbem Alexandriam colunt.
units.tr: "... gathered together for the ecclesiastical needs of the inhabitants living near the church, which in the native speech are called labrai by those who dwell in the city of Alexandria." Epiphanius's words in full: "For whatever church lies near Alexandria belongs to the catholic Church and is all under the archbishop; but especially the presbyters or elders are set over them, because of the ecclesiastical needs of the inhabitants who dwell near their church and of the surrounding regions or parishes, which in the native speech are called labrae by those who live in the city of Alexandria."

units.la: Ex his autem verbis facile intelligitur, qui fuerit olim Ecclesiarum ordoin amplioribus opidis: nam opida in labras (parochias hodie vocat) fuisse distributa, singulis labrae suum Presbyterium, omnibus autem simul Archiepiscopum & Antistitem præfuisse. Tum plerumque in summo labrae istius editissimóque loco fuit labrathá, sive Lebrathan de qua hic agitur, id est, synagoga, Ecclesia, locus conventui Ecclesiastico & scholastico dictus: atque hunc in locum sive conventum familiæ contributæ (παροικοι, parochi vulgo) appellabantur Lebrathenín, id est, Lebrathéni, qui corruptè (ut fit in migratione exterarum vocum & transplantationibus plurimùm) a Græcis dicti sunt Libertini.
units.tr: From these words it is easy to understand what the order of the churches once was in larger towns. For the towns were divided into labrae (today they call them parishes), each labra having its own presbytery, and over all of them together an archbishop and bishop presiding. Then, usually at the highest and most elevated point of that labra, was the labrathá, or Lebrathan, of which we are speaking here, that is, the synagogue, the church, a place named for ecclesiastical and scholastic assembly. And those families gathered together into this place or assembly (paroikoi, commonly called parochi) were called Lebrathenin, that is, Lebrathenes, who, by corruption (as happens very often in the migration and transplanting of foreign words), were called Libertini by the Greeks.

units.la: Sic enim illa Lucæ verba accipimus, Exorti sunt autem quidam e synagoga quæ dicitur Libertinorum tum Cyrenaorum tum Alexandrinorum, & eorum qui sunt ex Cilicia & Asia, altercantes cum Stephano, &c. Ab eadem origine sunt (ut cursim ea perstringamus quæ ad eruditæ antiquitatis intelligentiam faciunt) alia σύζυγα vel conjugata præfixum l habentia, aliáque carentia. Habent enim Ihæc nomina, λάβρος, fossa profunda, & Labarum sive λάβαρον Sozomeno, vexillum prætorium, principale, sive Augustale, ut antè dixinus. Sine l vero ex eodem fonte manantia leguntur ista: βήρυτος, Beryt sive Berútu, urbs Phœniciæ clarissima, ubi juridicam Academiam instituit Iustinianus
units.tr: For so we understand those words of Luke: "Then there arose certain men from the synagogue called that of the Libertines, both of Cyrenians and Alexandrians, and of those from Cilicia and Asia, disputing with Stephen," etc. From the same origin come other words, to touch briefly on what helps the understanding of learned antiquity, some with a prefixed l, others without. Those having it are: λάβρος, a deep ditch; and labarum, or λάβαρον according to Sozomen, the praetorian, principal or Augustal standard, as we said above. Without the l, coming from the same source, are the following: Beryt, or Berutu, the most famous city of Phoenicia, where Justinian established a school of law;

units.la: Act. 6. 9. Cæsar: Thabor mons Iudæx: Thabrus, qui vulgo Taurus mons, Ciliciam Armeniámque disterminans: & Atabyria, Plinio teste, olim Rhodus dicta. His adde coronidis loco cántabrum, vocem compositam, apud Tertullianum, Minutium, & aliosautores classicos: quo nomine significatur stylus, scapus, vel hastile labarorum, id est, signorum pensilium quæ Imperatoribus olim præferebantur, ritu ab Armeniis regibus translato. Hæc enim vexilla eo a cæteris commodè distinguebantur, quòd labara de suo kané, id est, scapo vel hastili deponi po-terant ut exemtilia, reliquaautem omnia erant operis continentis: ac propterea ubique vexillis cantabra opponuntur. Tertullianus Apologetico, Suppara illa Ꝑexillorum, & cantabrorum flola, crucium sunt. Minutius, Nam & signa ipsa, & cantabra, & vexilla caflrorum, quid aliud quàm inaurata cruces sunt & ornata? Sed ad rem.
units.tr: Act. 6. 9. Caesar: Thabor, a mountain of Judaea; Thabrus, commonly called Mount Taurus, dividing Cilicia from Armenia; and Atabyria, according to Pliny, formerly called Rhodes. To these add, as a crown, the word cantabrum, a compound found in Tertullian, Minucius and other classical authors, which signifies the stem, shaft or staff of the labara, that is, of the hanging standards which were once carried before the emperors, a custom taken over from the Armenian kings. For these standards were conveniently distinguished from others in that the labara could be removed from their kanē (that is, shaft or staff) as detachable pieces, while all the others were of one continuous piece. Therefore cantabra are everywhere set over against standards. Tertullian in the Apologeticus: "Those standards' ... and the flutter of the cantabra are crosses." Minucius: "For the very standards, and the cantabra, and the banners of the camps, what else are they but gilded and adorned crosses?" But to the matter.

units.la: Monastérium μοναστήριον, Græca appellatione ascetérium est vel phrontistérium monachorum, quos μοναστὰς, μοναχὰς, vel μοναζόντας antiquitas nuncupavit, id est, corum qui solitariam vitam colebant in Ecclesia vetere, ut pietatem semoti a reliquo mundo commodiùs exercerent, féque in contemplatione rerum sacrarum occuparent, donec legitimè ad sacras functiones & ministeria apta vocarentur.
units.tr: Monasterium (μοναστήριον) is, in Greek, an asketerion or phrontisterion of monks, whom antiquity called monastai, monachai or monazontes (μοναστάς, μοναχάς, μοναζόντας), that is, those who lived a solitary life in the early Church, so that they might more conveniently exercise piety, separated from the rest of the world, and occupy themselves in the contemplation of sacred things, until they were lawfully called to sacred functions and ministries suited to them.

units.la: Peripatos, περίπατος, Lycéi locus ἐγυμνάσιον, ut ab Aristotele sæpenumero appellatur, in quo ambulantes solébant agere de rebus philosophicis Peripatetici. Hæc enim ambulatio a rotunda ipsius forma dicta est illis περιπατοῦσι, aut etiam κυκλος, & ἐγκύκλιοι nimirum τὰ πάντα: Latini circum, vel circulum dicunt.
units.tr: Peripatos (περίπατος), the place of the Lyceum, which Aristotle often calls the gymnasium, where the Peripatetics walked and used to discuss philosophical matters. For that walking was named by them peripatousi, from the round shape of the place, or even kyklos and enkyklioi (κύκλος, ἐγκύκλιοι), namely all the branches of learning; the Latins say circum or circulus.

units.la: Stoa, στοά, cognomento ποικίλη dicta, poecile Spartiano, id est, varia, ubi depicti erant fortes illi & præstantes viri qui in pugna Marathonia pro patria occubuerant, gymnasium fuit Zenonis Stoicorúmque, situm ex adverso fermè ipsius Academiæ ad urbem Athenarum. Generatim verò porticum structurámque oblongam significat, qualia plerumque sunt basilicarum & magnificorum operum vestibula, a Stoæ illius Atticæ similitudine: ut Ioan.5.2.&10.23.
units.tr: Stoa (στοά), surnamed poikile (ποικίλη) by Spartianus, that is, varied, where the brave and distinguished men who had fallen for their country in the battle of Marathon were painted, was the gymnasium of Zeno and the Stoics, situated nearly opposite the Academy itself, near the city of Athens. In general it means a portico or long covered building, such as is usually the entrance hall of basilicas and magnificent structures, from its resemblance to that Attic Stoa; as in John 5:2 and 10:23.

units.la: Restant pauca nomina ex adjunctis attributa.
units.tr: A few names remain, given from the things attached to them.

units.la: Amalthea sive Amaltheum ἀμαλθεια, ἀμαλθεῖον, gymnasium Bibliotheca instructissimum & confertissimum,ex origine Hebrea dicitur. Nam vox Ɲ‎ālé Hebreis, & Syris significat plenum. Sic vocat Tullius in epistolis ad Atticum.
units.tr: Amalthea or Amaltheum (ἀμάλθεια, ἀμάλθεον), a gymnasium and library most richly furnished and crowded with books, takes its name from a Hebrew origin. For the Hebrew and Syriac word meaning "full" is the same. So Tully calls it in his letters to Atticus.

units.la: . Gymnásium, γυμνάσιον, proprie nominatur locus in quo nudi athletæ exercebantur,ut vocis notatio indicat: dicitur verò χ̓ὰ σωνκδοχῶ de quolibet exercitationis loco, & καὶ ἐχοχῶ de ludo literario & Academia. Nam huius in accessu erat gymnasium exercendis juvenum corporibus institutum, ne obtorpesceret assidua studiorum μελέτη. Pausanias in Atticis.
units.tr: Gymnasium (γυμνάσιον) properly names the place where naked athletes trained, as the etymology of the word shows. But it is used by synecdoche of any place of exercise, and of a school of letters and an Academy. For at its entrance there was a gymnasium set up for training young bodies, lest the constant practice of study should make them sluggish. Pausanias in Attica.

units.la: Heracleum, ἡρακλεῖον, alii ab Hercule Lybico dictum volunt, alii a statua Herculis quæ ante gymnasia solebat poni, ut fortes esse docerentur quicunque ad literarum studia accedebant: nam Hercules apud veteres dictus est μυσαγωγὸς. Sed Hercules unde? Phœnicia est & Punica appellatio,virum peregrinationibus variis cultum significans & versutum, qui orbem terrarum pedibus obierit, multiplicémque sibi peritiam rerum & doctrinam σὺν ἱστορίας comparaverit, ut de nomine Ἡρμῆς ante dicebamus. Nam ex eo quòd Hebræi virum peditem & vias tentantem explorantémque pedibus appellant Ragli, Phœnices & Pœni duxerunt nomen commune virorum omnium Regál vel Regla, quia solus ἀρχὴς ἱμπτετες aptus est, & τὸν ἑτερον nuncupauerunt Elragli: & inde ἡεχυλῆς. Atque hinc multæ Heraclea, & Heraclopoles in Asia tota, Ægyto, Græcia, & regionibus aliis, &c. ubi scholæ ad literarum studia floruerunt. Sed quia omnes putauerunt Herculem ante gymnasia in stadiis ascendicisque locis propter robur statui oportere, dedimus illud opinioni vulgi, ut hoc nomen gymnasiorum in numerum eorum conferremus quæ ex adjunctis ducta sunt.
units.tr: Some hold that the Heracleum (ἡρακλεῖον) was named after Hercules of Libya, others after a statue of Hercules which was customarily placed before the gymnasia, so that whoever came to the study of letters would be taught to be brave; for among the ancients Hercules was called mysagogos. But whence is Hercules? The name is Phoenician and Punic, signifying a man of much travel, skilled and shrewd, who has gone round the world on foot and acquired manifold experience and learning through inquiry, as we said earlier about the name Hermes. For because the Hebrews call a man who goes on foot, testing and exploring the roads, ragli, the Phoenicians and Carthaginians took regal or regla as the common name of all men, since he alone is fit to rule, and called the other one elragli; and from this comes [ἡεχυλῆς]. Hence there are many Heracleas and Heraclopoleis throughout Asia, Egypt, Greece and other regions, etc., where schools for the study of letters flourished. But since everyone thought Hercules had to be set up before gymnasia in the stadia and on rising ground for the sake of strength, we have yielded to popular opinion, so that this name is counted among those derived from attached things.

units.la: Xystus, ξυστὸς, lata porticus & ampla dicebatur, ubi exercebantur athletæ hiberno tempore, gymnasium tectum & quasi παράδεισος vestibulúmque Academiæ. Hinc Ἀλσ. συνεχοχῆς ipsam quoque Academiam nonnulli dixerunt Xystum. Sed hæc de nominibus plus satis.
units.tr: Xystus (ξυστός) was the name of a broad and spacious portico where athletes trained in winter, a covered gymnasium and almost a paradise and vestibule of the Academy. Hence some have also called the Academy itself the Xystus. But enough about names.

units.la: CAPUT TERTIUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER THREE.

units.la: Qua species Academiarum.
units.tr: Of the kinds of Academies.

units.la: EX tam multis σχολεῶν gymnasiorúmque appellationibus una hoc tempore cæteris anteponitur: & unum eorum genus est, quod ex communi usu jam sibi vindicat nomen Academiæ, proprio quodam & singulari jure, ut post dicturi sumus. Cùm igitur illud ipsum genus quod κατ' ἰδίαν vocatur Academia, justa legitimáque ratione postulet, ut inter se distinguantur gymnasiorum formæ: nunc videndum nobis est, quid sit id in quo Academia aliis antecellit, & quamobrem sibi hoc nomen arroget. Ac primùm quidem ponendum illud est, neque mechanica, neque palæstrica, neque παιγνιώδη, neque σωματικῆς ἀσκήσεως ullius gymnasia hic a nobis agi: sed ea spectari solùm in quibus animus humanus cognitione liberalium disciplinarum informatur, & ad veram pietatis formam, scientiæ, virtutisque ducitur.
units.tr: Of so many names for schools [σχολεῶν] and gymnasiums, one is at this time placed above all the rest, and it is a kind of these which, by common usage and by a peculiar and singular right, as we shall say later, already claims for itself the name of Academy. Since, then, that very kind which is called in particular [κατ' ἰδίαν] an Academy demands, on a just and lawful reasoning, that the forms of gymnasiums be distinguished from one another, we must now see what it is in which the Academy surpasses the others, and why it claims this name for itself. And first of all this must be laid down: that we are not here dealing with gymnasiums of the mechanical, the palaestric, the playful [παιγνιώδη] or the bodily exercise [σωματικῆς ἀσκήσεως] kind at all, but only those in which the human mind is formed by the knowledge of the liberal disciplines and led to the true form of piety, knowledge and virtue.

units.la: Prima igitur gymnasiorum distinctio a materia ducitur in hunc modum. Gymnasiorum alia sunt quæ dicuntur παιδαγωγικά, alia quæ ἐνκυκλοπαιδεία: illa minoribus erudiendis instituta, hæc grandioribus & provectioribus ætate studióque informandis plenius, ex quo principia in pædagogiis tradita belle ascequuti sunt. In pædagogiis autem duo traduntur potissimum: instrumenta doctrinarum, & principia sive rudimenta. Instrumenta appellamus linguas, artes instrumentales, & ornamenta earum historias. Linguas, Latinam & Græcam, omnis justa instituendi ratio pueris accuratè tradi postulat, & flagitat hæc memoria nostra: Hebræa non perinde ab omnibus desideratur. Desideratur tamen, eáque opus est plurimum: quod bonum antecedentium seculorum barbaries diu ignoravit, & impendens bellorum clades porrò impedit ura s., nisi Deus Christianum orbem respexerit misericorditer, & fortia juventutis piæ studia ad hoc officium accenderit, ut rumpatur Satan. Hic enim adversarius salutis nostræ jam fermè nihil tam molitur, quàm ut in sermone illo suo non audiatur Deus, quo sermone suavissima illa mysteria exoptatissimæ salutis nostræ olim tradita atque perscripta sunt. Artes instrumentales, nimirum Grammaticam verborum ex usu, Logicam veritatis ex ratione, & Rhetoricam communis cultus ad easdem res ex commoditate adhibendi artifices, necessarias esse qui ignorat, brutus est: suriosus, qui negat. Historias siqui his cum iudicio & ratione adjungunt, non mediocre juventuti allestamentum ad amorem literarum humaniorum præbent, & sermoni, rationi, cultui denique in pueris confirmanda.
units.tr: The first division of gymnasiums is drawn from their subject matter as follows. Some are called paedagogic [παιδαγωγικά], others encyclopaedic [ἐνκυκλοπαιδεία]. The former are established for teaching the younger pupils, the latter for training the older and more advanced in age and study more fully; from these, those who have well grasped the principles handed down in the paedagogies go on. In the paedagogies two things are chiefly taught: the instruments of learning, and the principles or rudiments. We call the instruments the languages, the instrumental arts, and their ornaments, the histories. Every proper method of instruction requires that Latin and Greek be taught to boys accurately, and our own memory insists on this. Hebrew is not equally demanded by all, yet it is demanded and is very much needed. The barbarism of past centuries long ignored it, and the impending ruin of wars hinders it further, unless God look mercifully on the Christian world and kindle the strong zeal of pious youth for this duty, so that Satan may be broken. For this adversary of our salvation now attempts almost nothing so much as that God should not be heard in that language of his in which those most sweet mysteries of our most desired salvation were once handed down and written. Whoever does not know that the instrumental arts are necessary, namely grammar for the correct use of words, logic for the truth by reason, and rhetoric, the skilled application of common refinement to these same things, is a brute; whoever denies it is mad. Those who join histories to these with judgment and reason give youth no small equipment for a love of the humane letters, and bring great help in strengthening speech, reason and, finally, refinement in boys.

units.la: {y} mando magnum adferunt adjumentum. Principia five rudimenta duum sunt generum, quæ in scholis prædagogicis si traduntur, bene est: si non traduntur, omnino tamen vnum eorum adhibeatur necesse est. Prius genus est pietatis, posterius philosophiæ. Pietatis rudimenta fermè cum lacte ipso sugiatque imbibi oportere, quisquis pius est fatebitur: & qua fronte, obsecro, officium illud in prædagogica institutione omittatur? qua negligatur fide? Philosophiæ non peregrinalia exponi, sed aditus pueris reserari cupio: non omneis, sed eos saltem qui sunt de moribus: quam ad rem Tullius libris illis suis quos scripsit de officiis juventuti maximè commodavit.
units.tr: The principles or rudiments are of two kinds. If they are taught in the paedagogic schools, it is well; if not, at least one of them must necessarily be used. The first kind is of piety, the second of philosophy. Whoever is pious will admit that the rudiments of piety ought to be imbibed almost with mother's milk. With what face, I ask, is that duty omitted in paedagogic instruction? With what faith is it neglected? As for philosophy, I do not want its remote matters expounded, but access to it opened for boys: not all of it, but at least that part which concerns morals. To this end Cicero especially adapted those books of his which he wrote on duties for youth.

units.la: Hoc ergo prædagogiorum opus: cui si acceßerit conveniens aliqua ad res Mathematicas (ut vocant) introductio, equidem juste prædagogium illud constitutum sensero, & quasi perfectum in suo genere. Quamquam non omnia prædagogia universo hoc instrumento sunt adornata, aut verò esse possunt: sed alia pro commoditate locorum, præceptorumque docentium, alia pro judicio variisque studiis hominum hanc aut illam partem depoposcerunt sibi, reliquas verò intactas sinunt. Exempli causa: literas quidem scire, id est, literaturam omnes fere cupiunt: sed linguam Latinam plerique, Græcam multi discunt, Hebræam paucissimi. Idem quoque euenit in tradendis artibus: passim Grammatica, multis in locis Logica & Rhetorica, sed quasi deartuata (ut ita dicam) exponitur, historia paucissimis. Sic gymnasia hæc prædagogica longè sunt alia præstantiora aliis: nempe quo melius felicius; instrumenta ac principia rerum & quædam velut femina doctrinæ teneris puerorum mentibus ingeniisque subactis & cultis inferuntur.
units.tr: This, then, is the work of the paedagogies. If a suitable introduction to mathematical matters (as they call them) were added, I would judge that paedagogy rightly established and, as it were, perfect in its kind. Yet not all paedagogies are, or indeed can be, furnished with this whole apparatus. Some, according to the convenience of places and of the teachers, and others, according to the judgment and varied interests of people, have claimed for themselves this or that part and leave the rest untouched. For example: nearly everyone wants to know letters, that is, literacy; many learn Latin, many Greek, but very few Hebrew. The same happens in the teaching of the arts. Grammar is taught everywhere, and logic and rhetoric in many places, but they are expounded as it were mangled (so to speak); history is taught to very few. Thus these paedagogic schools differ greatly in quality: the better and more fortunate ones convey the instruments and principles of things, and certain seeds of learning, into the tender minds and trained wits of boys.

units.la: Alterum autem illud gymnasticum genus, quod ex quam secundam philosophiam vocant ad res physicas pertinentem, eodemque ferme contextu τὰ ἀπλᾶ ὕλης, id est, materiam primæ, vt loquuntur, & reconditioris philosophiæ enucleat argutè, doctè, breviter, familiariter: iste vero τὰ ἠθικά, quibus circumscribuntur boni mores, sanctéque feruntur justi & injusti leges, ad singularem cujusque hominis institutionem, ad rem domesticam gubernandam, atque publicam necessarias. Succedunt tandem his facultates (ut appellantur) summæ, hominemque bene informatum & instructum in suo genere ad πρακτικὰ velut ducentes manu, θεολογικὴ, νομικὴ, ἰατρικὴ. Quarum illa quæ Theologia appellatur fontes suos non alibi quàm in cœlo habet, rivi in homines verbo & Scriptura sacra ex mera Dei gratia defluxerunt: Hæ vero fontes suos ab orbis condito in philosophiæ penetralibus, natura ipsa duce & teste habuerunt. Ethicam enim Iurisprudentia, Physicam Medicina quàm latissimè ad commoditatem generis humani privatim & publicè diduxerunt. Gymnasiorum igitur species ferme quatuor ex hoc ordine (nam totidem fuerunt olim) constitui possunt: prima, eorum in quibus linguarum doctrina fuit exposita: secunda, in quibus instrumenta subministrantur & artes ad philosophiam præviæ: tertia, in quibus aperiuntur studiosis & patescunt recessus philosophiæ: quarta denique eorum, in quibus summæ illæ facultates, quas postremo loco diximus, juventuti explanantur ex usu Reipub. Omnia autem inde a principio studiorum, ex quo Cadmus literas intulit, apud Græcos Cadmiæ sive Academiæ nomine donata sunt.
units.tr: The other gymnastic kind, which unfolds clearly, learnedly, briefly and familiarly the physical matters belonging to what they call second philosophy, and with almost the same scope the simple things of matter [τὰ ἀπλᾶ ὕλης], that is, the matter of first philosophy, as they say, and of the deeper philosophy. The ethical [τὰ ἠθικά] subjects, by which good morals are defined and the laws of just and unjust are rightly handed down, are necessary for the individual training of each person and for the management of household and public affairs. Then at last follow the so-called higher faculties, which lead the man who has been well informed and instructed in his kind, as if by the hand, to practical matters: theology, law and medicine. Of these, theology has its fountains nowhere but in heaven; its streams have flowed down to men from the pure grace of God, through the Word and Holy Scripture. The others had their fountains from the foundation of the world in the inner shrines of philosophy, with nature itself as guide and witness. For jurisprudence has spread out ethics, and medicine physics, as widely as possible, privately and publicly, for the benefit of the human race. Therefore four kinds of gymnasium (for there were as many of old) can be set up in this order: first, those in which the teaching of languages was set forth; second, those in which instruments and arts preparatory to philosophy are supplied; third, those in which the recesses of philosophy are opened and laid bare to students; and fourth, those in which the highest faculties we mentioned last are explained to youth for the use of the commonwealth. All of these, from the beginning of studies, when Cadmus introduced letters, were among the Greeks given the name Cadmea or Academy.

units.la: Quamquam, si litteraturam exceperis, gymnasia olim perpauca, ac penè nulla in Græcia tota exstiterunt, ubi traditus fuerit linguarum usus. Singuli enim philosophi & philosophorum principes in regiones quidem exteras commigrabant diligentissime, unde rerum scientiam apportarent: sed linguarum, quas una didicerant, notitiam dissimulabant strenuè multis nominibus. Primum illud est, quòd usque adeò sibi sapere videbantur ut res potius quàm linguas sua occupatione dignas judicarent.
units.tr: Although, if you leave out elementary literacy, there were in former times very few schools, and almost none in all of Greece, where the use of languages was taught. Individual philosophers and the chiefs of philosophers would migrate most diligently into foreign regions to bring back knowledge of things, but they strenuously concealed their knowledge of the languages they had learned there, for many reasons. The first is that they seemed to themselves so wise that they judged things, rather than languages, worthy of their attention.

units.la: Secundum, quòd istud doctrinæ genus magnis illis viris emporeticum magis esse quàm philosophicum videretur. Tertium, idque (ut mihi quidem videtur) maximè omnium verisimile, quòd mallent ipsi autores & inventores earum rerū quas docebant haberi apud suos, quàm aliis hominibus & linguis exteris laudem quam decerpebant tribuere: licet doctrinam suam, verissimam semetipsum laudum suarum, ab illis exteris accepisset. Itaque nec tum apud Græcos aliósve, nec diu post doctrina linguarum floruit, donec Romani scientiam exteram hausturi aliunde præceptores & interpretes linguarum habere in Repub. sua curaverunt. Primùm enim religionum suarum causa Oscam sive Ethruscam linguam a Phoenicibus ortam, quâ in Sibyllinis, Pompilianis, Saliaribus, & Auguralibus libris utebantur, deinde verò longo post intervallo Græcam visum est edisserere. Quapropter Catonem illum senem pro miraculo habebat poëta Ennius, quòd trilinguis homo, id est, linguarum trium cognitionem adeptus esset, Latinæ puta, id est, vernaculæ, Oscæq; & Græcæ. Adeo fera fuit linguarum disciplina.
units.tr: The second is that this kind of teaching seemed to those great men more a matter of trade than of philosophy. The third, and to me the most probable of all, is that the authors and inventors of the things they taught preferred to be held in esteem among their own people, rather than to give praise to other men and foreign tongues for what they were collecting; although they had received their true doctrine, the truest of their own praises, from those foreigners. So neither then among the Greeks nor others, nor long afterwards, did the teaching of languages flourish, until the Romans, who were to draw foreign learning from elsewhere, took care in their commonwealth to have teachers and interpreters of languages. For first, for the sake of their religious rites, they judged it proper to expound the Oscan or Etruscan language, which had its origin among the Phoenicians and which they used in the Sibylline, Pompilian, Salian and augural books; then, after a long interval, it seemed right to expound Greek as well. Hence the poet Ennius used to regard that old Cato as a marvel, because he was a trilingual man, that is, had attained knowledge of three languages: Latin, that is, his vernacular, Oscan and Greek. So crude was the discipline of languages.

units.la: Secundum genus, τὸ λογικὸν, floruit Athenis fuitque celebre, primùm quidem in Academia illa proprie apud Athenienses dicta, deinde verò in Lyceum & Stoam fuit derivatum. Etenim Lyceum, gymnasium alterum, omni instrumentorum & artium genere Aristoteles relicta Academia exornavit. Stoa vero Zenones duo, Citticus &c & Eleates auditor Parmenidis, & quicunque hos sequuti sunt, Megarici potiores argutioresque omnes illi τῆς λογικῆς καὶ σοφιστικῆς artifices: quos optimè Aristo quondam similes prædicabat esse edentibus cancros & aslacos, qui propter exiguum alimentum pertenui cum fructu in ossibus & testis plurimis occupantur. Atque hoc sero quoque in urbem Romam ingressum est: & ubi ingressum est, perdiu jacuit, nec ita magno in pretio fuit. Nam rhetorum turba referta fuerunt omnia, inquit Tullius in primo de officiis: merces vero dialecticorum mina fuit habita, donec succedente Grammaticorum grege aucta est dialecticorum auctoritas. Idem enim Romanis olim primò videbatur, ac eadem apud Athenæum, qui medicos omnium futuros fuisse miserrimos affirmabat, nisi manipuli Grammaticorum exstitissent. Tandem vero istud doctrinarum genus in pretio & honore fuit, si Suetonio credimus: etiamnunc quidem ea auctoritate est, ut nomen obtineat Academiæ.
units.tr: The second kind, the logical [τὸ λογικόν], flourished at Athens and was famous, first indeed in that Academy properly so called among the Athenians, and then was transferred to the Lyceum and the Stoa. For Aristotle, having left the Academy, adorned the Lyceum, the other gymnasium, with every kind of instrument and art. The Stoa had the two Zenos, Citticus, and the Eleatic, a hearer of Parmenides, and whoever followed them; the Megarians were the most powerful and subtle of all those artisans of logic and sophistry [τῆς λογικῆς καὶ σοφιστικῆς]. Aristo once used to declare them similar to crabs and aslaci, which, on account of their meagre nourishment, are kept busy with little flesh among many bones and shells. This also came late into the city of Rome, and when it came it lay neglected for a long time and was not held in great esteem. For, as Cicero says in the first book of On Duties, the crowd of rhetoricians filled everything; the wares of the dialecticians were priced at a single mina, until, with the arrival of the grammarian flock, the authority of the dialecticians increased. For the Romans at first took the same view as Athenaeus, who used to maintain that all physicians would be most wretched, unless bands of grammarians had arisen. At last, however, that kind of learning came into esteem and honour, if we believe Suetonius; even now it has such authority that it keeps the name of Academy.

units.la: Tertia gymnasiorum species φιλοσοφική, vetustissimè ex Athenensi illa & laudata Academia processit, quamvis ab exteris hausta & perecepta primùm, & in ea culta & conservata sit quam diutissimè: postea verò a Lyceo, Stoa, Cynosarge, aliisque; sed factionibus (ut de Cadmea progenie poetæ fabulati sunt) oppugnata est Academia, scilicet, & direxata maximè, ambitiosis multorum contentionibus. Tantus enim philosophorum estus περὶ καινῶν λογίων καὶ ματαιοτάτων fuit in suis dogmatis profundendis & pervicaciter asserendis, ut nationum fermè trecentarum examen in isto genere ad memoriam usque suam Themistius scripserit exstitisse. De hoc autem genere sic ait Tullius, Philosophia jacuit usque ad hanc aetatem, nec ullum habuit lumen literarum Latinarum: quae illustranda & excitanda nobis est, ut si occupati profiteamur ali-quid civibus nostris, prosimus etiam, si possumus, otiosi. In quo ea magis nobis est elaborandum, quod multi jam esse Latini libri dicuntur scripti inconsiderate ab optimis illis quidem viris, sed non satis eruditis, & quae sequuntur.
units.tr: The third kind of school, philosophy [φιλοσοφική], came down from very early times from that famous Academy of Athens, although it was first drawn from foreign sources and received there, and it was cultivated and preserved in that place for as long as possible. Afterwards, however, the Academy was attacked by the Lyceum, the Stoa, the Cynosarges and others, and was torn apart by factions, as the poets fabled of the offspring of Cadmus. Indeed the philosophers were so eager to pour out and stubbornly to assert their dogmas about novel and most vain doctrines [περὶ καινῶν λογίων καὶ ματαιοτάτων] that Themistius wrote that a trial of almost three hundred nations in this kind of thing had existed down to his own time. Of this kind of learning Tully speaks thus: "Philosophy lay prostrate down to this age and had no light of Latin literature.
