It is for us to illuminate and arouse it, so that if we, though busy, profess something to our fellow citizens, we may also, if we can, be of service even when at leisure. In this we must labour all the more because many books are now said to have been written in Latin, carelessly, by those indeed excellent men, but not learned enough," and what follows.

units.la: Quarta vero gymnasiorum species tum sane apud Graecos non potuit esse, quum summae illae (ut hodie vocantur) facultates nondum judicio publico ficesse constitutae ut sunt, aut ordo a literatis viris perceptus, dispositus, traditusque, aut potentiorum autoritate adusum publicum confirmatus. Nam ubi Theologia, praeterquam in populo Dei? Opiniones vero, superstitionesque gentium, & rituum interpretamenta a luce popelli & vulgi consuetudine ac conscientia tantum abfuerunt, ut contra omni tempore penes Hierophantas, mystas, pontifices, augures, divinaculos tecta omnia reconditaque permanserint. Testis universa antiquitas, Arnobius, Lactantius, Eusebius, Augustinus, caeteri. Similiter ubi Iurisprudentia? cujus corpus Athenis decem tabulis contineabatur; ratio penes ἀγοραστικὸς, judicii penes Areopagitas, Prytaneas, quingentos, Heliaftas erat: Romae verò xii. tabulis comprehensum, à Iurecoss. per responsa expositum, sine corpore, sine ordine, perdiu jacuit, ut ipse Tullius gravissime in libris de Oratore & de legibus conqueritur. Quid de Medicina dicam? quae ab Hippocrate primum Athenis inclaruit tempore pestilentiae: postea vero simulatque emerserat, in treis praecipuas veluti familias miscere dissecta vix tandem in unum corpus ante aliquot secula quasi adstricta est, & in unam docendi viam. Etsi haec quoque ipsa hodierno die a recentibus quibusdam ἰατρολόγοις non mediocriter oppugnatur, atque in vulgo traducitur. Harum igitur facultatum (quarum primam nefando quidem Athenienses & Romani olim audiverant, duas vero alias singuli fermè qui aliquid sibi sapere videbantur tractabant & tradebant arbitratu suo) harum inquam Academia ubi, quando, quomodo apud illos exstiterit, nemo (si bene memini) excertis autoribus demonstrare & probare potest, donec Romanum imperium aliquot jam seculis perdurasset, atque ἀπὸ τῆς οἰκουμένης πλάνης ad Christianam fidem transivisset, salutarisque & θεοπνεύστου sermonis veritatem. Quid igitur, dixerit quispiam, in hoc tempore est Academia? Academia est gymnasium literis, id est, cum linguis, artibus, & scientiis philosophiæ, tum summis illis facultatibus certo ordine & modo tradendis institutum, sanctisque prærogativis & privilegiis instructum justa autoritate publica, civili & Ecclesiastica.
units.tr: The fourth kind of school could certainly not exist among the Greeks at that time, since those highest faculties (as they are now called) had not yet been established by public judgment as they are now, nor had an order been conceived, arranged and handed down by learned men, nor confirmed for public use by the authority of the powerful. For where was theology, except among the people of God? The opinions and superstitions of the nations, and the explanations of rites, were so far from the light of the people and the common custom and conscience that, on the contrary, at all times everything was kept hidden and concealed among the hierophants, initiates, pontiffs, augurs and diviners. The whole of antiquity bears witness to this, as do Arnobius, Lactantius, Eusebius, Augustine and others. Likewise, where was jurisprudence? Its body was contained in ten tables at Athens; the reasoning was in the hands of the agoraios [ἀγοραστικὸς], the judgment in those of the Areopagites, the Prytanes, the Five Hundred and the Heliasts. At Rome it was comprehended in the Twelve Tables, expounded by the jurisconsults through responses, and for a long time it lay without a body and without order, as Tully himself complains most gravely in his books On the Orator and On the Laws. What shall I say of medicine? It first became famous at Athens through Hippocrates at the time of the plague; afterwards, as soon as it had emerged, it was divided into three principal families, as it were, and was only at last, some centuries ago, drawn together into one body and one way of teaching. Yet even this today is not a little attacked by certain recent iatrologists [ἰατρολόγοις] and is brought into popular ridicule. Of these faculties (the first of which the Athenians and Romans of old heard of with horror, while the other two were handled and taught almost by each individual who seemed to himself to be wise, at his own discretion), where and when and how the Academy of these faculties arose among those peoples, no one can show and prove from certain authors (if I remember rightly). It was only after the Roman empire had lasted for several centuries and had passed from the error of the world [ἀπὸ τῆς οἰκουμένης πλάνης] to the Christian faith, and to the truth of the saving and God-breathed [θεοπνεύστου] word. What then, someone may ask, is an Academy in the present age? An Academy is a school for letters, that is, a institution in which languages, arts and sciences of philosophy, as well as those highest faculties, are taught in a fixed order and manner, and which is furnished with holy prerogatives and privileges by due public authority, both civil and ecclesiastical.

units.la: Olim ergo doctorum hominum studia colentium docentiumque celebritas fecit Academiam: nunc autem Academiam facit judicii publici & summi autoritas. Et multa quidem fuerunt olim Academiarum genera: sed usus hoc tempore id fermè obtinet, ut quæ huiusmodi præsidio & autoritate fuerunt stabilitæ, ex singulari quodam jure & consensione publica nomen sibi vindicent Academiæ. Vera itaque proculdubio fuit olim Academia in populo Dei Hierosolymis, quam Deus lege imperaverat sanciveratque Deuteronomii 18. eaque post reversionem e Babylonia fuit restituta ex mandato Artoxerxis Regis & autoritate publica, Esdræ 7. ut in ea constaret doctrina certa sanctaque de rebus non Theologicis solùm, verumetiam politicis & ad jus civile pertinentibus. Postea vero imaginem potius & speciem Academiæ Iudæi habuerunt, quàm rei veritatem, ex quo labi cœpit Respublica & doctrina sacræ Theologiæ ad ambitionem, avaritiam, luxum, vanitatemque Scribarum & Pharisæorum traduci indignissimé. Eodem autem exemplo, postquam Romanum Imperium didicit fasces Christo Domino & Regi æterno submittere, Volaterranus autor est positam fuisse Bononiæ in Italia Academiam a Theodosio juniore; quam peridem ferme tempus Ambrosius scmirutæ potiùs urbis cadaver quàm urbem fuisse scribit. Sic Iustinianum Cæsarem mandavisse legimus, ut studium juris civilis a se compilati Romæ, Constantinopoli, Berytî, tanquam in Academiis Cæsarea autoritate sua fundatis docereturr: sic à Carolo magno Parisiensem, Papiensem, Ticinensem Academiam fuisse conditam historiæ narrant: Aurelianensem à Philippo Galliarum Regé, cui agnomen pulcro: Cracoviensem ab Vladislao Iagellone Rege Poloniæ: hanc Heidelbergensem à Ruperto primo, Electore Palatino, &c.
units.tr: In former times, therefore, the celebrity of learned men who cultivated and taught studies made an Academy; but now it is the authority of public judgment and of the highest power that makes an Academy. There were indeed many kinds of Academies in former times, but the custom of this age is for those established with such protection and authority to claim for themselves the name of Academy by a special right and public consent. Thus there was undoubtedly a true Academy of old among the people of God at Jerusalem, which God commanded and sanctioned by law in Deuteronomy 18, and which was restored after the return from Babylon by the command and public authority of King Artaxerxes, Ezra 7, so that a sure and holy doctrine might be established there not only on theological matters but also on political ones and those pertaining to civil law. Afterwards, however, the Jews had rather the image and appearance of an Academy than its reality, from which time the commonwealth began to slip and the doctrine of sacred theology was most shamefully turned to the ambition, avarice, luxury and vanity of the Scribes and Pharisees. In the same way, after the Roman Empire had learned to submit its rods to Christ the Lord and the eternal King, Volaterranus records that an Academy was established at Bologna in Italy by Theodosius the Younger; about which time Ambrose writes that the city was rather the corpse of a half-dead city than a city. Thus we read that the Emperor Justinian commanded that the study of civil law, which he had compiled, should be taught at Rome, at Constantinople and at Beirut, as in Academies founded by his imperial authority. Thus histories relate that the Academies of Paris, Pavia and Ticino were founded by Charlemagne; that of Orléans by Philip, King of the French, who had the surname "the Fair"; that of Kraków by Vladislaus Jagiełło, King of Poland; and that of Heidelberg by Rupert I, Elector Palatine, and so on.

units.la: Quæ cùm ita sint, justam Academiarum nostrarum materiam esse statuimus treis illas summas facultates præstantissimasque omnium, quæ in divinæ gratiæ, humanı juris, & curationis medicæ professionibus versantur: quarum elementa sunt artes & linguæ, rudimenta verò (sia Theologia discesseris) moralis & naturalis philosophia, Matheses adjumenta: formam verò non esse aliam, quàm publicum illum ordinem certis cancellis disclusum sapientissimè, & sanctas leges privilegiáque publica potentiorum autoritate attributa, & jure comprobata. Atque hinc duplex Academiarum distinctio nascitur: priòr a materia, posteriorque verò a forma ipsarum. A materia; tum quòd aliæ in una solùm facultate docenda occupantur, aliæ in duabus solùm, aliæ in omnibus; tum quòd aliæ præterea instructæ sunt documentis philosophiæ, velut optimis facultatum superiorum comitibus atque administris, aliæ idetiam obtinent juris, ut de linguis, artibus, mathematis, & rudimentis omnibus quæ ad tyrones sunt opus incunti cõsulant adolescentiæ. A forma autem distinguuntur Academiæ, non solùm quia varius est ipsarum ordo, prout à prima institutione & fundatione (ut vocant) placuit autoribus, aut post illud tempus reformare visum est ad commoditatem ipsarum & studiosæ juventutis bonum; verumetiam quia varia sunt earum jura & privilegia, his quidem ex communi solùm Academiarum lege concessa, illis verò amplius ex singulari quodam beneficio, & potentiorum, puta Cæsarum, Pontificum & omnium virorum principum indulgentia. Sed ab hiis omnibus, quia sunt singularia, perveltigandis hoc loco superscdebimus.
units.tr: These things being so, we determine that the proper subject matter of our Academies is those three highest and most excellent faculties of all, which are concerned with the professions of divine grace, of human law and of medical care. Their elements are the arts and languages; their rudiments, apart from theology, are moral and natural philosophy, and mathematics as aids. Their form is nothing other than that public order, wisely enclosed within fixed bounds, and holy laws and public privileges conferred by the authority of the powerful and confirmed by law. From this arises a twofold distinction of Academies: the first from their matter, the second from their form. They are distinguished by matter: partly because some are occupied in teaching only one faculty, some in only two, and some in all; and partly because some are furnished besides with the teachings of philosophy, as the best companions and servants of the higher faculties, while others also hold the right to consult on languages, arts, mathematics and all the rudiments needed by beginners entering upon youth. They are distinguished by form, not only because their order varies, as the founders have chosen it from its first institution and foundation (as they are called), or as it has seemed fit to reform it afterwards for the convenience of the Academies and the good of studious youth, but also because their rights and privileges vary: some are granted by the common law of Academies alone, others further by a special favour and the indulgence of the powerful, namely of emperors, pontiffs and all princely men. But since all these matters are particular, we shall pass over investigating them in this place.

units.la: CAPUT QVARTUM.
units.tr: CAPUT QVARTUM.

units.la: Quæ partes Academiarum.
units.tr: What the parts of the universities are.

units.la: ETsi ex iis rebus quas modò diximus, literato cuique homini satis exposita est sententia nostra de illis partibus in quas justa Academia distribui potest: tamen evidentiæ causa de hoc argumento aliquid amplius breviter & strictim attingemus, ut adumbrata quædam summæ hujusce informatio habeatur. Tria igitur capita sunt judicio meo in legitima nostrarum Academiarum forma & constitutione observanda, personæ, actiones earum, & leges ad utramque pertinentes: de quibus ordine deinceps quàm brevissimè ficri a nobis poterit, ὡς ἐν τάγῳ, non minutatim accurateque in hoc capite sumus perscripturi. Personarum genera sunt duo: unum docentium, discentium alterum. Nam ministeria quae ad hunc ordinem & corpus Academiarum adhibentur commoditatis ergo, quamvis mutatis nominibus, tamen communi sunt cum ordinibus ceteris instituto. Exempli causa, quum Academiae Cancellarium, Conservatorem privilegiorum, Syndicum, Collectorem, Bedellum, & siqua sunt alia id genus, appellamus: officia sunt in quavis Republ. ad commoditatem ipsius comparata. Quid enim Cancellarius, nisi custos annuli, ut olim dictus est Romanorum Caesarum temporibus? quid Conservator, nisi χαρτεφύλαξ, & actorum publicorum custos? Syndicum actuarium esse Academiae, Collectorem Quaestorem noverunt omnes. Bedellus vero (quem ego quidem voce Teuthonica Beutellum magis dixerim a mandatis perferendis) quid nisi apparitor, accensus, & stator dicendus est? His igitur omissis, virorum docentium, ut gymnasiorum, classes sunt quam plurimae: Hi enim suis in paedagogiis elementa, rudimenta, linguas, instrumenta scientiarum, & artes docent, illa accuratius & scrupulosius, has pinguius & crassius tyronibus exponentes: illi vero in altioribus gymnasiis, & grandiorum provectionumq; ἀβρηταϊοις. Et quemadmodum hi distincte per suas classes paedagogiam exercent, & ruditati puerorum accommodant suum institutionis modum: ficetiam illi per suos ordines studiis praesunt juventutis, eaque provehunt singuli suo doctrinarum genere. Nam linguas, artes, ipsamque adeo philosophiam exponunt auditoribus: linguas quidem & artes Magistri passim, hanc vero etiam Doctores philosophiae in Italia dicti. Summas vero facultates illas qui tradunt publice, etsi communi cum proxime praecedentibus appellatione Professores dicuntur in civili jure:
units.tr: Although my view of the parts into which a proper university may be divided should already be clear to any learned reader from what I have just said, for the sake of clarity I will briefly and concisely touch on this subject again, so that some outline of the whole matter is available. In my judgment there are three things to be observed in the lawful form and constitution of our universities: the persons, their activities, and the laws concerning both. I will set these out in order as briefly as I can, quickly [ὡς ἐν τάγῳ], and I do not intend to write about them in this chapter in minute and exact detail. There are two kinds of persons: teachers and learners. The offices that serve this order and body of the universities, though they bear different names, are for convenience' sake the same in kind as those of other bodies. For example, when we speak of the university's Chancellor, the Keeper of its privileges, the Syndic, the Collector, the Beadle, and any others of this sort, these are offices found in any commonwealth and designed for its convenience. For what is a Chancellor but the keeper of the seal, as he was once called in the time of the Roman emperors? What is a Keeper but a χαρτεφύλαξ [keeper of the records], the guardian of public documents? Everyone knows that the Syndic is the university's clerk and the Collector its treasurer. The Beadle (whom I would rather call, in German, the Beutell, the one who carries commissions) is nothing other than an attendant, an usher, and a macebearer. Setting these aside, there are very many classes of teachers in the schools. For in their elementary schools these men teach the rudiments, the languages, the instruments of the sciences, and the arts, expounding the former more carefully and scrupulously, and the latter more broadly and roughly, to beginners. Those in the higher schools teach the older and more advanced students [ἀβρηταϊοις]. And just as these teachers conduct their teaching in separate classes and adapt their method of instruction to the immaturity of the boys, so those others preside over the studies of the young through their own orders, and each advances them in his own branch of learning. For they expound to their hearers the languages, the arts, and indeed philosophy itself: the languages and arts are taught by masters everywhere, and philosophy also by those called doctors of philosophy in Italy. Those who publicly teach the highest faculties, although in common with the immediately preceding group they are called professors, are in civil law

units.la: { :1 Ii jure ; singularia tamen sunt nomina, quibus hi cum apud antiquos tum apud homines nostros distincti & insigniti sunt. Etenim vetera illa Imperatorum iura Antecessores eos appellarunt, id est, Kadmos sive Academos, ut res Romanas cum Phoeniciis, partum nempe cum suo parente, comparemus: his vero temporibus nostris id lex & consuetudo obtinet, ut Doctores vulgo, addé etiam (si placet) distinctionis ergo Doctores regentes (quod Gallia observat plurimum) nuncupentur. Quod epitheton profclassioribus in Academia docendae juventuti operam consumentibus eo apponitur, ut a Doctoribus aliis tum honorariis, quos vulgus Doctores bullatos vocat, tum creatis & renunciatis distinguantur, qui cognitione justa & solenni Academiae alicujus testificatione probati negotiis publicis implicantur, non otio Academico.
units.tr: {:1 These are called in law; yet these men have distinctive names by which they were marked out and honoured, both among the ancients and among our own people. For those old imperial laws called them Antecessores, that is, Kadmos or Academos, so that we may compare Roman affairs with the Phoenicians, namely the offspring with its parent. In our own times, however, law and custom have established that they are commonly called Doctors, and (if you like) for the sake of distinction, Doctors who regent [regentes] (a usage much observed in France). This epithet is added to the more distinguished men who spend their effort in teaching young people in the university, so that they may be set apart from the other doctors, both honorary doctors, whom the common people call "doctors with the bulla," and those who are created and proclaimed. The latter, after examination and the formal and solemn attestation of some university, are involved in public affairs, not in academic leisure.

units.la: Qui enim regentes sunt, ii non potentia Doctores solum, aut actuosi rerum quae ad publicum spectant procuratores sunt πραγματικοί, sed vocatione publica Academiae, actu, & legitima administratione docent quae suae facultatis sunt.
units.tr: For those who are regent are not merely doctors in power, or active managers of public affairs, the πραγματικοί [practical men]; they teach by public appointment of the university, actually and by lawful administration, what belongs to their faculty.

units.la: Horum vero Doctorum quos Hebraei Morim & Melammedim appellabant (unde natum est Palamedis nomen) aut etiam patrum, prout in rebus sacris fere ab inserioribus discipulisque vocabantur, numerus in prisciis illis Academiis pervarius & incertus fuit pro commoditate loci ubi instituebantur; sive facultates omnes in eis, sive una solum constituta esset. Principio enim singulis facultatibus ita prospectum est, ut Professores earum deni haberentur, qui singulas diei horas, antemeridianas & pomeridianas in explicandis facultatis suae dogmatis possent consumere. Ex eo autem numero ordinis & commoditatis causa unus aliquis deligebatur ex lege, collegio huic & corpori facultatis suæ præfuturus. Deligebatur autem sive pro ratione temporis quo in professione Academica versabatur (quod simplicissimum est, antiquissimum, & minus infestum ambitionibus) sive exate doctrinâve, quæ via ambitiosis factionibus magis est pervia. Quòd si per vices fiat, ut hic fit hodierno die, ea non electio, sed successio dicenda est. Huic ergo Decani vel Decurionis imponebatur nomen, quòd suæ decuriæ præses & moderator esset. Atque hinc factum illud est, quòd adhuc in Academiis nostris Decani parmanet appellatio. Posteaquàm verò numerus Academiarum auctus & amplificatus, deminuta commoda, & a potentioribus quacunque specie in rem suam versa sunt (cujus rei vestigium adhuc non obscurum exstat, quòd etiam hodierno die Ecclesiæ quædam collegiatæ plurimis in locis appellantur) detrahi necesse fuit in pædagogiis de præceptorum & παιδαγωγῶν, in Academiis de Professorum Doctorumque regentium numero, ut eadem opera & tenuitati Academiarum, & Professorum alimentis, & studiosorum commodis consuleretur. Alioqui enim Professoribus Academiæ & studiosi fuissent omnino caeruli, & humaniorum literarum studia jacuissent, facultatumque superiorum adjumenta. Interea verò Decani vel Decuriones dici perrexerunt hujus corporis in facultatibus singulis, quamvis deminutis numero, ταξιαρχῶν: sive antiquiores illi in sua professione essent (quod olim non imprudenter ambitionis prævertendæ & certæ commoditatis causa antiquitas factitavit) sive per vices in functione ista succederent annua, bima, trima, quadrima die.
units.tr: Of these doctors, whom the Hebrews called Morim and Melammedim [מורים ומלמדים] (from which the name Palamedes arose), or also "fathers," as in sacred matters they were usually called by their inferior pupils, the number in those early universities varied widely and was uncertain, according to the convenience of the place where they were set up, whether all the faculties were established in them or only one. At first each faculty was provided with ten professors, who could spend each hour of the day, morning and afternoon, in expounding the doctrines of their faculty. From this number, for the sake of order and convenience, one was chosen by law to preside over the college and body of his faculty. He was chosen either according to the length of time he had been engaged in academic teaching (the simplest and oldest method, and the least open to ambition), or according to his learning and teaching, which is the way more open to ambitious factions. But if it is done by turns, as is done today, this should be called not an election but a succession. This man was therefore called Dean or Decurion, because he was the president and director of his decury. And from this it comes that the title of Dean still remains in our universities. But after the number of universities grew and increased, their revenues were reduced and turned to their own advantage by the more powerful in various ways (a trace of which still clearly survives, since even today certain collegiate churches are called by that name in many places). So it became necessary to cut down in the schools the number of teachers and paedagogi, and in the universities the number of professors and regent doctors, so that the same measure would serve both the slenderness of the universities, the support of the professors, and the benefit of the students. Otherwise the professors of the university and the students would have been utterly sluggish, and the studies of the humane letters and the aids of the higher faculties would have lain neglected. Meanwhile, however, the deans or decurions of each faculty continued to be called, though now fewer in number, taxiarchs [ταξιαρχῶν]: whether they were the older men in their profession (which antiquity once wisely practised in order to forestall ambition and to secure a fixed advantage), or whether they succeeded one another in that office by turns, for one year, two, three, or four.

units.la: Discentium verò sive discipulorum auditorumque classes pro ratione temporis & profectus esse differentes res ipsa loquitur, & nos sequente capite, si Deus dederit, ostendemus. Etenim priscæ singularum Academiarum leges definitum dixerunt tempus; profectum vero discernit exploratio, quam lege & more fieri flagitat ratio in graduum, quos vocant, honoribus conferendis. Atque hunc quidem usum in populo Dei olim fuisse obseruatum ex Lege, nemini dubium esse potest qui librum quartum Mosis perlegerit: cùm in eo Sacerdotibus, Leuitis, & Dei administris tempora tyrocinii, progressus, ministerii, functionis, & vocationis ab ea præfigantur. Nam tyrocinio ad disciplinas quæ sunt opus percipiendas universum pueritiæ & adolescentiæ tempus, ad vigesimum vsque ætatis annum; tyrocinio ad ministerium capessendum præeunti proximè, anni quinque; ministerio succenturiato, anni totidem; functioni justæ & liberæ, viginti anni, puta a trigesimo ad quinquagesimum fuerunt deputati. Postremò autem vacatio a ministerio & laboriosa functione quavis, tamquam emeritis, data est quinquagenariis: non ut ventres otiosi essent, ut aves altiles in saginario aut in stara porci; sed ut doctrinæ solummodò tradendæ, ab obeundis laboribus cæteris immunes, attenderent. Hæc ergo legitima spatia jam olim a Deo in Iudæorum gente imperata. Sed quia certa quædam propriáque discentium discrimina per gradus honorum, veluti cancellos, sapienter disclusa sunt communi Academiarum lege, nos ea omnia in caput sequens certo consilio rejicimus, ubi diserte de discretione graduum & honorum collatione dicturi sumus.
units.tr: That the classes of learners, that is, of pupils and hearers, differ according to the length of time and their progress, the thing itself makes plain, and in the following chapter, God willing, I will show it. For the ancient statutes of the individual universities fixed the time; progress, however, is determined by the examination which reason requires to be carried out by law and custom in conferring the so-called degrees of honour. That this practice was observed among the people of God of old by the Law, no one can doubt who has read through the Fourth Book of Moses, since in it the times of apprenticeship, advancement, ministry, office, and the vocation that follows from it are prescribed for the priests, the Levites, and the servants of God. For the whole period of boyhood and adolescence, up to the twentieth year of life, was assigned to the apprenticeship in which the disciplines needed for learning are acquired; the five years immediately before taking up the ministry to the apprenticeship for the ministry; an equal number of years to service as an assistant; twenty years, that is from the thirtieth to the fiftieth year, to the true and free office. Finally, release from the ministry and from any laborious office was granted to those of fifty years, as to veterans: not so that they should be idle bellies, like fattened fowls in the coop or hogs in the sty, but so that, free from all other labours, they might attend only to the teaching of doctrine. These lawful spans were therefore long ago commanded by God among the Jewish people. But since certain definite and distinct divisions of learners have been wisely enclosed by degrees of honour, like barriers, by the common law of the universities, we deliberately reserve all these matters for the following chapter, where we shall speak expressly of the distinction of degrees and the conferring of honours.

units.la: Iam ergo id unum restat, ut de tertio loco, id est de legibus dicamus paucis. Quæcunque leges latæ sunt Academiis, aut ad officia & functiones pertinent eorum qui tamquam membra censentur in Academiarum corpore, aut ad iustum & decentem ordinem, aut ad beneficia & ornamenta in eas collata, quæ vulgo dicuntur privilegia.
units.tr: It now remains only for me to speak briefly about the third head, that is, the laws. Whatever laws have been enacted for the universities either concern the duties and functions of those who are counted as members of the body of the universities, or the just and proper order, or the benefits and ornaments conferred upon them, which are commonly called privileges.

units.la: Officia autem muneráque alia sunt eorum qui discunt, alia docentium. Auditorum, qui in stadio Academico decurrunt studiorum cursum, officia plurimùm describunt leges quædam communes omnium, & quædam speciales illius studii sive facultatis cui dant operam. Quo nomine sapienter sanè fuit illud a maioribus nostris institutum, ut communeis studiosorum leges, quas a singulis tenéri Academiæ ipsorúmque interest, omnibus palàm in Academia quotannis Rector; singularis verò atque priuatas facultatum, quisquis Decanus in ea futurus est præleget auditorum numero ad facultatem suam pertinenti. Nec absimilis est ratio in hominum docentium Professorúmque legibus. Nam harum aliæ consimiliter ad commune pertinent Academiæ, cuiusmodi eæ sunt quæ de Rectore, Senatu, consilio, administratione, & defensione totius universitatis vel Academiæ: aliæ ad proprium facultatis bonum & officium singulare, ut siqua de doctrinæ summa aut capite ullo, de professionum modo, ordine, tempore, loco, &c. de facultatis iure, & Professorum in ea commodis habenda erit consultatio: aliæ denique ad singulorum functiones spectant, ut si quando forte de lectionibus, doctrina, & circumstantiis omnibus præscribitur singulis quod facto opus est. Hæc enim venire interdum in quæstionem solent.
units.tr: The duties and functions of the students are of two kinds, as are those of the teachers. For the students who run the course of study in the academic arena, certain laws are common to all, and others are special to the particular study or faculty each one pursues. Our forebears wisely established that the general student laws, which every student is bound to observe and which concern the whole Academy, should be publicly read out to everyone in the Academy each year by the Rector. The private and particular laws of each faculty should be read by whichever Dean is to preside over it, to the students belonging to that faculty. The reasoning is much the same for the laws governing the teachers and professors. Some of these likewise concern the whole Academy, such as those on the Rector, the Senate, the council, and the administration and defence of the whole university. Others concern the proper welfare and special duties of a faculty, such as deliberation on the substance or any part of the doctrine taught, and on the manner, order, time and place of the lectures, and on the rights of the faculty and the advantages of its professors. Finally, others concern the functions of individuals, such as what is prescribed to each one concerning lectures, teaching and all the circumstances, as the situation requires. For these matters are sometimes brought into question.

units.la: Ordinem quia studiosa juventute in Academiis legitimè servari debet, commodéque potest, cùm in studiis colendis, tum in adipiscendis honorum gradibus, proximo capite exponemus. Quisnam autem sit Rectoris ordo in tota Academia, & facultatum inter se & uniuscujusque Decani in collegio facultatis suæ; id singulares Academiarum miarum leges præscribunt plurimùm, aut ex vetere & diu recepta in singulis consuetudine cognoscitur. Consuetudo enim (ut Iurecoss. aiunt) habetur pro lege, neque temere in hoc argumento perfringi debet: ne cujus ambitione publicus ordo dicatur violari, nève in gratiam ullius sternatur via ad alia consimilia, quæ bene instituta aut recepta non malè fuerint, perrumpenda.
units.tr: Because the order that studious youth must keep in the Academies ought to be observed lawfully and can be maintained conveniently, both in pursuing their studies and in attaining the degrees of honour, we shall set this out in the next chapter. As for the order of the Rector in the whole Academy, and of the faculties among themselves, and of each Dean in the college of his own faculty, the particular laws of our Academies mostly prescribe this, or it is learned from the old and long-established custom in each place. For custom (as the jurists say) is held to be law, and it ought not to be rashly broken in this matter, lest the public order be said to be violated through anyone's ambition, or lest a way be opened, by the favour shown to one person, for breaking into other similar arrangements that have been well instituted or received and have not been ill regarded.

units.la: Sed quid de beneficiis aut privilegiis Academiarum dicturi sumus? Exponemus paucis. Privilegiorum alia sunt ex communi, alia ex singulari iure attributa huic aut illi Academiæ. Hæc autem sapiens antiquitas literarum humaniorum alumnis concessit & dedit providentissimè, ut liberaliore bonorum studiorum cultura ampliùs accenderentur & inflammarentur ingenia juventutis ad res majores, & salutem Ecclesiæ commodáque Reipub. viri scientiis literarum auçti & ornati faciliùs ac meliùs proveherent. Hæc verò tempora, proh dolor, quę odio infestissimo & contemtu literarum indigno flagrant, non facilè ornant honoribus, & privilegiis augent Academias, intermorientibus scientiis, humanitate discedente, pietate profligata, invalescente barbarie, armis grassantibus. Verùm tamen, ut ad lineam, ex communi iure privilegia quæcumque habent & fruuntur Academiæ, duobus capitibus includi possunt: nempe vacatione ac immunitate ab oneribus, & commodorum prærogativis honorúmque accessionibus. Hæc enim duo capita fuisse olim gymnasiis & scholis in populo Dei attributa, aliquot in locis Moses demonstrat luculentissimè. Phœnices, Chaldæi, Indi, Ægyptii, alii honorem istum literarum studiis religiosè & semper habuerunt. Quid? quòd neipsi quidem Philistæi, quo tempore in tota fermè Iudæa poticbantur rerum, sacras Prophetarum
units.tr: But what are we going to say about the benefits or privileges of the Academies? We shall set them out briefly. Some privileges are granted to this or that Academy by general law, and others by special right. Wise antiquity, most providently, granted and gave these to the pupils of the liberal arts, so that by the more generous cultivation of the good studies the minds of young people would be kindled and inflamed the more towards greater things, and men enriched and adorned with the sciences of literature could more easily and better advance the welfare of the Church and the benefit of the commonwealth. But these times, alas, which burn with the most hostile hatred and contempt for literature, which is unworthy of them, do not easily adorn and enlarge the Academies with honours and privileges; the sciences die out, humanity departs, piety is overthrown, barbarism grows strong, and arms rage abroad. Nevertheless, to be brief, all the privileges that the Academies have and enjoy by general law may be included under two heads: namely, exemption and immunity from burdens, and the prerogatives of advantages and additions of honours. For these two heads were granted of old to the gymnasia and schools among the people of God, as Moses shows most clearly in several places. The Phoenicians, Chaldeans, Indians, Egyptians and others have always held this honour for the pursuit of letters with religious care. What of the Philistines themselves, who at the time when they held almost all of Judea in their power, did not dare to attack the sacred schools and retreats of the Prophets,

units.la: F scholas & asceteria ausi fuerunt infestare, sed Prophetis doctoribus atque discipulis locum suum, functiones, otia, honores integros & inviolatos permiserunt: hoc autem sacra historia priore libro Samuelis declarat evidentissime. Quantum gens Græca Academiæ & gymnasiis, Musarúmque delubris (ut Tullius ex vsu Græcorum vocat) in hoc genere indulserit nemo ignorat qui bonos autores legit: pleni sunt illorum libri, plenæ historiæ istius rei testimoniis. Quæ omnia Tullius ad Varronem scribens commodè elegantérque his verbis complexus est,
units.tr: but allowed the prophets, teachers and disciples their place, functions, leisure and honours, whole and unviolated? The sacred history declares this most evidently in the first book of Samuel. How much the Greek nation indulged the Academies, gymnasia and shrines of the Muses (as Cicero calls them, following Greek usage) in this respect, no one who reads the good authors fails to know: their books are full of it, and that history is full of testimonies to it. Cicero, writing to Varro, summed up all these things neatly and elegantly in these words:

units.la: Quæ studia, magnorum hominum sententia, vacationem habent etiam publici muneris, ut concedente Republica cur non abutamur? In primis verò testantur Græca & Romana jura, civilia & Ecclesiastica, Cæsarea & Pontificia: Pandectæ, Codex, Novellæ constitutiones, scriptáque & authenticæ, quibus iam olim ornata fuerunt & amplificata Academiarum iura. Hæc enim autoritate & consensu omnium, cum Ecclasiarum jure, tanquam sacra ad pios usus collata in Academias & instituta, comparantur. Merito id quidem: cùm Academiæ sint optima optimarum Rerumpub. primordia, Ecclesiarúmque seminaria, hæ verò fructuosi optimarum Academiarum partus.
units.tr: What studies, in the opinion of great men, have exemption even from public duty; why should we not make use of this, since the Republic concedes it? Above all, the Greek and Roman laws bear witness to this, civil and ecclesiastical, Caesarean and Papal: the Pandects, the Code, the Novels, the written and authentic constitutions, by which the rights of the Academies were long ago adorned and enlarged. For by the authority and agreement of all, these are compared with the rights of the Churches, as sacred things granted and set apart for pious uses in the Academies. And rightly so: for Academies are the best beginnings of the best commonwealths and the seedbeds of the Churches, while these are the fruitful offspring of the best Academies.

units.la: De singularibus autem privilegiis & prærogativis, quas huic aut illi Academiæ potentissimi Cæsares & fortissimi quique ac religiosissimi Principes piè tribuerunt scriptis certis & singularibus; de his igitur non est hic dicendi locus. Nam ea tantùm quæ sunt generalia percurrimus; & quo sunt notiora, eò leviore brachio perstringimus: quæ verò specialia & singularia sunt in Academiis, ea nec rimari cupimus, nec possumus percurrere, tum quia vix vnquam, ac ne vix quidem rerum singularium & individuarum (ut vocant) mens humana scientiam affequutura est, tum vero quia summa est earum in hoc tempore (ut Philosophi <bl>ἀεὶ τῶν ἀπμῶν</bl> dicunt) inconstantia & inftabilitas.
units.tr: As for the particular privileges and prerogatives that the most powerful Caesars, and the bravest and most pious princes, have granted to this or that Academy by certain and special documents, there is no place here to discuss them. For we run through only those things that are general, and the better known they are, the more lightly we touch on them. But the matters that are special and singular in the Academies we neither wish nor are able to investigate or run through, partly because the human mind will scarcely, if ever, attain knowledge of singular and individual things (as they are called), and partly because the sum of them at this time is, as the philosophers say, <bl>ἀεὶ τῶν ἀπμῶν</bl> [always of things in flux], inconstancy and instability.

units.la: CAPUT QUINTUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER FIVE.

units.la: Qui sint ordinarii gradus in Academia.
units.tr: Which are the ordinary grades in the Academy.

units.la: Omnia autem illa jura & beneficia ne forte in homines indignos, adde etiam ingratos, collata fuisse viderentur, piè sanè sapientérque majores nostri caverunt prospexerúntque, ut in literarum studiis, probationibus, testimoniis, honoribus certos gradus Academiæ observarent, quibus progressa ex ordine juventus studiosa ad legitimam quamdam studiorum suorum metam contenderet. Quæ res etsi interdum, præsertim magnis viris ludicram speciem aliquam παιγνιώδη puerilémque visa est habuisse, summa tamen cum dignitate ampliffimóque fructu peragitur, si bene & legitimè procuratur. Ac de studiis quidem, ordine, gradibúsque ipsorum in tertio cap. jam ante diximus ea prope omnia, quæ satis fermè ad institutum nostrum putamus pertinere. Nam studiorum gradus sunt in pædagogiis, sunt in gymnasiis scholisque maioribus, & Academiis: quos omneis gradus venerandailla antiquitas propterea disposuit & præfixit lege; ne imprudens & imperita ætas lubrico deciperetur, neve curiositate abrepta juventus aut præsumtione ebria (quam elegantissimè olim Democritus ἐγκαπλῶ θεσμοῖς appellabat) extra stadium plus satis excurreret magno malo literarum & suo. Nam hoc pacto fit ut vaga illa & instabilis ætas scipsam perdat, a curriculo suorum studiorum abludens, & illos amplissimos scientiæ thefauros illotis (quod ajunt) manibus contrectans inquinet turpissimé. Id ergo iuventuti videndum fuit, ut a carceribus ad calcem recta via compendióque perveniret: hoc autem quia nec bene nec semper aetas illa facit (faciunt enim paucissimi) majores legibus & quasi repagulis quibusdam positis bonae illi aetati prospectum esse voluerunt. Sic in paedagogiis pueritiae consulitur, ut certis principiis progressionibúsque ad certam aliquam linguarum scientiam perducatur per eas quas vocant classes: atque in eis rudimenta ἡ εἰσαγωγαί ad bonas artes & melioris scientiae instrumenta eidem aetati exponuntur. Sic in Academiis, ubi ex paedagogiis suis excessit adolescentia, traduntur progressiones certae ad instrumenta, artes, mathemata, ipsamque adeò philosophiam: quae spatia postquam justo legitimóque tempore decurrerunt juvenes studiosi, aditus ad facultates illas quas superiores dicunt permittitur. Vt ad facultates ventum est, non dispari quoque ratione & modo carceres, lineae, metae discendis & consequendis iis constitutae sunt.
units.tr: Lest all those rights and benefits should seem to have been conferred on unworthy men, or even ungrateful ones, our forebears wisely and piously took care and provided that in their literary studies, examinations, testimonials and honours they would observe certain grades of the Academy, by which young students, advancing in order, might strive towards a certain lawful goal of their studies. Although this arrangement has sometimes seemed to have a kind of playful and childish appearance, especially to great men, it is nevertheless carried out with great dignity and very ample benefit, if it is properly and lawfully managed. Concerning studies, their order and their grades, we have already said in the third chapter nearly everything that we think sufficiently pertains to our purpose. For there are grades of study in the paedagogia, in the gymnasia and greater schools, and in the Academies. Venerable antiquity arranged and prescribed all these grades by law, so that an unwary and inexperienced age might not be deceived by its slipperiness, nor youth, carried off by curiosity or drunk with presumption (which Democritus elegantly called "by fixed rules"), run out far beyond the course, to great harm both to letters and to themselves. For in this way that wandering and unstable age would ruin itself, departing from the racecourse of its studies, and would defile those vast treasuries of learning by handling them, as they say, with unwashed hands. Therefore youth had to be provided for, so that it might reach the goal from the starting gates by a straight and short path. But since that age does not do this well, or always (for very few do), our elders, having set up laws and, as it were, certain barriers, wished provision to be made for that good age. Thus in the paedagogia care is taken for boyhood, so that by fixed principles and progressions it is led to a certain knowledge of languages through the classes, as they call them; and in these the introductions [εἰσαγωγαί] to the good arts and the instruments of better learning are set before that same age. So in the Academies, where adolescence has left the paedagogia, fixed progressions are handed down to the instruments, the arts, mathematics, and philosophy itself. When young students have run through these stretches in the proper and lawful time, access to those faculties which they call higher is granted. When they came to the faculties, the barriers, lines and goals for learning and for attaining them were set up in no different manner or mode.

units.la: Ad haec vero studia, studiorúmq; gradus in Academiis commodè institutos accedunt tria illa quae totidem vocibus principio huius capitis perstrinximus, δοκιμή, πλᾶ ἡ ἴμαι, id est, probatio, testificationes, honorésque publico & solenni judicio in eos homines collati qui in literario hoc cursu constanter ex lege officióque perrexerint. Atque haec quidem singula etiam in populo Dei, quum Ecclesia Israëlitarum stetit, certo quodam modo fuisse observata non dubitaverim: quorum vestigia quaedam in Scripturis sacris comparent, nisi me animus & conjectura fallit. Sed quia vestigia illa quae dicimus obscurè adumbrantur magis quàm clarè exponuntur, ad alias historias & documenta istarum rerum venturi fumus,& trium illorum capitum quæ modò perstrinximus confirmationem ex eis ostensuri. Etsi quid hîc comprobatione opus in re tam honesta,utili,& necessaria? Probationem igitur illam,quam optimè Græci δοκιμὴν, recentiores nova & inaudita voce probam vel tentamentum dicunt, jam olim Academiæ optimæ habuerunt in Græcia,Latio,Gallia,& regionibus aliis;ut ex Iuvenalis versu quem supra cap 2.adduximus,vel pueri novisse possunt. Ejus autem (ne longiores simus) tria sunt genera: nimirum examen, disputatio,& lectio, quæ loci alicujus aut argumenti ad facultatem eamdem pertinentis enarratione & interpretatione concluditur. Examen, vt appellatur vulgo,præviuum illud est,quod à facultate,id est, à Doctorum Professoramque ad facultatem unam spectantium collegio & cœtu legitimè adhiberi solet, vt candidati juvenis peritia exploretur. Hoc duobus modis fieri assolet, potestq; commodè, αναλυτικῶς καὶ Δελε- κτικῶς. Analyticum examen est, in quo Decanus collegij totius nomine, aut cuicunque partes illas Decanus commendaverit, simpliciter hominem interrogat de summis capitibus scientiæ vel facultatis suæ. Exempli causa, si Theologiæ candidatus erit, facultas Theologica explorabit quid sentiat, & quid præstare possit in doctrina de Deo,de homine, de Scriptura sacra,de lege, de Evangelio, de fide & pœnitentia, &c. Si lurisprudêntiæ, inquiret de præceptis juris, de personis, rebus,actionibus; causis publicis & privatis, sacris & profanis, &c. Sin autem Medicinæ, rogabit de subiecto scientiæ illius, puta de corpore humano, partibus, affectionibus,curationibus, medicamentis, temperamentis, causis, &c. Alter vero examen quod Dialecticum appel-
units.tr: Besides these studies, and the grades of study rightly instituted in the Academies, there come those three things which we touched on at the beginning of this chapter in as many words: probation, testimonies, honours [δοκιμή, μαρτυρίαι, τιμαί], that is, examinations, attestations, and honours conferred by public and solemn judgment on those men who have persevered constantly in this literary course according to law and duty. And I would not doubt that each of these single things was also observed in some fixed manner among the people of God, while the Church of the Israelites stood; some traces of which appear in the sacred Scriptures, unless my mind and conjecture deceive me. But because those traces we speak of are shadowed obscurely rather than set forth clearly, we will come to other histories and documents of these matters, and from them show confirmation of those three things which we have just touched on. Yet what need is there of proof here, in a matter so honourable, useful and necessary? That probation, which the Greeks best call δοκιμήν, and which more recent writers, with a new and unheard-of word, call probam or tentamen, the best Academies of Greece, Latium, Gaul and other regions have had long ago, as even boys may know from the verse of Juvenal which we cited above in chapter 2. There are three kinds of it, namely examination, disputation, and lecture, which is concluded by the explanation and interpretation of some passage or argument pertaining to the same faculty. The examination, as it is commonly called, is the preliminary one, which is customarily held legitimately by the faculty, that is, by the assembly and company of the doctors and professors who look to one faculty, so that the young candidate's skill may be tested. This is usually done in two ways, and can be done conveniently, analytically and dialectically [ἀναλυτικῶς καὶ διαλεκτικῶς]. The analytic examination is that in which the Dean, on behalf of the whole college, or whomever the Dean has entrusted with that part, simply questions the man about the chief heads of his science or faculty. For example, if he is a candidate in theology, the theological faculty will explore what he thinks and what he can do in the doctrine of God, of man, of Scripture, of the law, of the gospel, of faith and repentance, and so on. If in jurisprudence, it will ask about the precepts of law, persons, things, actions, public and private causes, sacred and profane, and so on. But if in medicine, it will ask about the subject of that science, namely the human body, its parts, affections, cures, medicines, temperaments, causes, and so on. The other examination, which we call the dialectical one,

units.la: lamus,illud est quo Doctores & Professores in facultate singuli, prout libet, in contrariam sententiam cum suo candidato disputat de problematis & dogmatis, sive(ut dicuntur vulgo) de quæstionibus & decisionibus facultatis suæ, seque exercendis cum eo velitationibus literariis, tamquam levissima armaturæ, occupant: ut periculum hoc pasto faciant qua scientia, dexteritate, industriaque præditus ille sit qui adspirat ad certos honorum gradus. Hoc autem genus examinis non solùm est ex συνήμαt, certo definitoque inter agentes argumento, quum de aliqua materia proposita, condicta, & constituta studuit candidatus & de ea responsurus est, quam materiam facultas aut facultatis Decanus delegerit, verumetiam αὐτοσχεδίως in facultate adhibetur, quum Doctoribus, singulis qui in collegio facultatis versantur, licet quæstiones & argumenta quæcumque in mentem & buccam venerint afferre contrà, & respondentis candidati eruditionem variis problematis objectionibusque per satyram (ut aiunt) contari atque explorare. Optimum profectò cùm præsentis animi, tū fidelis in ea facultate studii, certissimúmq; solidæ eruditionis ac scientiæ documentum. Atque in uno quidem examine quod modò dicebamus, vel potiùs unica illius parte acquiescunt plurimùm Academiæ in Gallia, Italia, & regionibus aliis: quæ propter frequentiam & celebritatem locorum abundant majore candidatorum numero. His enim si tempus justum ad cæteros actus quos leges imperant tribui oporteret, neque dies anni peragendis iis ex lege sufficerent, neque habendis lectionibus ordinariis vacuum ullum tempus restaturum esset. Ordinarias quippe occupationes extraordinariæ plane interverterent. Quod autem illæ celebres Academiæ omittùt facere propter commoditatem, id Germania accurate seruat publici ordinis causa legūq; plurimùm. Nā Doctorū professorumq;,ut vocāt,Collegiatorū examen publicæ disputationes & lectiones solēt excipere. Ac disputationes quidē publicæ,ita se habēt ut de alteris modò dicebamus. Aliæ enim suum certumque περίβλημα ἐκ συωφήματος habent,id est,fiunt super thesibus(ut dicuntur vulgo) quæ de uno aliquo argumento disputandæ in publico proponuntur: aliæ verò sunt συμμικτοι καὶ αὐτοπροαίρετοι(quodlibeticas dicunt) id est,miscellæ siue commisculæ & collativæ disputationes ex infartilibus quæstionibus constitutæ; prout opponentibus de hac aut illa quæstione conferre;& candidati sciétiam obtrusis farctim materiis tentare placuerit. Harum autem disputationum priores magis sunt dialecticæ,posteriores ἐρεστικοί sophisticæque:ac proinde optimè à Nazianzeno Græca voce dicuntur ἐρεσχελίαι,cùm in eis candidatus magis(ut idem ait) ἐρεσχελεῖσθαι, quàm studiosus auditor οἰκοδομεῖται. Non enim id solum quæritur in hoc disputationis genere;ut innotescat hominis eruditio,sed etiam illud alterum,ut tentatis exploratisque illius moribus videatur,utrùm aptus sit nécne audiendis ferendisque aliorum communicationibus contrà sententientium,& hominum quamvis morosorum vitiis tolerandis inter disputandum & agendum. Doctum enim virum humanioribus literis imbutū ea modestia oportere esse apud omneis,Platone ipso & Cicerone testibus, ut & refellere paratus sit sine pertinacia, & refelli sine iracundia. Etsi ne hoc quidem ædificatione vacare potest, si cum opponentes juvenes modestiam & studium, tamen qui præsunt gravitatem autoritatemque adhibuerint: rebus in hoc genere præverrendis atque compescendis.
units.tr: is that in which the individual doctors and professors of the faculty, as each pleases, dispute with the candidate on the opposite side about problems and dogmas, or, as they commonly say, questions and decisions of their faculty, and occupy themselves with him in literary skirmishes, like light-armed troops, so that they may test by this experience with what knowledge, skill and diligence the man who aspires to certain grades of honour is endowed. This kind of examination is not only conducted by agreement [ἐκ συνθήματος], with a certain and defined argument agreed between the parties, when the candidate has studied a matter proposed, agreed and settled, and is to respond on a subject which the faculty, or the Dean of the faculty, has chosen; but it is also used extemporaneously [αὐτοσχεδίως] in the faculty, when each of the doctors who take part in the college of the faculty may bring against the respondent candidate any questions and arguments whatever that come into mind and mouth, and test and explore his erudition by various problems and objections, by satire, as they say. Certainly it is the best proof both of present wit and of faithful study in that faculty, and of very certain solid learning and knowledge. And in the one examination we have just mentioned, or rather in its single part, the Academies of France, Italy and other regions mostly rest content. Because of the frequency and fame of those places, they abound in a greater number of candidates. For if a proper time had to be given to the other acts which the laws prescribe, neither the days of the year would suffice for performing them according to law, nor would any free time remain for holding the ordinary lectures; for extraordinary business would plainly overturn ordinary business. But what those famous Academies omit for convenience, Germany keeps carefully, for the sake of public order and very much by law. For the examination of the doctors and professors, as they call them, the collegiate ones, is usually followed by public disputations and lectures. And public disputations are as I was just saying about the others. For some have their own fixed circumscription by agreement [περίβλημα ἐκ συνθήματος], that is, they are held on theses (as they commonly say) which are proposed in public to be disputed on one single argument; while others are mixed and voluntary [συμμικτοὶ καὶ αὐτοπροαίρετοι] (they call them quodlibetical), that is, miscellaneous or medley disputations composed of questions crammed together, so that the opponents may confer on this or that question, and the candidate may choose to try himself on subjects thrust in at random. Of these disputations the former are more dialectical, the latter more eristic and sophistical; and therefore they are rightly called by Nazianzen, in Greek, wranglings [ἐρεσχελίαι], since in them the candidate is (as the same writer says) rather wrangled with [ἐρεσχελεῖσθαι] than the studious hearer is built up [οἰκοδομεῖται]. For this kind of disputation seeks not only that the man's erudition become known, but also the other thing, namely, that when his character has been tried and tested it may be seen whether he is fit or not to hear and bear the arguments of others who think otherwise, and to tolerate the faults of men, however peevish, in disputing and in conducting himself. For a learned man, imbued with humane letters, ought to have such modesty before all people, as Plato himself and Cicero attest, that he is ready to refute without obstinacy and to be refuted without anger. Yet not even this can be free of edification, if the young opponents show modesty and zeal, while those who preside bring gravity and authority, in order to forestall and restrain matters of this kind.

units.la: Primùm igitur(vt missas faciamus promotiones illas pædagogicas quibus pueriles animi ad virtutē honorēq;, virtutis præmiū,non mediocriter accenduntur) qui pædagogicum studiū ἐν τοῖς λογικοῖς emensi sunt; iis postquā justo aliquo spatio audiendis lectionibus publicis in antegressis fuerunt confirmati, & scientiæ instrumenta hauserunt rudimentaq; philosophiæ, iis inquam bacca laurea decerni, & publicè tradi solet, tamquam fundamentorum bene feliciterque positorum in primis literarum humaniorum studiis. Atque hic primus est τῆς πλείστης βαθμός, vt dixerunt veteres, primus honorum in publico gradus, quem Nazianzenus σοφιστικὸν θρόνον eodem in loco quē paulo ante attingebamus appellavit. Qui enim ad hunc gradū pervenerant & in eo conquiescentes non adspirabant altiùs, σοφισταί dicebantur, vt qui non res sed verba, non philosophiam, sed instrumenta & quasi imaginem quādam philosophiæ in verbis positam profiterētur,nec ampliùs quàm τὰ λογικά profiteri possent Academiarū lege & more antiquissimo. Hoc modo Libanius & alii sophistæ dicti.
units.tr: First, then (to pass over those pedagogical advancements by which boyish minds are not a little stirred toward virtue and honour, the reward of virtue), those who have completed the pedagogical course [in the logical arts] are, after a suitable period of attending the public lectures in the earlier classes and of acquiring the instruments of learning and the rudiments of philosophy, awarded the bachelor's laurel, and it is customarily conferred publicly, as a sign that the foundations of the liberal studies have been well and happily laid. This is the first step [τῆς πλείστης βαθμός] of which the ancients spoke, the first public degree of honour, which Nazianzen, in the same place I touched on a little earlier, called the sophistic throne [σοφιστικὸν θρόνον]. Those who had reached this rank and rested there, without aspiring higher, were called sophists [σοφισταί], since they professed not things but words, not philosophy but its tools, and a kind of image of philosophy consisting in words; and by the most ancient custom and law of the Academies they could profess nothing beyond the logical arts [τὰ λογικά]. In this way Libanius and other sophists were so named.

units.la: His post legitimum tēporis spatium justúmque prosectū in gravioribus studiis philosophiæ, habita cognitione & probatione facta, si idonei comperti sint, secúdus gradus superiorq; tribuitur, data laurea, id est, corolla plexa ex lauro, quā vocant lauream Magisterii. Atq; hic summus gradus studii philosophici, ex quo in Germania & alibi Magistri, in Italia etiā Doctores philosophiæ nominantur, ubi assequuti sunt τὸ φιλοσοφικὸν δόγμα, editoq; eruditionis & scientiæ suæ specimine Magistri sive Doctores renunciati. Sic enim me autore apud Nazianzenum oportet legi pro eo quòd vulgo habetur δόγμα in istis verbis, quibus effert Basilium laudibus elegantissimè : ῥήτωρ &
units.tr: After a lawful period of time and a sound advance in the weightier studies of philosophy, and once knowledge and proof have been made, if they are found fit, the second and higher degree is conferred, with the laurel given, that is, a wreath woven of laurel, which they call the laurel of the Magistracy. This is the highest degree of philosophical study, from which in Germany and elsewhere they are called Magistri, and in Italy even Doctors of philosophy, when they have attained the philosophical doctrine [τὸ φιλοσοφικὸν δόγμα], and, having published a specimen of their learning and knowledge, are proclaimed Magistri or Doctors. For, on the authority of Nazianzen, I think this is how we should read, instead of what is commonly given as δόγμα, in those words in which he praises Basil most elegantly: ῥήτωρ &

units.la: G
units.tr: G

units.la: ῥήτορσι, ἢ περὶ τῶν σοφιστικῶν ἁρόνων φιλόσοφος ἐν φιλοσόφοις. ἢ περὶ τῶν ἐν φιλοσοφίᾳ δογμάτων τὸ μέγιστον, ἱερὸς ἐν χειρ-σιανοῖς, ἢ περὶ τῆς ἱερωσύνης. Summus,inquit,inter Rhetores Rhetor, etiā priusquàm sophisticos thronos adeptus esset: philosophus inter philosophos, etiam priusquàm renunciationes obtinuisset eas quæ in philosophicis usurpantur: denique quod omnium maximum, inter Christianos sacerdotes, etiam priusquàm functionem sacerdotii suscepisset.
units.tr: ῥήτορσι, ἢ περὶ τῶν σοφιστικῶν ἁρόνων φιλόσοφος ἐν φιλοσόφοις. ἢ περὶ τῶν ἐν φιλοσοφίᾳ δογμάτων τὸ μέγιστον, ἱερὸς ἐν χειρ-σιανοῖς, ἢ περὶ τῆς ἱερωσύνης. "He is the greatest," he says, "among rhetoricians a rhetorician, even before he had obtained the sophistic thrones; a philosopher among philosophers, even before he had obtained those proclamations which are used in philosophical matters; and finally, what is greatest of all, a priest among Christian priests, even before he had undertaken the office of the priesthood." [ῥήτορσι, ἢ περὶ τῶν σοφιστικῶν ἁρόνων φιλόσοφος ἐν φιλοσόφοις. ἢ περὶ τῶν ἐν φιλοσοφίᾳ δογμάτων τὸ μέγιστον, ἱερὸς ἐν χειρ-σιανοῖς, ἢ περὶ τῆς ἱερωσύνης.]

units.la: Hic autem ritus, quem hodierno die nostræ observant Academiæ, longè amplius simplicitatis, honestatis, & gravitatis habet, quàm vetus ille mos à Kadmi posteris seu Academicis observatus apud Athenienses, & inde ad gentes alias translatus: puta quum solenni pompa cādidatus in balneum sive lavacrum duceretur, fierentq; cetera quæ ibidem ab eodem Nazianzeno copiosè his verbis exponuntur: ἑπαταὶ ὁ ἐρεσχελήμενος προμαθεῖα ἀπὸ τῆς ἀγορᾶς ἐπὶ τὸ λουτρὸν παραγόμενον. ἡ προμαθή. Ἀρματίζαντες ἑαυτὸς ... ἐπὶ τὸ λουτρὸν ... κελεύει ἡ βοὴ μὴ παραβαίνειν, ἀλλ' ἴσαθαι, ὡς τὰ λαμπρὰ σφᾶς ... πάντων ... Καὶ τὰ τοῦ ἑαυτοῦ ... τῆς πόλεως τὸ πρυτανεῖον, &c.
units.tr: Yet this ceremony, which our Academies observe today, has far more simplicity, honesty and dignity than that old custom observed at Athens by the descendants of Cadmus, that is, by the academics, and from there carried over to other nations: namely, when the candidate was led to the bath or washing-place in solemn procession, and the other things that Nazianzen sets out at length in the same place, in these words: "Then the one who has been put through the disputations is led from the marketplace to the bath, in procession. ... They arm themselves ... to the bath ... the cry bids them not to step aside but to stand fast, since the bright ... of all ... and the things of their own ... the city's prytaneum, etc." [ἑπαταὶ ὁ ἐρεσχελήμενος προμαθεῖα ἀπὸ τῆς ἀγορᾶς ἐπὶ τὸ λουτρὸν παραγόμενον. ἡ προμαθή. Ἀρματίζαντες ἑαυτὸς ... ἐπὶ τὸ λουτρὸν ... κελεύει ἡ βοὴ μὴ παραβαίνειν, ἀλλ' ἴσαθαι, ὡς τὰ λαμπρὰ σφᾶς ... πάντων ... Καὶ τὰ τοῦ ἑαυτοῦ ... τῆς πόλεως τὸ πρυτανεῖον, &c.]

units.la: Postquàm verò, inquit, contentionibus exagitatus est, procedit pompæ solennis ritu, & per forum ipsum ad balneum sive lavacrum deducitur. Hic autem est pompæ modus. Disponunt seipsos per intervalla suis ordinibus binos qui candidato juveni honoris ergò præunt, & ipsum ad lavacrum procedentem sic deducunt pompali modo.vt autem accesserunt propiùs,clamore magno & exsultationibus utuntur velut lymphati. Sed jubet vox (opinor τὰ πεσφαγωγὲ quem vulgo promotorem vocant, aut certè Professoris alterius) ne progrediantur ulterius, sed ibi consistant, ut pote cùm non sit eos capturum balneum. Tum itaque simulac pulsaverunt fores, complosione juveni injiciunt metum, deinde faciût ingrediendi copiam. Hoc demum modo receptum, Professores putã, dant ei libertatem, eumque honoris ex æquo consortem velut unum de suo numero excipiunt ex lavacro illo procedentem. Atque hæ quidem sunt initationis partes candidatis illis jucundissime, &c. Iam verò tempus est veniamus ad facultatum illarum gradus quæ superiores appellantur.
units.tr: "But after he has been worn down by the contests," he says, "he proceeds with the solemn rite of the procession and is led down through the forum itself to the bath or washing-place. Now this is the manner of the procession. They arrange themselves by intervals in their own ranks, two by two, who go before the candidate youth as a mark of honour, and lead him as he advances to the bath in procession fashion. But when they have come nearer, they make use of a great shout and exultation, as if they were frenzied. But the voice (I suppose of the one they commonly call the promoter, or certainly of another Professor) bids them not to advance further, but to halt there, since the bath is not going to receive them. Then, as soon as they have knocked at the doors, they strike fear into the youth by a clash, and then they grant him the opportunity to enter. Once he has been received in this way, the Professors, I think, give him liberty, and receive him as an equal sharer in honour, as one of their own number, as he comes out of that bath. And these are indeed the parts of the initiation, most pleasant for the candidates, etc." Now it is time to come to those grades of the faculties which are called the higher ones.

units.la: Post elementorum ergo, rudimentorû,instrumentorum,doctrinarumq; omnium perceptionem legitimam quas superioribus illis facultatibus oportet ancillari; studia demum graviora in Theologia, Iurisprudentia, Medicináve occupantur, velut scientiis cum publico humani generisufu & bono conjunctissimis. Ac sacræ quidem Theologiæ studiosos & rebus divinis daturos operam fiz olim quasi deductos fuisse manu in populo Dei per certos legitimosque gradus, exempla & leges Israelitarum docent. Exemplo fit Samuel, & quicunque a primis annis Deo fuerunt consecrati legitima, aut etiam votiva consecratione. Legem superiore capite evidenter expositimus, judicio meo. Nam ad vigesimum vsque ætatis annum instruebantur illis præeuntibus ad rem divinam adjumentis, rudimentisque doctrinæ cælestis. Hic primus studiorum gradus. Inde ad vigesimum quintum in rerum ampliorum cognitionem & scientiam provehebantur: ut eo demum anno confortes essent. honoris alicujus & ministerii, sed tamen secundarii. Hic fecundus, & quasi Licentiæ (ut appellatur) gradus.
units.tr: After the legitimate perception of the elements, the rudiments, the instruments and all the branches of learning, which ought to serve those higher faculties, the more serious studies are at last taken up in Theology, Jurisprudence or Medicine, as sciences most closely bound up with the public use and good of the human race. That those who studied sacred Theology and were going to devote themselves to divine things were once, as it were, led by the hand into the people of God through certain lawful degrees, the examples and laws of the Israelites teach. Samuel is an example, and all who from their earliest years were consecrated to God by a lawful or even votive consecration. I have set out this law clearly in the previous chapter, in my judgment. For up to the twentieth year of age they were instructed, with those going before them as helps to the divine service, and with the rudiments of heavenly doctrine. This is the first grade of study. Then up to the twenty-fifth year they were advanced into a wider knowledge and understanding of things, so that only in that year would they be partners in some honour and ministry, though a secondary one. This is the second grade, as it were of Licentiate (as it is called).

units.la: Tandem vero quum ad trigesimum ætatis annum pervenissent, renunciabātur ὁμόπμοι, juftamq; suæ functionis ἐλεξθεῖαν adipiscebantur, ut Deus ipse Mosi præceperat. In lurisprudētiæ autē studio non ita fuit olim conftituta ratio, quū per annos magis numeraretur studii illius cursus, quàm ratio profectus (ut profectō opus est) haberetur. Etenim primo anno, quo juri primùm juvenes dabāt operam, priùs Dupondii per contemtum, post Iuftiniani novi ex rescripto fuerunt appellati, fecundo Edictales, tertio Papinianiftæ, quarto Λύτης quasi jam apti solvendis quæstionibus ex iure propositis, five (vt hodie vocantur) licentiati, quinto ἀπόλυτης ac velut Doctores creati & pronunciati sunt. Nec diversam fuisse Medicorum studii rationem est verisimile, ex quo publica auctoritate constitutum est Medicinæ corpus, discidiaque nationum medicarum vtcunque sublata.
units.tr: But when they had reached their thirtieth year, they were proclaimed ὁμόπμοι [homoioi?] and obtained the lawful ἐλεξθεῖαν [elexthein?] of their office, as God himself had commanded Moses. In the study of jurisprudence, however, the method was not so fixed in those days, when the course of that study was reckoned more by years than by the measure of progress, which indeed must be taken into account. For in the first year, when young men first gave themselves to law, they were called Dupondii, in contempt, and afterwards Justiniani novi from the rescript; in the second year Edictales; in the third Papinianists; in the fourth Λύτης [Lytes], as if now fit to resolve the questions proposed from the law, or, as they are called today, licentiates; in the fifth ἀπόλυτης [apolytes], and they were created and proclaimed as it were Doctors. It is likely that the method of study for physicians was not different, since the body of medicine was established by public authority and the divisions among the medical nations were somehow abolished.

units.la: Nostræ vero Academiæ inde a Caroli magni Cæsaris temporibus sanè commodiorem quamdam viam in his rebus videntur inivisse, vt non æquè temporis ac profectus & scientiæ ratio in candidatis haberetur.
units.tr: But our Academies, from the times of the emperor Charlemagne onward, seem certainly to have taken a rather more convenient path in these matters, so that in candidates the measure was not so much of time as of progress and knowledge.

units.la: Tres enim gradus ad has facultates singulas fuerunt instituti, infimus, medius, fummus, ad diuinæ legis imitationem. Infimus gradus eorum appellatur, qui in locorum (ut vulgo dicuntur) communium, & primarum institutionum intelligentia scientiaque adeò provexerunt, ut de sententia judicioque Collegii ducantur aliquo honore digni pro studiorum suorum fide, quæ in divina, civili, medicâve scientia naviter occupaverint. His bacca laurea symbolum honoris tradebatur, olim Apollini & Musis sacra: & ex ea dicti Baccalaurei, ut ante diximus, non autem (ut leve Magistellorum vulgus exi-stimat) Bacularii. In Academiis fiunt Baccalaurei; in sylvis sunt Bacularii, qui ligneos vient fasciculos, ut a Iurecos. nominantur. Medius gradus eorum dicitur, qui in suae facultatis studiis tantas progressiones fecerunt, ut de sententia Collegii sive facultatis suae judicentur idonei quibus liceat docere elementa & instituta prima facultatis suae, & de caetero exercere ea munera extra Academiam quae facultati suae coniuncta sunt, atque ad gradum summum, quum erit animus & commoditas, contendere. Horum itaque capiti imponebatur laurea libertatis index, quam dicunt licentiam, eo quòd libertatem illam in ea facultate quam colebant tum denum adipiscerentur, licet a caeteris commodis abstinerent quae in summum gradum tantummodo conferri solent. Summus vero gradus eorum est, qui in iisdem studiis ita sunt versati, & Collegio facultatis: quasi plenam & absolutam eruditionem suam ita in eo genere probaverunt, ut dignissimi ab eo pronuncientur palàm qui & doceant & exerceant omnia ad suam illam facultatem pertinentia, & secundùm divina humanáq; jura omnes honores, dignitates, officia, beneficia, & commoda obtineant quae literatissimis viris, Doctoribus meritissimis, & Professoribus lectissimis fuerunt attributa. His autem symbola jam olim plurima, & a plurimis collegiatis (ut vocant) ὡς νομίμως πλέτως de more & instituto collata sunt: plurima quidem, ut quàm plurima hujus summi gradus cum officia, tum ornamenta designarent: a plurimis vero, ut singulis qui in collegio suae facultatis erant hac solenni administratione suae partes essent, & singuli consensionem suam judiciúmque legitimum testificarentur in ea novi Doctoris renunciatione. Etenim, probi & sciti Doctoris officium libro & cathedra, ornamenta & commoda pileo cingulo annulóque, consensionem εἰς τὴν ὁμοίωμον osculo & benedictione confirmabant. Librum a Doctoribus versari & teri quis nescit oportere?neque id tantùm ut fiant ipsi in dies assidua lectione & studio doctiores, sed etiam ut in cathedram suggestúmque conscendant ubicunque vocatio legitima fuerit oblata, & ex eo superiore loco doceant pro autoritate queipsis judicio publico attributa est,& pro ea quam dederunt fide. Pileo libertatem ;cingulo militiam, annulo dignitatem, consociationem & pacem gratulationémque osculo, benedictione denique consecrationem quamdam significabant in novo munere, & partis susceptísque Dei ope & gratia honoribus. Atque hæc a singulis singula olim collata, posterioribus seculis ad commoditatem uni soli cuncta fuerunt demandata, re tamen integra permanente. Sic igitur uno eodémque tempore tria illa simul conjuncta sunt quæ principio capitis distinximus. Nam & studiorum antecedentium progressus legitimè cognoscûtur, & ea cognita legitimam suam testificationem consequuntur, & ornata suo testimonio ἀξιῶς τῆς πολιτείας ad legitimos honores & jura literarum studiis & summo eorum gradui attributa promoventur quàm honestissimè ex communi jure, & laudabili majorum nostrorum instituto.
units.tr: For three grades were instituted for each of these faculties, the lowest, the middle and the highest, after the pattern of the divine law. The lowest grade is called that of those who have advanced so far in the understanding and knowledge of the commonplaces (as they are commonly called) and the first principles, that, by the judgment and opinion of the College, they are deemed worthy of some honour, for the faithfulness of their studies, which they have diligently devoted to divine, civil or medical learning. To these a symbol of honour was given, the bachelor's laurel, once sacred to Apollo and the Muses; and from it they were called Baccalaurei, as I said before, and not (as the shallow crowd of little Magistri thinks) Bacularii. In the Academies they become Baccalaurei; in the woods there are Bacularii, who carry bundles of sticks, as they are called. The middle grade is that of those who have made such progress in the studies of their faculty that, by the judgment of the College or faculty, they are judged fit to teach the elements and first principles of their faculty, and to exercise outside the Academy the offices joined to their faculty, and to press on to the highest grade when they have the will and opportunity. So to the heads of these was imposed the laurel, the sign of freedom, which they call the licence, because they then obtained that freedom in the faculty which they cultivated, although they abstained from the other privileges which are usually conferred only on the highest grade. The highest grade is that of those who have been so practised in the same studies, and so have proved their learning in the College of the faculty as complete and perfect in that kind, that they are publicly pronounced most worthy to teach and to exercise everything pertaining to their faculty, and, according to divine and human law, to obtain all the honours, dignities, offices, benefices and advantages which were assigned to the most learned men, most deserving Doctors, and most select Professors. To these, in former times, many symbols were given, and by many of the so-called collegiates, according to custom and institution, in a lawful and solemn manner [ὡς νομίμως πλέτως]: many, indeed, so that they might signify as many offices and ornaments of this highest grade; and by many, so that each of those who were in the College of their faculty might have his part in this solemn administration, and each might testify his consent and lawful judgment in the proclamation of the new Doctor. For the duty of a good and learned Doctor was confirmed by a book and a chair, and his ornaments and advantages by a cap, a belt and a ring, and his consent to the fellowship [εἰς τὴν ὁμοίωσιν] by a kiss and a blessing. Who does not know that a book ought to be handled and worn by Doctors? And not only so that they may grow more learned every day by constant reading and study, but also so that they may mount the chair and the rostrum wherever a lawful summons is offered, and from that higher place teach with the authority given them by public judgment and by the trust they have given. The cap signified liberty, the belt military service, the ring dignity, the kiss fellowship, peace and congratulation; finally the blessing signified a kind of consecration to the new office and to the parts and honours undertaken with God's help and grace. These things, once conferred one by one by different people, in later centuries were all entrusted to one person for convenience, while the substance remained intact. Thus those three things which we distinguished at the beginning of the chapter are joined together at one and the same time. For both the progress of the earlier studies is lawfully recognised, and, being recognised, they obtain their lawful attestation, and, adorned with that testimony, are advanced, as worthily as possible by common law and by the praiseworthy institution of our ancestors, [ἀξιῶς τῆς πολιτείας] to the lawful honours and the rights of the literary studies, and to their highest grade.

units.la: CAPUT
units.tr: CHAPTER

units.la: CAPUT SEXTUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER SIX.

units.la: Quae causa & effecta graduum in Academiis.
units.tr: The causes and effects of degrees in the Academies.

units.la: ATque hi quidem gradus honorésque recepti in Academiis, & legitimè jam olim a maioribus instituti. Sed quæ causa? dixerit quispiam. Quid opus fuit hos gradus eo ordine conferri? quid obseruari has ceremonias? Cur distincti honorum gradus in eos homines fuerint collati, qui certa studiorum suorum stadia constanti ingenuóque labore decurrerint, tria potissimùm fuerunt in causa judicio meo: primum, ut ipsis de perfuncto strenuè studiorum cursu darentur honorum præmia: secundum, ut aliis omnibus studiosis exemplo consuleretur: tertium denique, ut illa publica & solenni Academiarum testificatione quódam singulari modo & via commoda Rebuspub. caveretur. Qui enim ad illas statas definitásque studiorum metas summo labore & diligentia pervenerunt, ii non mediocrem illorum fructum percipiunt animo, quum & anteacto labori suo in studiis literarum consumto honorem haberi vident, & testimonium præberi scientiæ quam suo illo labore diligentiáque paraverunt, & legitimas insuper commoditates ad transigendam cum honore vitam sperant & statuunt accessuras. Ac hono-rem quidem haberi antegressis studiis quantum momenti habeat in publicis & privatis rebus, ut adea porrò provehenda, res bene gerendas, vitámque honestè instituendam bonorum animos excitet, inflammet, urat; nemo nisi ignavus & excors ignorare potest.
