Demonstrant illud puerulorum igniculi, ac potius animorum ingenuorum faces, ad honorem atque gloriolam in oculis sodaliùm & congerronum suorum inardescentes: demonstrant adolescentum ἀεὶ ἀγωνία ἐς ἡμᾶς (quas promotiones dicunt) in vnoquoque studiorum genere ad quod genus animum suum appulerint: demonstrant etiam juvenum virorúmque fortissimorum exempla, quorum mentes & animos vel theatricæ laudationes in vulgo imperitáque plebecula, acclamationes, plausus, significationes faustæ affecerunt recreaverúntque. Quòd si hæc natura velut esca virtuti humanæ data atque oblata est ut sese honore pascat, augescat, confirmetur; in primis autem eo honore qui præterito jam labore industriáque partus & quæsitus fuerit: qui honor, Deus bone, præ theatrico illo clamore & ventosis vocibus futurus est, si decursus ille studiorum ad suas usque metas feliciter perductorum non in cavea aut circoab instabili vulgo & imperito numero, sed in Musarum choro a probis & literatisviris afficitur honore meritissimo? Præsertim si non solùm præterito labori suum illud præmium honoris tribuitur, sed indoli, ingenio, & scientiæ: quæ res bonum illum & laudatum juvenem semper comitantur, præcunt, ducunt, regunt, ac confirmant in amplissimis & optimis studiorum suorum fructibus percipiendis cum voluptate, & collocandis cum utilitate publica & sua. Nam his etiam illud accedit tertium, quòd jure & lege viris ejusmodi scientia, probitate, & virtute instructis commoda tribuuntur, quæ omnibus quidem optare datum est, sed literatis solis & testimonio publico ornatis assequi via legitima. Quænam autem illa sunt? officia nempe & beneficia, laudatæ illorum virtutis & honoris illius publici præmia. Officia enim & functiones honestissimæ quibus, obsecro, magis legitimè tum in Academiis, tum in optima quavis Repub. adeóque in Ecclesia offerri & deferri possunt, quàm iis qui sementem laborum suorum literarioque huic agro ad pietatem, virtutem, & utilitatem publicam crediderunt? Hæc certè justissima est (ut ita dicamus) illorum messis, quam denuò serunt in functionibus justis oportuno tempore ab Academiis, Rebusp ub. & Ecclesiis demetendam. Beneficia verò sive (ut dicuntur vulgo) privilegia cùm publica ex communi jure, tum etiam pro conditione & statu uniuscujusque singularia, quæ & quanta ad ipsos perveniant, neque enumerare hoc in loco possumus, neque libet perstringere: id enim versatur in oculis omnium, & bonos malim ex facto ea cognoscere experientiáque suâ; quàm inaniter discere prædicatione mea. Sanè ut a bonis viris seruntur officia, sic demetuntur ab illis ex jure beneficia: si non, saltem consolatur ipsos laboris bene occupati, rerumque benegestarum conscientia: præsertim cùm illud optimè noverint, nihil a viro bono nisi culpam præstari oportere.
units.tr: These degrees and honours, conferred in the Academies, have long been lawfully instituted by our forefathers. But what was the reason, someone may ask? Why was it necessary to confer these degrees in this order, and to observe these ceremonies? In my judgement there were chiefly three reasons why distinct degrees of honour were conferred on those who had run the set course of their studies with steady and honest labour: (1) that rewards of honour should be given to them for having vigorously completed the course of their studies; (2) that an example should be offered to all other students; and (3) finally, that by this public and solemn testimony of the Academies the commonwealth might be provided for in a singular manner and by a convenient means. Those who have reached those fixed and defined goals of study by great labour and diligence do not gain a small fruit from them in their minds, since they see honour paid to their past labour spent on letters, and see testimony given to the learning which they acquired by that labour and diligence, and they hope and expect that lawful advantages will also come to them for passing their lives with honour. That the honour of past studies has great weight in public and private affairs, and that it excites, inflames and fires good minds to advance further, to carry out their affairs well and to live honourably, no one but a lazy and foolish man can fail to know. Sparks in little boys, or rather the torches of noble minds, blazing with desire for honour and small glory in the eyes of their companions and fellow students, show this; the cries of young men at each stage of study (which they call promotions) in whatever kind of study they have turned their minds, show this; and so do the examples of brave young men and the most courageous men, whose minds and spirits were refreshed and gladdened by the applause, acclamations and joyful signs of the common and ignorant crowd, as at the theatre. But if this nature has been given and offered to human virtue as food, so that it may feed, grow and be strengthened on honour, and especially on the honour won and sought after labour and industry already past, then how much greater, good God, will that honour be which is given not by the shouting of the theatre and empty voices, nor in the amphitheatre or circus by an unstable and ignorant mob, but in the company of the Muses, by upright and learned men, as a most deserved honour? Especially if this reward of honour is given not only for past labour but also for natural aptitude, talent and knowledge, which always accompany such a good and praised young man, go before him, lead him, guide him and strengthen him in gathering the richest and best fruits of his studies with pleasure, and in putting them to use for the public good and his own. For to these is added a third thing: that by law and right, conveniences are granted to men thus furnished with knowledge, uprightness and virtue, which indeed everyone is allowed to wish for, but which only the learned and those adorned with public testimony can attain by lawful means. What are these? Namely offices and benefits, the rewards of praised virtue and of that public honour. For what honourable offices and functions, I ask you, can be offered and conferred more lawfully, whether in the Academies, in any good commonwealth, or indeed in the Church, than to those who have entrusted the seed of their labours and their learning to this field for piety, virtue and public usefulness? This is surely the most just harvest of such men (so to speak), which they sow again in just functions, to be reaped at the proper time from the Academies, the commonwealths and the Churches. As for benefits, or (as they are commonly called) privileges, both public ones from common law and particular ones according to each man's condition and status, what and how great they are, which come to such men, we can neither enumerate in this place nor do we wish to touch on them: for that lies in the sight of all, and I would rather that good men learn them from fact and their own experience than vainly from my preaching. Certainly, as offices are borne by good men, so benefits are reaped by them from the law; if not, at least the consciousness of work well employed and of affairs well managed consoles them, especially since they know very well that nothing should be given by a good man except what is owed.

units.la: Quod autem re viros illos bonos, fortes, & constantes juvat, id alios quoque exemplo permovet. Nam si cuius fides & diligentia in studiis nostris adhibita judicio & authoritate communi literati confessus in Academia probatur palàm; si prædicatur eruditio, doctrina, scientia, virtus summo labore ac vigiliis maximis comparata; si vehementes honoris stimuli & calcaria ad res porrò bene agendas atque procurandas publicè & priuatim admoventur; si honores amplissimi, officia laudatissima, gravissima beneficia, summáque commoda ex lege & more ostenduntur iis qui tam bene fortiterque versati fuerint in Academiis: quis nisi saxum aut stipes non permoveatur exemplo utili? quis non inardescat & desiderio rapiatur totus, ut suâ studia, mores, vitam denique totam instituat in eum modum, & conformet laudatissimis doctorum hominum exemplis, consiliis bonorum salutaribus, & piis Academiarum nostrarum institutis? Themiftoclem illum Atheniemfem non sivit quiescere tropæum Miltiadis: & juventutem literarum humaniorum studiis consecratam sinant quiescere a vigiliis, & inignavia desidiáque obscura torpescere, tam multa & gravia optimorum doctissimorúmque virorum & fortissimorum hominum documenta æternis laudibus dignifllma? quorum materia his ipsis studiis literarum parta, in florentiffimis Academiis educata, certis honorum gradibus confirmata, in Ecclesiis denique ac Rebuspub. fata & posita, ipsis incredibilem suavissimúmque existimationis fructum, Rebuspub. & Ecclesiis utilitatem maximam, Deo autori omnis boni honorem pepererunt & gloriam amplifllmam. ἀρχὴ δ' ἡμισυ παντὸς, inquit Hefiodus.
units.tr: But what helps those good, brave and steadfast men in fact, moves others also by example. For if anyone's faith and diligence in our studies is openly approved in the Academy by the judgement and authority of the learned community; if erudition, learning, knowledge and virtue won by great labour and vigils are proclaimed; if strong spurs and goads of honour are applied to carry on and pursue affairs well, both public and private; if the highest honours, most praiseworthy offices, weighty benefits and great advantages under law and custom are shown to those who have so well and bravely conducted themselves in the Academies: who, unless he were a stone or a stump, would not be moved by such useful example? Who would not take fire and be wholly carried away by desire, to order his studies, his morals, and indeed his whole life, in that manner and to conform it to the most praiseworthy examples of learned men, the wholesome counsels of good men, and the pious institutions of our Academies? Themistocles of Athens was not allowed to rest by the trophy of Miltiades; and shall we let the youth dedicated to the humane studies rest from their vigils, and grow numb in idleness and dull sloth, when there are so many and such weighty teachings of the best and most learned men and the bravest heroes, worthy of eternal praise? Their material, won by these very studies of letters, educated in the most flourishing Academies, confirmed by fixed degrees of honour, and at last placed and set down in the Churches and commonwealths, has brought forth for themselves an incredible and most sweet fruit of esteem, for the commonwealths and Churches the greatest usefulness, and for God, the author of every good, honour and most ample glory. The beginning is half of the whole [ἀρχὴ δ' ἡμισυ παντὸς], says Hesiod.

units.la: Præcipuè verò singulare illud est Academiarum erga Respublicas & Ecclesias Christi officium, quòd & homines commodi agendis rebus utilésque futuri miniftrantur, ac testimonio publico ostenduntur eis, & ab incommodis viris atque ineptis ad capessendas functiones publicas præcavetur. Hîc verò non agimus de illis Academiis, in quibus Doctores & Profeffores, fi forte, neglecta publici officij fui & fidei quam Academiæ dederunt ratione id unum curant, ut ex promotionibus frequentibus ac tumultuariis potiùs quàm legitimis commoda sua promoveant, & ex dispendio publico suum faciant compendium. Id enim qui faciunt, cùm iacturam faciunt fidei & existimationis suæ, tum malo maximo Ecclesias Réfquepub. afficiunt turpissimé. Atque hoc vitium, αἰχροκερδῶν personarum est, non optimarum legum: pfeudoacademicorum, ac non Academiarum culpa. Sed nos hîc de ordine publico loquimur, déque fidelibus eorum officiis, qui Spartam hanc, in qua exculti fuerunt ipsi, excolunt seduló. Magnum profectò præ-fidiunu fidium est & firmamentum Reipub. Academia bene instituta, instructáque legibus & viris suarum legum studiosis observantibúsque: vbi probantur & commendantur apti, inepti vero quasi à tergo relinquuntur, quòd Reipub. aut non satis utiles, aut planè inutiles, aut etiam damnosi futuri essent. Ac propterea etiam in ea gradus honorum legitimi & quidam velut cancelli fuerunt dispositi, scientiæque distributæ, ut quis quam ad rem quousque Reipublicæ utilis esse posset, doctissimorum, peritissimorum, optimorúmque virorum iudicio publico & testificatione communi teneretur. Quas ob res non possum equidem quin hoc loco eos moneam, horter, & obsecrem, quibus hæc cognitio iure, lege, & more permissa est, & quorum iudicio, consensione, ac autoritate fretæ Respublicæ, amplissimæ, Principéisque fortissimi viros testimoniis Academiarum ornatos ad functiones vocare solent, & consiliis sacris publicisque gubernaculis adhibere; quàm diligentissimè reputent, expendant, & videant quodnam sit officium suum, & quæ religio officii, quæ Rerumpublicarum & Ecclesiarum communis expectatio, quæ præstitæ & servatæ fidei in probationibus iudiciisque ipsorum utilitas, quæ denique sequuntur malorum Ilias, si fidem neglexerint, aut parui unquam secerint in hoc argumento: in quo tam necessaria est religio & fides, quàm ubi maximè. Hac enim culpa commissa, dum student sibi prodesse miseri, eadem opera & suam ipsorum evertunt fidem, & Academiarum dignitatem, honorem, autoritatémque proterunt, & obsunt Reipub. & Ecclesiis Dei: quod crimen impunè abire non sinet unquam Dominus. Sed hæc satis.
units.tr: Especially peculiar, however, is the duty of the Academies towards the commonwealths and the Churches of Christ, namely that they supply men who will be useful and fit for conducting affairs, and show them to be such by public testimony, and guard against unsuitable and inept men taking up public functions. Here, however, we are not speaking of those Academies in which the teachers and professors, if perhaps, neglecting the reason of their public office and of the trust which the Academies have placed in them, care only for this: that they advance their own interests by frequent and tumultuous promotions rather than lawful ones, and make their own profit at public expense. For those who do this, while they suffer loss of their faith and reputation, also inflict most shameful harm on the Churches and commonwealths. And this vice belongs to the persons, greed for shameful gain [αἰσχροκερδῶν], not to the good laws: it is the fault of pseudo-academics, not of the Academies. But we are speaking here of the public order, and of the faithful duties of those who diligently cultivate this Sparta in which they themselves were trained. A well-founded Academy, equipped with laws and with men who are zealous and observant of its laws, is a great bulwark and firm support of the commonwealth: where the apt are approved and commended, and the inept are, as it were, left behind, because they would be either not useful enough, or wholly useless, or even harmful, to the commonwealth. And for this reason, in the Academy also, the lawful degrees of honour and certain lattice-like barriers were arranged, and the sciences distributed, so that how far anyone could be useful to the commonwealth should be held by the public judgement and common testimony of the most learned, most skilled and best men. For these reasons I cannot but here advise, exhort and beseech those to whom this recognition is permitted by right, law and custom, and on whose judgement, consent and authority the commonwealths, the most ample ones and the bravest princes, are accustomed to call men adorned with the testimonies of the Academies to offices, and to employ them in sacred and public governance: that they consider, weigh and see most diligently what their duty is, and what the sanctity of office is, what the common expectation of the commonwealths and Churches is, what advantage comes from faith kept and observed in their examinations and judgements, and finally what Iliad of evils follows if they neglect their trust or make little of it in this matter, in which religion and faith are as necessary as anywhere. For by committing this fault, while wretchedly seeking to benefit themselves, they at the same time overthrow their own faith, trample on the dignity, honour and authority of the Academies, and harm the commonwealths and the Churches of God; a crime which the Lord will never allow to go unpunished. But enough of this.

units.la: Ceremoniæ autem aspectabiliáque symbola quibus
units.tr: The ceremonies and visible symbols which the universities use

units.la: utuntur Academiæ, etsi his superflua, illis ridicula videtur esse: cùm tamen in rebus fermè omnibus quæ publicam autoritatem desiderant, nonnulla soleant adhiberi, & in his ipsis actionibus jam olim citra superstitionem more & lege fuerint usurpata: non video quid sit in hoc toto actionum genere, quod homines severi magnopere exagitent, aut a quo boni abhorreant. Contrà enim si boni sunt, facile acquiescent rebus in quibus nihil est mali: sin mali erunt, quid istis cum Academia? Ac in omnibus quidem actionibus publicis aliquid ejusmodi fermè adhiberi nemo homo nescit, nemo vir bonus improbat. Nam humanæ functiones quæcunque sunt, forenses, castrenses, & domi, & foris, publicæ autoritatis symbola & testimonia publica post omnem hominum memoriam inde a prima institutione sua semper habuerunt. Regum diadema fuit: Imperatorum, paludamentum: Consulum & Prætorum, fasces: Ædilium, currus eburnei: Centurionum, vites: omnium in foro, toga: militiæ; baltheus cum gladio: & sexcenta alia. Atque hinc Græcis & Latinis cingendi & discingendi verba, pro eo quod est aptum militiæ hominem renunciare, aut ineptum indignum ve militia. In sacris functionibus & Ecclesiasticis, longè plures adhuc religionis ergò occupatæ fuerunt ceremoniæ, testæ universa Scriptura sacra, testibus historiis. Harum autem numero comprehendi oportet Academicas atque scholasticas: quæ vel ab vno Elisæi Prophetæ exemplo (ut taceamus cætera) commonstrantur. Duo enim fuerunt symbola quæ in hunc Elias contulit: unum fuit unctio, donum significans: alterum, abolla prophetica, qua vocationem ejus obsignavit: atque hæc per intervalla ipsi fucfuerunt data. Quid ergo? an more solùm exemplóque ceremonias defendimus? aut an omniufu carent? Neutrum profectò dicimus. Etsi hoc in symbolis a Deo imperatis agnoscimus singulare, quòd veritatem suam habebant conjunctissimam: absit autem, ut humanis signis dignitatem eamdem arrogemus. Verumtamen id de humanis symbolis certò possumus confirmare: quæcunque olim fuerunt in his rebus, aut hoc etiam tempore usurpantur symbola & ceremoniæ, iis aut habitum functionemque designari, aut dignitatem beneficiaque dono & functione coniunctæ, aut denique vocationem & initiationem (ut vocant) in ea functione cujus symbola tribuuntur. Hic verò habitum (quem in rebus sacris singulari quadam ratione donum vocari animadvertimus) habitum inquam liber in Academia, functionem auctoritatemque cathedra, dignitatem pileus annulusque; & (quo multi non utuntur hodierno die) cingulum, vocationem & initiationem osculum ac benedictio fausta significant. His rebus quid simplicius afferri potest? quid cum eã re quæ agitur convenientius? At profuerunt vetera, quæ Scriptura teste) olim mandabat Deus: quid prosunt ista? inquies. Primùm ut nihil per se juvant aut prosunt, sic nihil nocent aut obsunt cuiquam, quòd lege imperata sunt & recepta antiquo more sine offensa pietatis aut jactura conscientiæ. Deinde prosunt initiato: nam magis afficitur horum omnium sensu confirmatúrque, si justam interpretationem adjeceris. Tùm prosunt spectantibus & audientibus: singula enim oculis ipsorum subjecta symbolicè plus eos permovent, quàm si assa voce & nuda in frequente observantium corona proponerentur. Postremò autem prosunt Reipub. quæ hac publica testificatione magis confirmatur de commoditate eorum hominum, quorum operam ad utilitates publicas conducit adhiberi, quàm si incertis facultatis unius literis ab Academia clam & obscurè datis instructi essent. Literas enim legere & intelligere doctifolùm; hæc omnes etiam indoctissimi videre possunt: & illas quidem aut precariò aut furtim vir mendax obtinere, perscriptásque falsarius dare; hæc nunquam nisi præsentes, videntes, scientes prudentes viri boni & docti conferre possunt. Quæ cùm ita sint, non possumus bona fide, quin sapientissimæ illius antiquitatis prudentiam summam & circumspectum judicium in eo ipso admiremur, quod alii contemnendum, alii abolendum grandi supercilio putant.
units.tr: may seem superfluous to some and ridiculous to others. Yet in almost every matter that requires public authority, some such things are customarily employed, and in these very actions they have long been used, by custom and law, without superstition. I do not see what there is in this whole class of actions that serious men so greatly condemn, or from which good men shrink. On the contrary, if they are good, they will readily acquiesce in things that contain no evil; but if they are bad, what have they to do with the university? Indeed, everyone knows, and no good man disapproves, that in almost all public actions something of this kind is employed. For whatever human functions there are, whether judicial, military, at home or abroad, have always had public symbols and public tokens of authority, from the first institution of each, within the memory of all men. Kings had the diadem; emperors, the military cloak; consuls and praetors, the fasces; aediles, ivory chairs; centurions, the vine staff; all men in the forum, the toga; the military, the belt with sword; and countless other things. Hence the Greeks and Latins have phrases for girding on and taking off the belt, meaning to dismiss a man as fit or unfit for military service. In sacred and ecclesiastical functions, there were far more ceremonies for the sake of religion, as the whole of Holy Scripture attests, with the histories as witnesses. Among these we must count the academic and scholastic ceremonies, which are shown by the example of the prophet Elisha alone (to say nothing of the rest). For two symbols were given to him by Elijah: one was the anointing, signifying the gift; the other was the prophetic mantle, by which his calling was sealed; and these were given to him at different times. What then? Do we defend ceremonies merely by custom and example, or are they without any use? We certainly say neither. Although we acknowledge that in the symbols commanded by God this is unique, that their truth was most closely joined to them, far be it from us to claim the same dignity for human signs. Yet this we can certainly affirm about human symbols: whatever symbols and ceremonies there were in these matters in former times, or are still used at this time, they designate either a habit and function, or the dignity and benefits joined with a gift and a function, or finally the calling and initiation (as they are called) into that function to which the symbols are assigned. Here, the habit (which in sacred matters we notice is called a gift by a peculiar reason) — I say, the habit: the gown in the university; the function and authority: the chair; the dignity: the cap and ring; and (which many do not use today) the belt; the calling and initiation: the kiss and the blessing of good fortune signify. What could be presented more simply than these things? What could be more fitting to the matter at hand? But, you will object, the ancient things which God commanded by Scripture were useful: what use are these? First, just as they do not help or benefit in themselves, so they do not harm or hinder anyone, since they were commanded by law and received by ancient custom without offence to piety or loss of conscience. Second, they benefit the initiated: for their sense is more impressed and confirmed by all these things, if you add a correct interpretation. Then they benefit the onlookers and listeners: for when single things are set before their eyes symbolically, they move them far more than if they were proposed by bare voice and naked words in the crowd of observers. Finally, they benefit the commonwealth, which is more firmly assured by this public attestation of the fitness of those men whose labour it hires for public advantage, than if they were equipped with the uncertain letters of a single faculty, given secretly and obscurely by the university. For reading and understanding letters is the privilege of the learned; all, even the most unlearned, can see these symbols. A lying man may obtain those letters by begging or by stealth, and a forger may hand over written ones; but only men present, seeing, knowing, wise, good and learned can confer these. Since these things are so, we cannot in good faith but admire the great prudence and careful judgment of that most wise antiquity in this very thing, which others, with great disdain, think should be despised and abolished.

units.la: CAPUT SEPTIMUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER SEVEN.

units.la: Quæ sint adjuncta studiorum in Academiis, & quæ pugnantia.
units.tr: What are the accompaniments of studies in the Academies, and which are hostile to them.

units.la: NVNC restat, ut quæ adjuncta studiorum in optimis Academiis, & quæ pugnantia sint, explicemus. Etsi autem hic totus de adjunctis locus ad dicendum est uberrimus: quia tamen Athenis perdiu studia floruerunt, ac propterea eo in loco (si alibi usquam) de adjunctis ad studia literarum commodis prospectum est diligentissimè: propterea nos, omissis cæteris, ex Pausania solum dicturi sumus quæ adjunctorum ratio priscis philosophis olim placuerit, prout ab ipsis ad laudatam illam Academiam fuerunt constituta. Adjunctorum igitur alia fuerunt in Academia, & alia foris. Intus quasi in sacrario Academiæ, tria visebantur, Minerva, Hercules, olea. Primum igitur & omnium potentissimum significatum illud est, Deum ipsum autorem ac ducem studiorum esse: quod impiæ
units.tr: NOW it remains to explain what the accompaniments of study were in the best Academies, and which things are hostile to it. Although the whole topic of accompaniments is very rich for discussion, yet because studies flourished at Athens for a long time, and so in that place, if anywhere, provision was made most carefully for the conveniences that attend literary study, we shall, leaving aside the rest, speak only from Pausanias about what principle of accompaniments the ancient philosophers once approved, as they established it in that famous Academy. Some accompaniments, then, were inside the Academy and others outside. Inside, as it were in the sanctuary of the Academy, three things could be seen: Minerva, Hercules, and the olive. The first and by far the most powerful meaning is that God himself is the author and leader of studies. The impious nations indeed signified this by the name and image of Minerva, said to have been born of Jove, but they obscured the truth and overthrew it through ignorance of the true God.

units.la: illæ gentes & ἀγῶσι Minervæ olim sive Palladis Iove natæ nomine & simulacro figurabant quidem, sed veritatem obscurabant evertebantque veri Dei ignoratione. Quapropter etiam illa ipsa Minerva (ut idem in Bæoticis auctor est) Siga, id est, magna apud Cadmi posteros Phœnicia vel Syra voce dicebatur. Huic autem suberat draco pervigil, ad studia literarum vigilias adhiberi monstrans oportere. Hic enim, ut quum maximè, Deus laborantes adjuvat, κῆρι τὰ μὲν φαλλὸς, inquit Plutarchus, τὰς ἀμεταλλάκτους φόβοις, τὰ δ᾽ χαλεπὰ τῆς ἀνθρωπείας ἀλύσεως. Secundum fuit Herculis signum: illius puta Libyci, qui cum doctrinæ laude fortitudinem conjunxerat. Est enim Minerva, ut idem Pausanias loquitur, ἡ ἐγκλᾶ σύμμαχος fortitudo adhæret literarum studiis, sive colas ea apud te & Musas, ut loquebantur veteres, sive in officiis & functionibus justis eadem occupes: τὸ δ᾽ ἀρχαῖον μέσον studiorum venenum est. Tertium fuit olea, insigne pacis. Quantum vero pax ad studia juvanda faciat, me tacente res ipsa loquitur: & funesta hæc nostra tempora, quæ per impunem armorum licentiam nefarie insultant literis, hoc ipsum commonstrant (proh dolor) evidentissime. Atque hæc quidem intestina literarum bona: quorum unum si fregeris, earum studia fregeris atque suffuleris. Ad reliqua veniamus.
units.tr: For this reason that same Minerva (as the same author reports in the Boeotica) was called Siga, that is, in the Phoenician or Syrian tongue, great among the descendants of Cadmus. Beneath her lay a watchful dragon, showing that watches must be kept for the study of letters. For God, as always, helps those who labour: for some things are unchangeable through fears, while others are hard, being bonds of human servitude [κῆρι τὰ μὲν φαλλὸς ... τὰς ἀμεταλλάκτους φόβοις, τὰ δ᾽ χαλεπὰ τῆς ἀνθρωπείας ἀλύσεως], says Plutarch. The second sign was that of Hercules, that is, of the Libyan Hercules, who had joined strength of courage to the praise of learning. For, as the same Pausanias says, Minerva is the ally that clings to the pursuit of letters, whether you cultivate them with her and the Muses, as the ancients put it, or occupy yourself with the same in just duties and functions [ἡ ἐγκλᾶ σύμμαχος]; but the ancient middle course [τὸ δ᾽ ἀρχαῖον μέσον] is the poison of studies. The third was the olive, the emblem of peace. How much peace helps the study of letters, the thing itself speaks, though I say nothing; and these our grievous times, in which unpunished licence of arms shamelessly attacks literature, show this most clearly (alas). These are the inner goods of letters, and if you break one of them, you will break and undermine their studies. Let us come to the rest.

units.la: In ipso aditu vestibuloque Academiæ stabat Mercurius, pater (ut quidem volebant illi) eloquentiæ, atque ex eo Ἑρμῆς quasi interpres appellatus. Proximum igitur Academici & literarii illius studii ornamentum est eloquentia & commoda rerum enarratio: qua plurimum juventus solet ad studia excitari, studentes adjuvari; & viri boni doctrina præstantes emenso studiorum curriculo prodesse quàm plurimis, obcssè nemini. Ante hunc stabant castæ illæ fororesMusæ, humanitatisindices, & animi non immemoris beneficiorum quæ per literarum monumenta ad genus humanum pervenerunt: hæ enim Mnemosynes filiæ,id est,memoriæ dicebantur. Hæc ergo proximè adstat eloquentiæ, & humaniorum literarū studia cohonestat,gratiámq, & autoritatem maximam conciliat eis. Studia enim perpetuam quasi adsestricem humanitatem habent, humanitatem coluntstudiosissimè, & vicissim ab humanitate colunthonestissimè, omnibus officiis: unde λαδψίεια,liberalia & humaniora dicnntur vulgo. Tertium adjunctum, quod positum fuit ulterius petentibus Academiam, fuit ara Promethei:quoex locostudiosi juvenes cum ardentibus facibus ad urbem vsque solebant currere cursu perpetuo: sed hac lege tamen,ut faces currentium non exstinguerentur; aut eas aliis ex ordine ferendas traderent,usquedum aliquis ardente adhuc lampade in urbem decurrisset, victoriamque hoc signo comparavisset. Atque hinc illud proverbium quod vulgo dici solet, lampada tradere. Huiusautem rei totius significatum est, prudentia exercita & labore culta. Prudentia enim si non colitur, torpescit: si colitur & subacto ingenio jungitur, facile victrix exsistit omnium,&palmam obtinet in suo genere. Quid autem Epimetheo,& bardo rupici(ut ita dicamus)cum literarum luce? Quartum ante ingressum in Academiam fuit Amoris signum cum ara,quod signū Charmus dedicaverat. Amoris autem intelligimus pudici & casti: vt significaretur animus propensus & singulare studium, quo literati homines ergo literarum studia magis ac magis inardescunt, ex quo gustum aliquem ceperunt illius sapientiæ,quæ & paratur,& augetur, & occupatur ad justos usus suos publicos & pvatos earum beneficio. Quintum, & quidem in primis nobile atque copiosum instrumentum, fuit a monumentis, hinc quidem virorum fortium qui res præclaras pro patria gerentes fortiter occubuerât, illinc vero doctorum hominum philosophorumque summorum, qui scientiæ facem in publico accenderant, & omnibus præluxerant. Hoc autem documentum fuit ab exemplis: quæ in rebus humanis posiunt quàm plurimùm tum ad incitandos, tum ad retrahendos & inhibendos eorum animos qui incumbūt scientiis & in actionibus earum occupantur. Historia enim exemplorum index & magistra vitæ, maximum est profecto ad vitam bene instituēdam, literas excolendas, & functiones quasq; publicè atq; privatim obeūdas cum ratione & modo adjumentum. Extimum verò adjūctorum omnium ante Academiam illud fuit, quo significabatur, imperabatur juventuti, observabaturq; corporum exercitatio: sine qua etiam præclara quævis ingenia solent torpescere. Atque hinc factum est, ut rudes & illiterati homines ἀπάλαυστοι Græcis dicerentur. Hujus exercitationis corporibus salutaris, animis verò non inutilis documenta fuerunt duo ad Academiam. Vnum fuit Dianæ scptum, cum signis(ait Paufanias) Ἀξίσης καὶ Καλλίσης, vel potius ordine inverso, Καλλίσης καὶ Ἀξίσης (sic enim magis dixerunt Græci καλὸς καγαθὸς quàm contrà): id est, Dianæ honestissimæ & optimæ, non autem inhonestæ & sceleratæ exercitationis, literis humanioribus, earumque castitatiinimicissimæ. Alterum fuit palestræ sive gymnasij proprie appellati, cui vacans à studiis juvenitusaliquid temporis commodè utilitérque solebat tribuere. Sic & equestris, ut ad venationem est, & pedestris, ut ad palæstram, exercitatio salubris maximè adhibebatur, quod sine damno incommodóq; studiorum poterat fieri. Atque hæc quidem adjuncta Atticæ illius Academiæ fuerunt ornamenta: quæ siquis a nostris Academiis abesse volet, ne ille funditus eas everterit.
units.tr: At the very entrance and vestibule of the Academy stood Mercury, the father (as those people believed) of eloquence, and from this he was called Hermes, as it were the interpreter [Ἑρμῆς]. Next to this study of the Academy and of letters, then, is the adornment of eloquence and the agreeable narration of things, by which young people are especially stirred to study and studious men are helped; and good men who excel in learning, having completed the course of their studies, should benefit as many as possible and harm no one. Before him stood those chaste sisters, the Muses, the indicators of humanity and of a mind not forgetful of the benefits that have come down to the human race through the monuments of literature; for these were called the daughters of Mnemosyne, that is, of memory. These, therefore, stand next to eloquence and grace the studies of the humane letters, and win for them favour and the greatest authority. For studies have, as it were, a constant companion in humanity: they cultivate humanity most diligently, and in turn are cultivated by humanity most honourably, in all duties; whence they are commonly called the liberal and humane studies. The third accompaniment, which was placed further on for those seeking the Academy, was the altar of Prometheus, from which studious young men were accustomed to run with burning torches all the way to the city in continuous relay, on this condition, however: that the torches of the runners should not go out, but that they should hand them on in turn to others, until someone had run into the city with the lamp still burning and had won the victory by this sign. Hence comes the proverb commonly used, to hand on the torch. The meaning of the whole matter is practised prudence and cultivated labour. For if prudence is not cultivated, it grows dull; if it is cultivated and joined to a trained talent, it readily emerges victorious over all and wins the palm in its own kind. But what has Epimetheus, or the dull rustic (as we may say), to do with the light of letters? The fourth sign before entering the Academy was the emblem of Love with an altar, which Charmus had dedicated. By love we understand a chaste and pure love, signifying a mind inclined and a singular zeal, by which literary men are kindled more and more toward the studies of letters, since they have tasted something of that wisdom which is both acquired and increased, and is employed for its just public and private uses through the benefit of letters. The fifth, and indeed the chief and most abundant instrument, was the place of monuments: on the one side, of brave men who had performed illustrious deeds for their country and had fallen bravely; on the other, of learned men and the greatest philosophers, who had kindled the torch of knowledge in public and shone a light upon all. This instruction came from examples, which in human affairs have very great power, both to spur on and to restrain and check the minds of those who apply themselves to the sciences and are occupied in their practice. For history, the witness and teacher of life, is truly a very great help for ordering life well, cultivating letters, and discharging the duties both public and private, with reason and measure. The last of all the accompaniments before the Academy was that which signified, and enjoined on the young, the exercise of the body; without which even the most outstanding talents are wont to grow dull. Hence it came about that rude and unlettered men were called unacquainted with the palaestra [ἀπάλαυστοι] by the Greeks. Two examples of this exercise, wholesome for the body and not useless for the mind, were at the Academy. One was the shrine of Diana, with the statues (as Pausanias says) of Axiê and Kallisê, or rather, in reverse order, Kallisê and Axiê (for the Greeks spoke in this way of kalos kagathos rather than the reverse): that is, of Diana most honourable and best, not of dishonourable and wicked exercise, hostile to humane letters and most inimical to their chastity. The other was the palaestra, or what is properly called the gymnasium, to which the young, when free from their studies, were accustomed to give some time conveniently and usefully. So also horse-riding, as for hunting, and foot exercise, as for the wrestling-ground, were applied as a healthy practice, which could be done without loss or hindrance to studies. These were indeed the accompaniments and adornments of that Attic Academy; and if anyone should wish these to be absent from our Academies, let him beware lest he utterly overturn them.

units.la: Quid enim? nónne literarii hujus studii autor est Deus, & pietas in Deum arx quædam & caput literariæ illius sapientiæ? nónne cætera illa quæ modò fuerunt a nobis posita tam sunt ad hanc rem necessaria, sed suo tamen ordine singula, quàm quæ maximé? Fortes animi contendúnt strenuè & feliciter assequúntur, quod ignavi ne per somnium quidem cogitant. Pax & ἀπραγία studia literarum promovet, quæ frangit perturbatio. Eloquentia juventutem suaviter perducit cò liberalitate & comitate juncta, unde morosa deterret barbaries atque asperitas. Studia humanitate juvantur, eaque vicissim juvat & comit (ut ita dicamus) humanitas. Prudentiam humanæ scientiæ principem in cernendis & agendis rebus summa consensione veteres appellabant: eamdem vero scientiam aries inimicissimus labefactat & perdit, imprudentia. Amore & ardente studio foventur literæ: sed quid odio tetrius? quid tam exitiale est quàm invidia studiis humanioribus? Exempla honorum, & honores ipsi (ut vulgo dici solet) alunt artes: at inscientia pereunt, contemtu fordescúnt, & rubigine quadam obducuntur indignissimé. Denique honesta & mediocri exercitatione juvantur animi ad literarum studia: verùm si ad laborem plus æquo contenderis, franguntur: si plus remiseris, segnescunt & otio diffluunt in perniciem suam.
units.tr: For what? Is not God the author of this literary study, and piety toward God a certain citadel and head of that literary wisdom? Are not those other things just now set forth by us as necessary to this matter, each in its own order, as much as the greatest? Brave spirits strive vigorously and attain success, which the idle do not even dream of. Peace and freedom from business advance the study of letters, which disturbance breaks. Eloquence leads youth pleasantly, joined with liberality and courtesy, whereas barbarism and harshness, which are sullen, deter. Studies are helped by humanity, and in turn humanity helps and adorns them (as we may say). The ancients, with the greatest agreement, called prudence the prince of human knowledge in discerning and doing things; but the most hostile enemy of that same knowledge, imprudence, weakens and destroys it. Letters are fostered by love and eager zeal; but what is more foul than hatred? What is so deadly to humane studies as envy? Examples of honour, and honours themselves (as is commonly said), nourish the arts; but for lack of knowledge they perish, through contempt they grow foul, and they are covered with a certain rust, most unworthily. Finally, minds are helped toward literary studies by moderate and honest exercise; but if you press them to labour beyond measure, they break; if you relax them too much, they grow sluggish and dissolve in idleness to their own ruin.

units.la: Vtriusq; verò argumenti, adjumētorum inquâ eorum quæ proficiunt, & impedimētorum quæ officiunt studiis humanioribus atq; adversantur, exempla evidentissima hæc nostra memoria suppeditat. Iādiu enim sæculo amplius uno floruerūt literæ, ex Græcia in Italiā primū, inde autem autè in regiones finitimas singulari Dei beneficentia cōmigrantes. Sed ex quo tempore impietas revicta autoritate Dei & Scripturæ sacræ incepit furere, qui tandē studiorū fructus? qui Academiarum cultus percipi aut sperari potest? Grassatur impietas plus quàm Liciniana foris: intus ignavia (si dicere fas est) Libethria hodierno die invadit omnes plateas, & in domibus pene singulis sobolescit: perpetuum est turbarum aestuarium & insanus quidam Euripus, quem foris perflans a Gigantibus & Centauris omni ex parte Caecias permovet, intus ambitiosorum & ἀσπνδῶν hominum intemperantia. Proba, sana illa, & incorrupta Atticorum prisco rum eloquentia & lepos Atticus jam ferme exsulat, & a duro parasitorum & scurrarum ore frigidam potentioribus suffundentium adeò miscere profligatur, ut nihil praeter illud Aristophanis ἀπλχὴν βλέπως mox fit futurum reliqui, nisi Deus prospexerit, & bonos confirmaverit salutari manu. Humanitatem inhumanitas expellit palàm, motuum frequentia, armorum licētia, assentatorum ἀλλαζόνων fumo, potentiorum tyrannide: qui tum demum homines sibi videntur esse, quum (ut Aristodemus ille Cumanus apud Dionysium Halicarnassēum) id unū satagunt, ut literarum studia intercidant, & homines facti ad imaginem Dei in brutas pecudes transformentur. Praecoci prudentiae, & civili, & sanctae succedit scelerosa, profana, demens imprudentia, & juvenile consilium, tyrannidi & licentiae cuivis conuenientissimum. Succrescit odium & invidia in literas & literatos omnes per imperitiam vulgi, Suffenorum cacozeliam, importunorumque ἀρεταλόγων malitiam, veneno calumniae & detractionis omnia quamvis purissima inficientium. Honores auferuntur dignis, indignis scurris & libidinis voluptatumq; administris certatim offerūtur. Deniq; comissationes, cōpotationes, alcationes, tesserę, ludi ἀπλαγῆ, omnia ἀπλαγῆ & Sybaritica curātur potiùs, quā honestæ corporū exercitationes ad animi confirmationem pertinentes, studiorumque sanctorum adjumentum. Histot & tantis malis quis non indolescat bonus? quis Academias intermorientes non lugeat?
units.tr: Of the examples of both kinds, both of what helps and advances the liberal studies and of what hinders and opposes them, our own memory supplies the most evident instances. For more than a century letters have flourished, first migrating from Greece into Italy and from there, by the singular goodness of God, into the neighbouring regions. But from the time when impiety, having cast off the authority of God and of holy Scripture, began to rage, what fruit of study, what cultivation of the universities can be gained or hoped for? Impiety rages more than the Licinian [plague] abroad; at home, idleness (if it is lawful to say so) today invades every square and grows up in almost every house like Libethrian [pests]. It is a perpetual seething of disorders and a kind of mad Euripus, which, when the Giants and Centaurs blow upon it from outside, is stirred up on every side, and inside is churned by the intemperance of ambitious and [unruly] men. The honest, sound and uncorrupted eloquence of the ancient Attic writers and their Attic charm is now almost exiled, and is being so thoroughly mixed and trampled by the harsh mouths of parasites and buffoons, who pour cold flattery upon the powerful, that nothing will soon remain of it except that saying of Aristophanes, "to look at the ceiling," unless God looks down and confirms the good with his saving hand. Inhumanity openly drives out humanity: by the frequency of tumults, the licence of arms, the smoke of flatterers and boasters, and the tyranny of the powerful. Men seem to themselves to be men only when, as that Aristodemus of Cumae in Dionysius of Halicarnassus did, they labour at this one thing, that the study of letters should perish, and men made in the image of God be transformed into brutish beasts. Wicked, profane and mad imprudence succeeds to early prudence, and civil and holy [wisdom]; and a youthful plan, most suited to tyranny and to every kind of licence, takes its place. Hatred and envy against letters and all literary men spring up through the ignorance of the crowd, the bad taste of the Suffeni, and the malice of importunate boasters, who stain all things, however pure, with the poison of calumny and detraction. Honours are taken from the worthy and offered eagerly to unworthy buffoons and servants of lust and pleasure. Finally, drinking parties, carousing, dicing, games of chance, and everything Sybaritic are cared for more than honest bodily exercises, which pertain to strengthening the mind and to the furtherance of holy studies. At such great evils, who that is good would not grieve? Who would not mourn the Academies dying away?

units.la: Quæ cùm ita sint, nunc certè, siullo unquam tempore, necesse est omnes ii qui boni esse & haberi volunt, neruos omneis contendant ingenii, ut his legitimis omnibus adjumentis, seposito omni privato studio & perturbatione, confirment labentes Academias, earumque elementa, instrumenta, disciplinas, facultates, honores, ornamenta, commoda, pro eo ac possunt, promoveant quàm fidelissimè, atque a fraudibus Satanæ, inimicorum impressiones, & hypocritarum cuniculis defendàt propugnentque religione summa. In primis autem Deum studiorum nostrorum autorem, ducem, & arbitrum singuli studiosè castè adeuntes orent, vt misertus istorum miserrimorum funestissimorúmque temporum nutantes Academias & gravem ruinam minantes statuminet, collapsas erigat, omneis vindicet ab omni malo, eásque bonis omnibus augeat quæ ad gloriam suam, communebonum, & suorum salutem novit pertinere. Tuigitur, Domine aspice & fac. Amen.
units.tr: Since these things are so, now surely, more than at any time, it is necessary that all who wish to be and be considered good should strain every nerve of their talent, so that, with all these lawful aids, setting aside all private pursuits and disturbances, they may strengthen the tottering Academies and advance their foundations, instruments, disciplines, faculties, honours, ornaments and advantages as faithfully as they can, and defend and protect them with the utmost religious devotion against the frauds of Satan, the attacks of enemies, and the mines of hypocrites. Above all, let each one who studies, approaching with a pure heart, pray earnestly to God, the author, leader and judge of our studies, that, taking pity on these most wretched and deadly times, he would steady the wavering Academies that threaten grievous ruin, raise up those that have fallen, defend all from every evil, and enlarge them with every good thing that he knows pertains to his glory, the common good, and the salvation of his people. Look upon us therefore, O Lord, and grant it. Amen.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: THE END.

units.la: TYPOGRAPHVS LECTORI.
units.tr: THE PRINTER TO THE READER.

units.la: EDITO elegantissimo hoc D.D. Junij de Academia libello, visum est singularum Academiarum quae in orbe Christiano sunt breviter subiungere catalogum: quo patria earum nomina, ortus, & situs ex Ptolemaeo describuntur. Vale.
units.tr: Now that this most elegant little book, Academia, by the Reverend Junius, has been published, it seemed good to add briefly a catalogue of the individual universities that exist in the Christian world, in which their home cities, founding dates and locations are described after Ptolemy. Farewell.

units.la: ANGLIAE.
units.tr: ENGLAND.

units.la: OXONIENSIS, Ptol. Caleva, vulgo Oxforde: quam instituit Aluredus, Saxonum Rex, anno Christi 872. Postea vero ex multorum Principum & Praesulum beneficentia, amplissimis structuris, redditibus, & privilegiis ornatur: habetque iam collegia xvi. aulas etiam viii. singula aedificiorum splendore magnificentissima, ac bonarum literarum artiumque omnium studiis florentissima.
units.tr: OXFORD, Ptolemy's Caleva, commonly called Oxford: founded by Alfred, King of the Saxons, in the year of Christ 872. Afterwards, through the generosity of many princes and prelates, it has been adorned with very ample buildings, revenues and privileges. It now has 16 colleges and 8 halls, each most magnificent in the splendour of its buildings, and most flourishing in the study of good letters and of all the arts.

units.la: Cantabrigiensis, vulgo Cambridge: in qua primum Collegium instituit Batsomus, Eliensis Episcopus, anno 1274. Habet iam collegia xi. aulas etiam 1.11. eaque omnia aedificiorum celebritate praestantissima. Habuit etiam antea scholam publicam peraugustam (in qua philosophia, humanioresque disciplinae tradebantur) a Sigeberto, Estanglorum Rege, constitutam, anno 637.
units.tr: Cambridge, commonly called Cambridge: in which the first college was founded by Bishop Batsomus of Ely in the year 1274. It now has 11 colleges and 1.11 halls [sic], all of them most outstanding for the renown of their buildings. It also had earlier a very famous public school (in which philosophy and the humane disciplines were taught), established by Sigebert, King of the East Angles, in the year 637.

units.la: BOHEMIAE.
units.tr: BOHEMIA.

units.la: Pragensem, Prage, exstructam a Carolo Quarto Imperatore, anno 1370 teste Aenea Sylvio de gestis Bohemicis. eius long. 32. grad. lat. 50. grad. 6. minut.
units.tr: Prague, Prague, built by the Emperor Charles IV in the year 1370, according to Aeneas Sylvius in his deeds of the Bohemians. Its longitude 32 degrees, latitude 50 degrees 6 minutes.

units.la: GALLIAE.
units.tr: FRANCE.

units.la: Andegavensem, Angiers, in Comitatu Andegavorum. eius long.13.49.lat.460.
units.tr: Andegavensem, Angiers, in the County of Anjou. Its long. 13.49, lat. 460.

units.la: Aucnionensem, Auignon, in Gallia Narbonensi, ad Rhodanum. Huc Ioannes xxii.Pontifex Max.curiā Pōtificiam Roma transtulit, quæ annos 60.ibi mansit, floruitque tū Academia,anno 1360.eius long. 22.lat.45.52.
units.tr: Avenionensem, Avignon, in Narbonese Gaul, on the Rhône. Here John XXII, the Supreme Pontiff, transferred the papal court from Rome. It remained here sixty years, and the university flourished then, in 1360. Its long. 22, lat. 45.52.

units.la: Aurelianensem, Orleans, ad Ligerim fl.in Ducatu Aurelianensi: constructam ab Aureliano Duce, anno 1276. eius long.15.36.lat.47.13.
units.tr: Aurelianensem, Orleans, on the river Loire, in the Duchy of Orléans, founded by Duke Aurelian in 1276. Its long. 15.36, lat. 47.13.

units.la: Bituricensem, Bourges, quam ante multos annos construxit Dux quidam Bituricensis. eius long. 18. lat.45.30.
units.tr: Bituricensem, Bourges, which a certain Duke of Bourges built many years ago. Its long. 18, lat. 45.30.

units.la: Burdigalensem, Bourdeaux, ad Garumnæ fl.oftium, in Ducatu Aquitanico.eius long.18.lat.45.30.
units.tr: Burdigalensem, Bordeaux, at the mouth of the river Garonne, in the Duchy of Aquitaine. Its long. 18, lat. 45.30.

units.la: Dolanam, Dole,in Burgundiæ Comitatu, ubi pro toto Comitatu celebratur Parlamentum.eius long.21.25.lat. 45.10.
units.tr: Dolanam, Dole, in the County of Burgundy, where the Parlement for the whole county is held. Its long. 21.25, lat. 45.10.

units.la: Duacensem, Douay, in finibus Hannoniæ & Artesiæ. Hanc instituit Philippus Hispan. Rex, sub annum 1558. eius long. 24.30.lat.52.50.
units.tr: Duacensem, Douai, on the borders of Hainault and Artois. King Philip of Spain founded it around the year 1558. Its long. 24.30, lat. 52.50.

units.la: Montem Pessulanum, Montpelier, in Provincia Narbonensi,olim Iurisprudentiæ, nunc Medicinæ studio florentem. eius long.20.46.lat.43.5.
units.tr: Montem Pessulanum, Montpellier, in the Province of Narbonne, once flourishing in the study of law, now in the study of medicine. Its long. 20.46, lat. 43.5.

units.la: Nannetas, in Britannia superiori versus Oceanum Cantabricum, vulgò Nantes. eius long.1.6.lat.48.12.
units.tr: Nannetas, Nantes, in Upper Brittany, towards the Cantabrian Ocean. Its long. 1.6, lat. 48.12.

units.la: Parisiensem,seu Lutetianam, Paris. Hanc Alcuinus in Grandcheftria, Britonum Academia, prope eam quæ nunc Cantabrigia dicitur, educatus, instituit; Consummauit autem Carolus Magnus, anno 791. teste Volaterrano. eius long.17.8.lat.47.55.
units.tr: Parisiensem, or Lutetianam, Paris. Alcuin, educated in Grandcheftria, the British academy near the place now called Cambridge, founded this one. Charlemagne completed it in 791, according to Volaterranus. Its long. 17.8, lat. 47.55.

units.la: Pictauiensem, Poitiers, Ptol. Augustoritum ; Picto-nuna num metropolin. fita eft in Piētonum Comitatu. eius long.17.50.lat.48.20.
units.tr: Pictauiensem, Poitiers, Ptol. Augustoritum; the metropolis of the Pictones. It is situated in the County of Poitou. Its long. 17.50, lat. 48.20.

units.la: Rhemenicēm, Reims, Campaniæ metropolis, in qua Reges Franciæ confecrantur. hanc ante paucos annos erexit Carolus Lotharingiæ Cardinalis. eius long. 18.55. lat.48.45.
units.tr: Rhemensem, Reims, the metropolis of Champagne, where the Kings of France are consecrated. Charles, Cardinal of Lorraine, established it a few years ago. Its long. 18.55, lat. 48.45.

units.la: Tolosanam, Toulouse, in Comitatu Tolosano, in qua maximè floret iurisprudentia. Hæc statim post Lutetianam incepit. eius long.17.lat.43.32.
units.tr: Tolosanam, Toulouse, in the County of Toulouse, where the study of law especially flourishes. This one began immediately after the Parisian. Its long. 17, lat. 43.32.

units.la: Valentinam, Valence, prope Rhodanum fl. in Allobrogum Ducatu, qui nunc Sabaudiam & Delphinatum completitur. eius long.26.9.lat.42.6.
units.tr: Valentinam, Valence, near the river Rhône, in the Duchy of the Allobroges, which now embraces Savoy and Dauphiné. Its long. 26.9, lat. 42.6.

units.la: GERMANIÆ.
units.tr: GERMANY.

units.la: Argentinensem, alias Argentoratensem, Strasburg, in Alsatia, eius long.24.30.lat. 48.5.
units.tr: Argentinensem, also Argentoratensem, Strasbourg, in Alsace. Its long. 24.30, lat. 48.5.

units.la: Basilicnsem, Basel, quam Pius 2. qui ex Concilij Basilicnsis scriba electus est Papa, erexit anno sui Pontificatus 2. id est,1459. vt ex eiusdem literis confirmatoriis patet. eius long.24.22.lat.47.41.
units.tr: Basiliensem, Basel, which Pius II, who was chosen pope from the secretaries of the Council of Basel, founded in the second year of his pontificate, that is, in 1459, as his confirmatory letters make clear. Its long. 24.22, lat. 47.41.

units.la: Coloniensem, Colen, ad Rhenum fl. instituta anno 1398. sub Urbano Pontifice. eius long.23.28. lat.51.
units.tr: Coloniensem, Cologne, on the river Rhine, founded in 1398 under Pope Urban. Its long. 23.28, lat. 51.

units.la: Dilinganam, Dilingbe, in Bavaria superiori, Iesuitarum insigne asylum. Hanc instituit Episcopus quidam Augustanus, anno 1549.
units.tr: Dilingam, Dillingen, in Upper Bavaria, a famous asylum of the Jesuits. A certain Bishop of Augsburg founded it in 1549.

units.la: Elmstadianam, Elmstad, in Ducatu Brunsvicensi, quam ante sexennium fundavit Iulius iam Dux Brunsvicensis, à quo etiam Iulia dicitur. eius long. 28. lat.
units.tr: Helmstadiensem, Helmstedt, in the Duchy of Brunswick, which Julius, then Duke of Brunswick, founded six years ago, and from whom it is also called Julia. Its long. 28, lat.

units.la: 62 · 63 Francfordiensem, Franceford,ad Viadrum fl.in Marcha Brandeburgensi conftructam anno 1206. eius long. 32. 34.lat. 52.33.
units.tr: 62 · 63 Francofordiensem, Frankfurt, on the river Oder, in the March of Brandenburg, built in 1206. Its long. 32.34, lat. 52.33.

units.la: Friburgensem, Friburg,in Brisgoia Rhetia: quam condidit Albertus Auftriacus, anno1460. eius long.24. 38. lat.48.13.
units.tr: Friburgensem, Freiburg, in the Breisgau, in Rhaetia, which Albert of Austria founded in 1460. Its long. 24.38, lat. 48.13.

units.la: Gripfvvaldensem Gripzwald, in Ducatu Pomeraniæ. Initium cepit anno1457. vt scribit Bentherus in Ephem. Hist.cius long.31.56. lat.54.18.
units.tr: Gripswaldensem, Greifswald, in the Duchy of Pomerania. It began in 1457, as Bentherus writes in his Ephemerides historicae. Its long. 31.56, lat. 54.18.

units.la: Heidelbergensem, Heydelberg, quam exstruxit Rupertus I. Palatinus Rheni, anno 1387. cius long.25.38. lat. 49.45.
units.tr: Heidelbergensem, Heidelberg, which Rupert I, Count Palatine of the Rhine, built in 1387. Its long. 25.38, lat. 49.45.

units.la: Ingolstadiensem,Inglestad, in Ducatu Bavariæ: quæ ex Viennensi Austriæ incœpit anno 1210.eius long.29.6.lat. 48.42.
units.tr: Ingolstadiensem, Ingolstadt, in the Duchy of Bavaria, which began in 1210 out of the Viennese one of Austria. Its long. 29.6, lat. 48.42.

units.la: Lipsensem, Leipzig, in Misnia, quam Teutones, supra duo millia, propter exortas Hussitarum contentiones, à Praga uno die discedentes,triúmque dierum itinere illinc profecti, erexerunt, anno1408. eius long. 29.58. lat.51.14.
units.tr: Lipsiensem, Leipzig, in Meissen, which the Teutons, more than two thousand of them, founded in 1408, when they left Prague on a single day, because of the disputes that had arisen with the Hussites, and set out from there on a three-day journey. Its long. 29.58, lat. 51.14.

units.la: Lovaniensem, Louen, quam instituit Iohannes Dux Brabantiæ,anno 1426.eius long.20.36.lat.59.59.
units.tr: Lovaniensem, Louvain, which John, Duke of Brabant, founded in 1426. Its long. 20.36, lat. 59.59.

units.la: Lugdunensem, seu Logodunensem Batavorum, Leyden: prope occidentale Rhenioftium, à Gulielmo Aurasino Principe inauguratam, circiter annum 1574. eius long.26. 40. lat.53.30.
units.tr: Lugdunensem, or Logodunensem Batavorum, Leiden, near the western mouth of the Rhine, inaugurated by William of Orange, Prince, around the year 1574. Its long. 26.40, lat. 53.30.

units.la: Marpurgensem,Marpurg, in Hassia, institutam à Philippo Lantgravio, anno 1535.eius long.25.45.lat.51.
units.tr: Marpurgensem, Marburg, in Hesse, founded by Landgrave Philip in 1535. Its long. 25.45, lat. 51.

units.la: Moguntinam, Mentz, Germanicarum ferc antiquissimam: in qua laudabilis illa, & utilissima ars impressoria per Iohannem Faustum inventa est, circiter annum 1453.eius long.25.4.lat.50.8. Montem Regalem, Konigsberg, in Pruffia, quam condidit Albertus Dux Brandeburgenfis, anno 1544. teste Ebero in Calend. eius long. 41.16. lat. 54.17.
units.tr: Moguntinam, Mainz, almost the oldest in Germany, where that praiseworthy and most useful art of printing was invented by Johann Faust, around the year 1453. Its long. 25.4, lat. 50.8. Montem Regalem, Königsberg, in Prussia, which Albert, Margrave of Brandenburg, founded in 1544, according to Ebero in his Calendar. Its long. 41.16, lat. 54.17.

units.la: Roftochiensem, Roftock, in Ducatu Mechelburgio, quae ex Erphordiensi initium cepit. anno 1419. eius long. 30.14. lat. 54.36.
units.tr: Rostochiensem, Rostock, in the Duchy of Mecklenburg, which began out of the one at Erfurt in 1419. Its long. 30.14, lat. 54.36.

units.la: Treverensem, Trier, inter Germanicas vetustissimam. eius long. 26. lat. 49.10.
units.tr: Trevirensem, Trier, the oldest among the German ones. Its long. 26, lat. 49.10.

units.la: Tubingensem, Tubinghe, in Ducatu Wirtenbergenfi, quam exstruxerunt Euerardus Comes Wittenbergenfis, eiusque mater Melchtildis, anno 1447. eius long. 26. 23. lat. 48.38.
units.tr: Tubingensem, Tübingen, in the Duchy of Württemberg, which Count Eberhard of Württemberg and his mother Mechtild founded in 1447. Its long. 26.23, lat. 48.38.

units.la: Viennensem, Viena, in Pannonia superiori, Austriae Metropolin, constitutam à Rodolpho Austriaco, anno 1363. eius long. 35.8. lat. 48 22.
units.tr: Viennensem, Vienna, in Upper Pannonia, the metropolis of Austria, established by Rudolph of Austria in 1363. Its long. 35.8, lat. 48.22.

units.la: Wittenbergensem, Wittenberge, in Ducatu Saxoniae: quae sub Frederico Saxoniae electore incoepit, anno 1502. eius long. 30.30. lat. 51.50.
units.tr: Wittenbergensem, Wittenberg, in the Duchy of Saxony, which began under Frederick, Elector of Saxony, in 1502. Its long. 30.30, lat. 51.50.

units.la: HISPANIAE.
units.tr: SPAIN.

units.la: Complutensem, vulgò Alcala, de henares regno Castiliae, quam instituit Episcopus quidam Toletanus. eius long. 10.20. lat. 41.40.
units.tr: The Complutensian academy, commonly called Alcalá (de Henares), in the kingdom of Castile, founded by a certain Bishop of Toledo. Its longitude 10.20, latitude 41.40.

units.la: Granatensem, Granada, Ptol. Illiberin, in Hispania Be-tica. eius long. 8.34. lat. 39.50.
units.tr: The Granadan academy, Granada, Ptolemy's Illiberis, in Spanish Baetica. Its longitude 8.34, latitude 39.50.

units.la: Leridensem, Lerida, Ptol. Ilerda: in Hispania Tarraconensi. eius long. 56. lat. 41.46.
units.tr: The Lérida academy, Lérida, Ptolemy's Ilerda, in Tarraconensian Spain. Its longitude 5.6, latitude 41.46.

units.la: Oftensem, seu Oscensem, vulgò Huesca, in Hispania Siguntiêscem,vulgò Ciguenca.eius lõg.14.50.lat.39.30. Toletanam, Toledo,in regno Castellæ:ubi Alfonsus 10. Hispaniarum rex.29. tabulas Astronomicas fecit circiter annum 1260.eiuslong.9.4.lat.39.55.
units.tr: The Huesca (Oscensis, or Oscensis) academy, commonly called Huesca; in Spanish Sigüenza, commonly called Cuenca; the Toledo academy, Toledo, in the kingdom of Castile, where Alfonso X, king of the Spains, made the Astronomical Tables around the year 1260. Its longitude 9.4, latitude 39.55.

units.la: Vallifolitanam ,seu Pinciensem, vulgò Valladulit,in Castellæ regno. eiuslong. 10.10. lat.42.0.
units.tr: The Valladolid academy, or Palencia, commonly called Valladolid, in the kingdom of Castile. Its longitude 10.10, latitude 42.0.

units.la: Lullianam, in urbe Mallorca, infulæ Maioricæ (quæ altera est Balearidum) metropoli : nomen perrò sumsitâ Raymundo Lullio,qui ibidem natus & educatus est.eius long.16.45.lat.39,15.
units.tr: The Lullian academy, in the city of Palma de Mallorca, metropolis of the island of Majorca (which is the second of the Balearics); it took its name from Raymond Lull, who was born and educated there. Its longitude 16.45, latitude 39.15.

units.la: Italiæ.
units.tr: ITALY.

units.la: Bononiensem,olim Bolonia,vulgò Bologna la grassa,in Romandiola: quam ædificauit Theodosius Imperator, circiter annum 447. vt scribit Volater. Sed temporis progressu fere dirutam ,restaurauit Carolus Magnus, circiter annum 806.eiuslong.32.5.lat.43.54.
units.tr: The Bolognese academy, formerly Bologna, commonly called Bologna la Grassa, in Romagna; it was built by the Emperor Theodosius around the year 447, as Volaterranus writes. But over time it was nearly destroyed, and Charlemagne restored it around the year 806. Its longitude 32.5, latitude 43.54.

units.la: Ferrariensem, Ferraria, in Ducatu Ferrariensi. eius long.32.15.lat.44.23.
units.tr: The Ferrara academy, Ferrara, in the Duchy of Ferrara. Its longitude 32.15, latitude 44.23.

units.la: Florentinam, vulgò Florentia,in Tuscia.eiuslong. 33. 30. lat.43.4.
units.tr: The Florentine academy, commonly called Florence, in Tuscany. Its longitude 33.30, latitude 43.4.

units.la: Mediolanensem, vulgò Mylano,in Langobardia.hæc Virgilij etiam tempore, quem in ea boni literis operam navasse scribunt, fuit percelebris. eius long.28. 20. lat.45.6.
units.tr: The Milanese academy, commonly called Milan, in Lombardy. It was very famous even in the time of Virgil, who is written to have worked at good letters there. Its longitude 28.20, latitude 45.6.

units.la: Patavinam,vulgò Padua,in Marchia Trevizana,à Casolo Magno institutam, anno 791. in hac urbe natus est historiæ parens,Titus Livius. eiuslong.32.50.lat.44.30.
units.tr: The Paduan academy, commonly called Padua, in the March of Treviso, founded by Charlemagne in the year 791. In this city was born Titus Livy, father of history. Its longitude 32.50, latitude 44.30.

units.la: Papiensem, vulgò Pauia, in Langobardia. Hanc urbem Carolus Magnus, ab Adriano Pontifice in Italiam, adversus Desiderium Regem Langobardicum evocatus, obsedit ; anno 773. ibique nobilem posteà Academiam constituit, circiter annum 800. eius long.28.22 lat.44.50.
units.tr: The Pavian academy, commonly called Pavia, in Lombardy. Charlemagne, summoned into Italy by Pope Adrian against Desiderius, king of the Lombards, besieged this city in the year 773, and there afterwards founded a noted academy, around the year 800. Its longitude 28.22, latitude 44.50.

units.la: Perufinam, Ptol.Perufia Augusta, vulgò Perufca, in Tufcia.eius long 35.18.lat.42.56.
units.tr: The Perugian academy, Ptolemy's Perusia Augusta, commonly called Perugia, in Tuscany. Its longitude 35.18, latitude 42.56.

units.la: Pifanam, Pisa, in Tufcia, quam Volaterranus scribit à Pontifice Max.fuisse inauguratam, anno 1339. eius long. 31.28.lat.42.22.
units.tr: The Pisan academy, Pisa, in Tuscany, which Volaterranus writes was inaugurated by the Supreme Pontiff in the year 1339. Its longitude 31.28, latitude 42.22.

units.la: Romanam, Roma, olim terrarum Dominam. Hæc primò (vt habent annales, & Historici) ex Athenarum resquiis Academia esse cœpit, anno 700. Postea verò paulatim corruentem instauravit auxitque Eugenius 4. qui passim in Europa Academias ornavit & instituit, vt scribit Sabellicus. eius long. 36.40.lat.41.40.
units.tr: The Roman academy, Rome, once mistress of the world. This, as the annals and historians report, first began to be an academy out of the remains of Athens, in the year 700. Later, however, when it was gradually falling into ruin, Eugenius IV restored and enlarged it; he also adorned and founded academies in many places throughout Europe, as Sabellicus writes. Its longitude 36.40, latitude 41.40.

units.la: Senensem, vulgò Sena, in Tuscia : ab urbe Roma centum miliaribus dissitam.eius long.348.18.lat.42.50.
units.tr: The Sienese academy, commonly called Siena, in Tuscany, a hundred miles distant from the city of Rome. Its longitude 348.18, latitude 42.50.

units.la: Taurinensem, Ptol.Augusta Taurica, vulgò Turin, in Ducatu Pedemontano: quæ olim, cum Duces Allobrogum eam tenuerunt, erat florentissima.eius long.30.32. lat.43 40.
units.tr: The Turin academy, Ptolemy's Augusta Taurinorum, commonly called Turin, in the Duchy of Piedmont. Once, when the Dukes of the Allobroges held it, it was most flourishing. Its longitude 30.32, latitude 43.40.

units.la: LVSITANIAE.
units.tr: PORTUGAL.

units.la: Conimbriensem, seu Colimbriensem, vulgò Coymbre; propè littus Oceani Occidentalis. Hanc autem fundauit Iohannes 111. Rex Portugalliæ. xv. & Catharina eius uxor, soror Caroli.v. circiter annum 712. eius long. 11. 48 lat.40.3.
units.tr: The Coimbra academy, or Colimbria, commonly called Coimbra, near the shore of the Western Ocean. It was founded by John III, king of Portugal, and by Catherine his wife, sister of Charles V, around the year 712. Its longitude 11.48, latitude 40.3.

units.la: POLONIAE.
units.tr: POLAND.

units.la: Cracoviensem, seu potiùs Graccoviensem à Graccho potiùs triviales, quàm academias numeranda. eius long. 35.18.lat.52.4.
units.tr: The Kraków academy, or rather Gracovia, named from Gracchus, is to be counted among the trivial schools rather than among the academies. Its longitude 35.18, latitude 52.4.

units.la: SCOTIAE.
units.tr: SCOTLAND.

units.la: Aberdoniensem, Aberdein: portū habet ad littus maris Germanici optimum. hanc Alexander Rex, cum sorore Isabella, ab Anglia tum nuper reversa, multis ornavit privilegiis circiter annum 1240. eius long. 19.146.lat.64.15.
units.tr: Aberdeen University, Aberdein: it has an excellent harbour on the shore of the German Sea. Alexander the King, together with his sister Isabella, who had then recently returned from England, adorned it with many privileges around the year 1240. Its longitude 19.146, latitude 64.15.

units.la: Glasquensem, Glasquo, institutam à Turnbullo, Glasquensi Episcopo, anno 1454. eius long. 16.43.lat.59.40.
units.tr: Glasgow University, Glasquo, founded by Turnbull, Bishop of Glasgow, in the year 1454. Its longitude 16.43, latitude 59.40.

units.la: S. Andreæ, S. Adrewes, quæ sub Iacobo Rege, in Anglia profugo, inaugurata est, anno 1411. eius long. 18.29. lat. 61.3.
units.tr: St Andrews, S. Adrewes, which was opened under King James, while he was in exile in England, in the year 1411. Its longitude 18.29, latitude 61.3.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: THE END.
